items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
Use this section after understanding the clinical material. Each trial is linked; the result, endpoint and important limitation are given so a neutral primary outcome is not mistaken for equivalence.

| **Study (linked)** | **Population/intervention** | **Main result and implication** |
|---|---|---|
| [ARDSNet low VT, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200005043421801) | 861 ALI/ARDS patients, 6 versus 12 mL/kg PBW strategy | Mortality 31.0% vs 39.8%; establishes protective VT. Cannot conclude PEEP or all other settings alone caused the difference. |
| [PROSEVA, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214103) | Early prolonged proning in severe ARDS | Marked mortality reduction in protocolised severe ARDS; effect not transferable to brief or casual proning. |
| [EOLIA, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800385) | Early VV-ECMO vs conventional rescue in very severe ARDS | 60-day mortality 35% vs 46%, P=.09; 28% control crossover. Primary endpoint not statistically significant; supports expert referral alongside broader evidence. |
| [CESAR, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736%2809%2961069-2) | ECMO-centre referral vs conventional management | Better survival without severe disability in referral arm; measures specialist-centre strategy, not isolated efficacy of cannulation. |
| [FACTT, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa062200) | Conservative vs liberal fluid after initial ARDS resuscitation | More ventilator-free/ICU-free days with conservative fluid; avoid applying during uncontrolled shock. |
| [ACURASYS, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1005372) | 48-h cisatracurium in early severe ARDS with deep sedation | Suggested benefit after adjusted analysis; era-specific sedation and comparator matter. |
| [ROSE, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1901686) | Routine NMBA/deep sedation vs usual care with lighter sedation | No significant 90-day mortality benefit; do not paralyse all severe ARDS patients routinely. |
| [OSCILLATE, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1215554) | High-frequency oscillation in early ARDS | Higher mortality with early HFOV strategy; do not use routinely. |
| [ART, 2017](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.14171) | Aggressive recruitment/PEEP titration vs conventional low PEEP | Increased mortality/barotrauma in intervention group; argues against prolonged high-pressure recruitment manoeuvres. |
| [FLORALI, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1503326) | HFNC vs standard O₂ vs facemask NIV in nonhypercapnic hypoxaemia | Primary day-28 intubation 38% vs 47% vs 50%, P=.18; secondary 90-day mortality favoured HFNC. Do not claim proven primary intubation benefit from this trial alone. |
| [3CPO, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0707992) | CPAP/NIV versus oxygen in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema | Faster physiological/symptom improvement, no significant seven-day mortality advantage; useful mechanism and tolerance data. |
| [HOT-ICU, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2032510) | Lower vs higher PaO₂ target in acutely hypoxaemic ICU adults | No statistically significant difference in 90-day death; a single oxygen target does not suit all phenotypes. |
| [LOCO₂, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1916431) | Conservative vs liberal oxygen in ARDS | Stopped early for safety concerns; avoid extreme oxygen restriction in severely hypoxaemic patients. |
| [REDUCE, 2013](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2013.5023) | 5 vs 14 days prednisone in AECOPD | Five days noninferior for re-exacerbation in trial population, with less steroid exposure; supports contemporary short course. |
| [PEITHO, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1302097) | Tenecteplase vs placebo in intermediate-risk PE | Fewer haemodynamic collapses but more major bleeding/stroke; no routine lysis in stable intermediate-risk PE. |
| [PREPIC2, 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.3780) | Retrievable IVC filter plus anticoagulation vs anticoagulation alone | Did not reduce recurrent symptomatic PE in selected patients; filters are not routine with adequate anticoagulation. |
| [RECOVERY respiratory support / NIV trials — review](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajrccm/aamag302) | Modern synthesis across NIV, CPAP and HFNC | ATS 2026 guideline integrates multiple trials; not itself a single trial. For hypercapnia, NIV has strongest direct outcome evidence. |
| [SBT strategy evidence — AARC 2024 review](https://doi.org/10.4187/respcare.11735) | Guideline synthesis of adult weaning trials | RSBI not necessary for SBT readiness; low PSV or no PSV acceptable. This is a guideline, listed here for its direct exam utility. |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## BJA Education: targeted reading (primary learning texts)

- **1.** [Morris T, Young A, Thomas C. Causes and management of impaired gas exchange in critically ill patients (BJA Education 2025;25:90–98)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.11.001). **Read for:** physiology linking V/Q, shunt, CO₂ elimination and bedside respiratory support. Best complement to Chapters 1, 3 and 4.
- **2.** [Offer J, Sampson C, Charlton M. Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe acute respiratory failure (BJA Education 2024;24:138–144)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001). **Read for:** VV-ECMO circuit, sweep/blood-flow determinants, indications, troubleshooting and complications (Chapter 5).
- **3.** [Jayasimhan D, Matthay MA. Corticosteroids in adults with acute respiratory distress syndrome and severe pneumonia (BJA Education 2023;23:456–463)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.08.005). **Read for:** inflammatory injury and why steroid timing/population matter; read alongside 2024 ATS ARDS update.
- **4.** [Jayasimhan D, Young PJ. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (BJA Education 2025;25:391–399)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.07.002). **Read for:** ventilator biofilm, diagnostic uncertainty, prevention bundles and antimicrobial stewardship (Chapter 8).
- **5.** [Airway management in critically ill patients (BJA Education 2025;25:375–381)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.05.003). **Read for:** physiologically difficult intubation, preoxygenation and haemodynamic management (Chapters 2–3).
- **6.** [Pippalapalli J, Lumb AB. The respiratory system and acid–base disorders (BJA Education 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.002). **Read for:** ABG physiology, compensation and hypercapnic failure (Chapter 1).
- **7.** [Acute respiratory distress syndrome (BJA Education 2017;17:161–165)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2058534917300501). **Read for:** classical ARDS teaching, supplemented by 2024 Global definition and ATS guideline; **some older statements on corticosteroids have been superseded**.
- **8.** [Lyons C, Badiger S. Jet ventilation (BJA Education 2025;25:131–138)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.11.004). **Supplementary**, for ventilation failure and shared-airway specialist contexts; the full jet-ventilation LO belongs elsewhere.

## ANZCA Blue Book and examination material

- [Kim JCH, Lau LSY. B-lines and beyond: Lung ultrasound for the perioperative clinician — Australasian Anaesthesia 2025](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1378). Directly relevant to differentiating pneumothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia and oedema; read the examination protocol and limitations, rather than memorising B-lines in isolation.
- [ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia 2025 — complete volume](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1305). College reference resource; the lung ultrasound chapter above is the most directly relevant verified chapter for Set 3.

2026.1 Final Examination report (provided in this project): COPD medical viva required severity, exacerbation history, malnutrition/frailty, RHF signs, interpretation of investigations and optimisation. Anaesthesia viva explicitly examined recognition of hypoxia and a blocked/displaced tracheostomy. These are incorporated as practical standards in Chapters 2, 6 and 9.

2023.1 and 2022.2 ANZCA final reports (project): reinforce the need to interpret gas exchange, clinical risk and ICU management rather than offer isolated treatment lists.

## Current specialist recommendations

- [2026 ATS: Noninvasive respiratory support in acute respiratory failure](https://doi.org/10.1093/ajrccm/aamag302) — the current distinctions between HFNC, NIV, CPAP, preoxygenation and high-risk postextubation support.
- [2024 ATS: Update on ARDS management](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.202311-2011ST) — protective ventilation, PEEP, proning, NMBA, corticosteroids and selected ECMO.
- [2024 Global ARDS definition](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.202303-0558WS) — HFNC inclusion, S/F and lung ultrasound.
- [2026 GINA Strategy Report](https://ginasthma.org/2026-gina-strategy-report/) — current asthma prevention and acute-exacerbation management.
- [GOLD 2026 Report / guideline overview](https://www.guidelinecentral.com/guideline/2231686/) and [NZ COPD Quick Reference](https://nzmj.org.nz/journal/vol-134-no-1530/new-zealand-copd-guidelines-quick-reference-guide) — COPD pharmacology, short steroids, controlled oxygen, NIV and risk reduction.
- [2026 AHA/ACC multisociety acute PE guideline](https://professional.heart.org/en/science-news/2026-guideline-for-the-evaluation-and-management-of-acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults) — new A–E categories, thrombosis decisions and reperfusion.
- [2024 AARC Spontaneous Breathing Trial Guideline](https://doi.org/10.4187/respcare.11735) — readiness screening, SBT approach and RSBI limitations.
- [National Tracheostomy Safety Project algorithms](https://tracheostomy.org.uk/healthcare-staff/emergency-care) — tracheostomy versus laryngectomy emergencies.
- [ANZCOR resuscitation guidance](https://www.anzcor.org/home/) — respiratory arrest and advanced life support, use current local algorithms.

### Additional reference standards used in the expanded chapters

- [ERS/ATS 2022: Pulmonary function test interpretative standard](https://doi.org/10.1183/13993003.01499-2021) — Flow–volume loops, LLN, TLC, bronchodilator response and DLCO.
- [ASA: Practice guideline for perioperative OSA](https://www.asahq.org/≈/media/sites/asahq/files/public/resources/standards-guidelines/practice-guidelines-for-the-perioperative-management-of-patients-with-obstructive-sleep-apnea.pdf) — OSA assessment, airway strategy, extubation and recovery; older guideline, interpret with current practice.
- [ATS/IDSA: HAP/VAP management guideline](https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/hap_vap/) — Respiratory sampling, antimicrobial spectrum, de-escalation and duration.
- [AARC 2024: Spontaneous breathing trial guideline](https://doi.org/10.4187/respcare.11735) — Readiness, low-pressure-support SBTs and limitations of RSBI.
- [2026 AHA/ACC: Acute PE guideline](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.005) — A–E PE severity, risk and advanced reperfusion decisions.
- [2024 ATS: ARDS management update](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.202311-2011ST) — VT, Pplat, PEEP, prone, corticosteroids, NMBA and VV-ECMO.

items.title: What is your immediate response to a sudden fall in SpO2 under anaesthesia?
items.q: What is your immediate response to a sudden fall in SpO2 under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Tell the team, give 100% oxygen and hand-ventilate.
- Check the probe, circuit, tube position and ETCO2.
- Auscultate and look for bronchospasm or pneumothorax.
- Use bronchoscopy, ultrasound and a gas if unresolved.

> **Closing point:** Oxygenate first, then search systematically.

items.title: What are the causes of intraoperative hypoxaemia by site?
items.q: What are the causes of intraoperative hypoxaemia by site?
items.a:
- Equipment: oxygen supply, circuit and ventilator.
- Airway: tube displacement, obstruction, laryngospasm.
- Lung: bronchospasm, pneumothorax, atelectasis, aspiration, embolism.
- Circulation and metabolism: low output, anaphylaxis, methaemoglobin.

> **Closing point:** Work from gas supply to the tissues.

items.title: How do you check for endobronchial intubation?
items.q: How do you check for endobronchial intubation?
items.a:
- Unilateral breath sounds and chest movement.
- Rising airway pressure and falling SpO2.
- Fibreoptic view of the carina.
- Withdraw the tube and recheck.

> **Closing point:** Bronchoscopy confirms it.

items.title: What mechanisms cause hypoxaemia in general anaesthesia?
items.q: What mechanisms cause hypoxaemia in general anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Atelectasis and shunt.
- V/Q mismatch.
- Hypoventilation.
- Reduced cardiac output and mixed venous saturation.

> **Closing point:** Atelectasis is the most common.

items.title: How does a high peak pressure with a normal plateau differ from both being high?
items.q: How does a high peak pressure with a normal plateau differ from both being high?
items.a:
- High peak only: raised airway resistance.
- Both raised: reduced compliance.
- Resistance causes: tube, bronchospasm, secretions.
- Compliance causes: pneumothorax, abdomen, oedema.

> **Closing point:** Peak versus plateau separates the diagnosis.

items.title: What are the causes of a sudden rise in airway pressure?
items.q: What are the causes of a sudden rise in airway pressure?
items.a:
- Tube kinking, biting or herniated cuff.
- Bronchospasm or anaphylaxis.
- Tension pneumothorax or endobronchial tube.
- Surgical pneumoperitoneum, packs or light anaesthesia.

> **Closing point:** Hand-ventilate to find out.

items.title: How do you treat intraoperative bronchospasm?
items.q: How do you treat intraoperative bronchospasm?
items.a:
- 100% oxygen and deepen anaesthesia.
- Salbutamol via the circuit.
- Adrenaline if severe or anaphylaxis.
- Magnesium and ketamine for refractory cases.

> **Closing point:** Remove the trigger and dilate.

items.title: What are the causes of a rising end-tidal CO2?
items.q: What are the causes of a rising end-tidal CO2?
items.a:
- Increased production: malignant hyperthermia, sepsis, laparoscopy, tourniquet release.
- Reduced elimination: hypoventilation, dead space.
- Rebreathing: exhausted soda lime, faulty valve.
- Equipment faults.

> **Closing point:** Production, elimination, rebreathing.

items.title: How do you recognise malignant hyperthermia early?
items.q: How do you recognise malignant hyperthermia early?
items.a:
- Rising ETCO2 despite ventilation.
- Tachycardia and masseter rigidity.
- Temperature rise is a late sign.
- Stop triggers, give dantrolene.

> **Closing point:** ETCO2 rise is the early clue.

items.title: What are the effects of hypercapnia?
items.q: What are the effects of hypercapnia?
items.a:
- Respiratory acidosis and right shift of the curve.
- Sympathetic stimulation then depression.
- Cerebral vasodilatation and raised ICP.
- Pulmonary vasoconstriction.

> **Closing point:** Brain, heart and lung effects.

items.title: What are the causes of a low or absent end-tidal CO2?
items.q: What are the causes of a low or absent end-tidal CO2?
items.a:
- Disconnection or oesophageal intubation.
- Cardiac arrest or severe low output.
- Pulmonary embolism, including air.
- Iatrogenic hyperventilation.

> **Closing point:** Fall in ETCO2 means ventilation or perfusion failure.

items.title: What are the effects of hypocapnia?
items.q: What are the effects of hypocapnia?
items.a:
- Cerebral vasoconstriction.
- Left shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve.
- Reduced ionised calcium.
- Reduced cardiac output.

> **Closing point:** Cerebral ischaemia risk.

items.title: What is the role of PEEP and recruitment under anaesthesia?
items.q: What is the role of PEEP and recruitment under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Reduces atelectasis and improves oxygenation.
- Use 5 to 10 cmH2O.
- Recruitment can lower blood pressure.
- Use lower FiO2 to limit absorption atelectasis.

> **Closing point:** Balance recruitment against haemodynamics.

items.title: What is lung-protective ventilation under anaesthesia?
items.q: What is lung-protective ventilation under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Tidal volume 6 to 8 mL/kg ideal body weight.
- PEEP 5 to 10 cmH2O.
- Limit driving pressure.
- Avoid high FiO2.

> **Closing point:** Small tidal volumes with PEEP.

items.title: How do you define type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure?
items.q: How do you define type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure?
items.a:
- Type 1: PaO2 below 8 kPa with normal or low CO2.
- Type 2: PaCO2 above 6.5 kPa.
- Acute or chronic compensated.
- Check the bicarbonate and pH.

> **Closing point:** Hypoxaemic versus hypercapnic.

items.title: What are the mechanisms of hypoxaemia?
items.q: What are the mechanisms of hypoxaemia?
items.a:
- V/Q mismatch.
- Shunt.
- Diffusion impairment.
- Hypoventilation and low inspired oxygen.

> **Closing point:** Shunt does not correct with oxygen.

items.title: How does the A-a gradient help?
items.q: How does the A-a gradient help?
items.a:
- PAO2 = PiO2 minus PaCO2/R.
- Normal in hypoventilation.
- Raised in V/Q mismatch and shunt.
- Rises with age.

> **Closing point:** Separates lung from ventilatory causes.

items.title: What are the causes of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
items.q: What are the causes of hypercapnic respiratory failure?
items.a:
- Central depression from drugs or brainstem lesion.
- Neuromuscular weakness.
- Chest wall disease and obesity.
- COPD and increased dead space.

> **Closing point:** Hypoventilation or dead space.

items.title: What oxygen target do you use in COPD?
items.q: What oxygen target do you use in COPD?
items.a:
- SpO2 88 to 92%.
- Avoid excess oxygen.
- Mechanisms: V/Q worsening and Haldane effect.
- Check gases after changes.

> **Closing point:** Titrate, do not abolish drive.

items.title: When do you intubate in respiratory failure?
items.q: When do you intubate in respiratory failure?
items.a:
- Worsening acidosis or exhaustion.
- Reduced conscious level.
- Failure of NIV.
- Airway protection needs.

> **Closing point:** Do not wait for arrest.

items.title: What are the advantages of high-flow nasal oxygen?
items.q: What are the advantages of high-flow nasal oxygen?
items.a:
- Provides heated humidified flow.
- Delivers FiO2 reliably.
- Generates a small PEEP and dead space washout.
- Reduces intubation versus standard oxygen in some trials.

> **Closing point:** Comfort plus modest support.

items.title: How do you interpret an arterial gas in chronic hypercapnia?
items.q: How do you interpret an arterial gas in chronic hypercapnia?
items.a:
- Raised bicarbonate.
- Near-normal pH.
- A new CO2 rise and acidaemia suggest deterioration; exclude a mixed metabolic disorder.
- Compare with baseline.

> **Closing point:** Compare pH, bicarbonate, CO2 and baseline together.

items.title: What is the difference between volume and pressure control?
items.q: What is the difference between volume and pressure control?
items.a:
- Volume: set volume, pressure varies.
- Pressure: set pressure, volume varies.
- Pressure control limits peak pressure.
- Monitor tidal volume in pressure control.

> **Closing point:** One variable fixed, the other varies.

items.title: What is pressure support ventilation?
items.q: What is pressure support ventilation?
items.a:
- Patient-triggered breaths.
- Set inspiratory pressure.
- Tidal volume depends on effort and compliance.
- Comfortable and used in weaning.

> **Closing point:** Needs spontaneous effort.

items.title: What are the criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial?
items.q: What are the criteria for a spontaneous breathing trial?
items.a:
- Cause improving; oxygenation adequate.
- Haemodynamically stable with adequate drive.
- Minimal sedation.
- Low PEEP and FiO2.

> **Closing point:** Assess readiness daily.

items.title: What is the rapid shallow breathing index?
items.q: What is the rapid shallow breathing index?
items.a:
- Respiratory rate divided by tidal volume in litres.
- Below 105 is a historical predictive threshold with limited standalone accuracy.
- Measure at 1 minute.
- Not required to determine SBT readiness (AARC 2024).

> **Closing point:** Rate over volume.

items.title: Why can weaning fail?
items.q: Why can weaning fail?
items.a:
- Respiratory muscle weakness.
- Cardiac dysfunction.
- Sepsis, delirium or secretions.
- Excess sedation or metabolic problems.

> **Closing point:** Look for a reversible cause.

items.title: What is auto-PEEP and how do you manage it?
items.q: What is auto-PEEP and how do you manage it?
items.a:
- Incomplete expiration before the next breath.
- Causes include obstruction and high rate.
- Lower rate and tidal volume; lengthen expiratory time.
- Disconnect briefly in an emergency.

> **Closing point:** Give time to exhale.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic effects of positive pressure ventilation?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic effects of positive pressure ventilation?
items.a:
- Reduced venous return.
- Raised pulmonary vascular resistance.
- Reduced LV afterload.
- Worse with hypovolaemia.

> **Closing point:** Preload falls.

items.title: What are the complications of mechanical ventilation?
items.q: What are the complications of mechanical ventilation?
items.a:
- Barotrauma and volutrauma.
- Ventilator-associated pneumonia.
- Haemodynamic compromise.
- Muscle weakness and delirium.

> **Closing point:** Ventilate gently.

items.title: How do you prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
items.q: How do you prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
items.a:
- Head-up position.
- Daily sedation interruption.
- Oral hygiene and subglottic suction.
- Minimise ventilation days.

> **Closing point:** Bundle of care.

items.title: What are the ventilation targets in neurological injury?
items.q: What are the ventilation targets in neurological injury?
items.a:
- Normocapnia unless herniating.
- Avoid hypoxia.
- Short-term hyperventilation as a bridge.
- Check plateau pressure.

> **Closing point:** Protect the brain.

items.title: What is the Berlin definition of ARDS?
items.q: What is the Berlin definition of ARDS?
items.a:
- Onset within 1 week.
- Bilateral opacities.
- Not explained by cardiac failure.
- PaO2/FiO2 300 or less with PEEP 5.

> **Closing point:** Severity by P/F ratio.

items.title: What are the causes of ARDS?
items.q: What are the causes of ARDS?
items.a:
- Direct: pneumonia, aspiration, contusion.
- Indirect: sepsis, trauma, pancreatitis.
- Transfusion and burns.
- Cardiopulmonary bypass.

> **Closing point:** Direct lung injury or systemic.

items.title: What ventilation strategy is used in ARDS?
items.q: What ventilation strategy is used in ARDS?
items.a:
- Tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted weight.
- Plateau below 30 cmH2O.
- Driving pressure below 15.
- Permissive hypercapnia and PEEP titration.

> **Closing point:** ARDSNet is the foundation.

items.title: What is the evidence for prone positioning?
items.q: What is the evidence for prone positioning?
items.a:
- PROSEVA: P/F below 150.
- Generally at least 16 hours per prone session when indicated.
- Mortality about 16% versus 33%.
- Improves V/Q matching.

> **Closing point:** Early and prolonged.

items.title: What is the evidence for neuromuscular blockade in ARDS?
items.q: What is the evidence for neuromuscular blockade in ARDS?
items.a:
- ACURASYS: benefit in severe ARDS.
- ROSE: no mortality benefit.
- Use for dyssynchrony.
- Risk of weakness.

> **Closing point:** Selective use.

items.title: Which adjuncts have not improved mortality in ARDS?
items.q: Which adjuncts have not improved mortality in ARDS?
items.a:
- High-frequency oscillation.
- Inhaled nitric oxide.
- Routine surfactant.
- Statins.

> **Closing point:** Improved oxygenation is not benefit.

items.title: What are the indications for ECMO in respiratory failure?
items.q: What are the indications for ECMO in respiratory failure?
items.a:
- Severe potentially reversible failure.
- P/F below 80 despite optimal care.
- Uncompensated hypercapnia.
- Bridge to transplant.

> **Closing point:** EOLIA criteria.

items.title: What is the difference between VV and VA ECMO?
items.q: What is the difference between VV and VA ECMO?
items.a:
- VV: gas exchange only.
- VA: circulatory and respiratory support.
- VA risks limb ischaemia.
- Harlequin syndrome in peripheral VA.

> **Closing point:** VV supports lungs, VA lungs and heart.

items.title: What factors define severe COPD preoperatively?
items.q: What factors define severe COPD preoperatively?
items.a:
- FEV1 below 50%.
- Home oxygen or hypercapnia.
- Frequent exacerbations.
- Cor pulmonale and poor exercise capacity.

> **Closing point:** Function, gas exchange and exacerbations.

items.title: How do you optimise a COPD patient before surgery?
items.q: How do you optimise a COPD patient before surgery?
items.a:
- Stop smoking.
- Treat infection.
- Optimise bronchodilators and steroids.
- Pulmonary rehabilitation and physiotherapy.

> **Closing point:** Delay elective surgery for an exacerbation.

items.title: How do you ventilate a patient with COPD?
items.q: How do you ventilate a patient with COPD?
items.a:
- Low respiratory rate.
- Prolonged expiratory time.
- Avoid auto-PEEP.
- Accept mild hypercapnia.

> **Closing point:** Time to exhale.

items.title: What are the features of acute severe asthma?
items.q: What are the features of acute severe asthma?
items.a:
- Unable to complete sentences.
- Heart rate above 110.
- Peak flow 33 to 50%.
- Silent chest is life-threatening.

> **Closing point:** Recognise the severity.

items.title: Why avoid nitrous oxide in COPD?
items.q: Why avoid nitrous oxide in COPD?
items.a:
- Bullae can expand.
- Risk of pneumothorax.
- Reduces oxygen fraction.
- Use air and oxygen.

> **Closing point:** Air spaces expand.

items.title: What is the role of preoperative spirometry?
items.q: What is the role of preoperative spirometry?
items.a:
- Not routine for general surgery.
- Assess severity of disease.
- Lung resection planning.
- Compare with baseline.

> **Closing point:** Use for known disease and resection.

items.title: How do you manage severe asthma in ICU?
items.q: How do you manage severe asthma in ICU?
items.a:
- Oxygen and continuous salbutamol.
- Ipratropium, steroids and magnesium.
- Ketamine or volatile agents.
- Careful intubation and permissive hypercapnia.

> **Closing point:** Bronchodilate and avoid hyperinflation.

items.title: How do you intubate a patient with severe asthma?
items.q: How do you intubate a patient with severe asthma?
items.a:
- Use an experienced operator.
- Ketamine induction and a large tube.
- Pre-oxygenate and use a low rate.
- Monitor for hypotension and auto-PEEP.

> **Closing point:** Prepare for collapse.

items.title: What are the triggers of perioperative bronchospasm?
items.q: What are the triggers of perioperative bronchospasm?
items.a:
- Airway instrumentation.
- Light anaesthesia.
- Drugs including beta-blockers and some muscle relaxants.
- Anaphylaxis and aspiration.

> **Closing point:** Anticipate and remove.

items.title: How do you recognise a tension pneumothorax?
items.q: How do you recognise a tension pneumothorax?
items.a:
- Rising airway pressure and falling SpO2.
- Hypotension and tachycardia.
- Absent breath sounds on one side.
- Late tracheal deviation.

- Do not wait for late tracheal deviation or imaging when tension physiology is suspected.

> **Closing point:** Clinical diagnosis.

items.title: How do you decompress a tension pneumothorax?
items.q: How do you decompress a tension pneumothorax?
items.a:
- Finger thoracostomy in the 4th/5th space.
- Or large-bore needle in the 2nd space.
- Insert a chest drain.
- Reassess and obtain an X-ray.

- Use the fastest appropriate technique and expertise, reassess effectiveness and provide definitive pleural drainage.

> **Closing point:** Treat before imaging.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic considerations for a known pneumothorax?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for a known pneumothorax?
items.a:
- Insert a drain before positive pressure.
- Avoid nitrous oxide.
- Keep the drain below the chest.
- Monitor airway pressures.

- Individualise small stable cases; avoid clamping an active air leak or prescribing suction automatically.

> **Closing point:** Positive pressure converts to tension.

items.title: How do you manage aspiration at induction?
items.q: How do you manage aspiration at induction?
items.a:
- Head-down and suction.
- Secure the airway.
- Bronchoscopy if particulate.
- No routine steroids or antibiotics.

> **Closing point:** Clear gross contamination promptly, but never delay life-saving oxygenation.

items.title: What are the features of Mendelson syndrome?
items.q: What are the features of Mendelson syndrome?
items.a:
- Chemical pneumonitis.
- Acidic aspirate can cause chemical injury; severity also depends on composition and host response.
- Historical experimental volume thresholds are not bedside diagnostic cutoffs.
- Hypoxia and bronchospasm.

> **Closing point:** Acid injury to the lung.

items.title: What causes negative pressure pulmonary oedema?
items.q: What causes negative pressure pulmonary oedema?
items.a:
- Forced inspiration against obstruction.
- Often laryngospasm.
- Fit young men.
- Treat with relief of obstruction and CPAP.

- Diuretics are selective for overload; reassess cardiac, aspiration and retained-pack alternatives.

> **Closing point:** Resolves quickly.

items.title: How do you manage laryngospasm?
items.q: How do you manage laryngospasm?
items.a:
- 100% oxygen and CPAP.
- Jaw thrust.
- Deepen with propofol.
- Suxamethonium if persistent.

- Remove the stimulus, suction safely and escalate promptly if oxygenation or ventilation is failing.

> **Closing point:** Escalate quickly.

items.title: How do you stratify severity in pulmonary embolism?
items.q: How do you stratify severity in pulmonary embolism?
items.a:
- High risk: shock.
- Intermediate: RV dysfunction or troponin.
- Low risk: neither.
- Use sPESI and echo.

- Add clinical severity and respiratory status; RV strain alone does not mandate thrombolysis.

> **Closing point:** Haemodynamics and RV strain.

items.title: What are the gas exchange effects of pulmonary embolism?
items.q: What are the gas exchange effects of pulmonary embolism?
items.a:
- Increased dead space.
- Raised arterial-end-tidal gradient.
- V/Q mismatch and hypoxaemia.
- Shunt via PFO.

- PaCO2 may be normal or low from compensation; a low ETCO2 can conceal a widened gradient.

> **Closing point:** Dead space dominates.

items.title: What is the treatment of severe community-acquired pneumonia?
items.q: What is the treatment of severe community-acquired pneumonia?
items.a:
- Early beta-lactam plus macrolide.
- Cover Legionella and influenza.
- Hydrocortisone in severe cases.
- Respiratory support and shock management.

- Steroid guidance is conditional and excludes severe influenza; antibiotics and organ support remain essential.

> **Closing point:** Treat quickly and support.

items.title: How do you use severity scores for pneumonia?
items.q: How do you use severity scores for pneumonia?
items.a:
- CURB-65 for severity.
- IDSA/ATS for ICU admission.
- Look for sepsis.
- Guides disposition.

- A score supports judgement but must not delay ICU escalation for unstable physiology.

> **Closing point:** Score then escalate.

items.title: What is your approach to intraoperative cardiac arrest?
items.q: What is your approach to intraoperative cardiac arrest?
items.a:
- Stop surgery, call for help, start CPR.
- Defibrillate shockable rhythms.
- Give adrenaline per ALS.
- Search for reversible causes.

> **Closing point:** Treat the arrest and the cause.

items.title: What are the reversible causes of arrest under anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the reversible causes of arrest under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Hypoxia and hypovolaemia.
- Tension pneumothorax and tamponade.
- Anaphylaxis and local anaesthetic toxicity.
- Gas embolism, PE and malignant hyperthermia.

> **Closing point:** 4 Hs and 4 Ts, adapted to theatre.

items.title: What is the role of capnography in CPR?
items.q: What is the role of capnography in CPR?
items.a:
- Confirms tube position.
- Reflects compression quality.
- ETCO2 trends help assess pulmonary blood flow and CPR; no single threshold determines success or termination.
- Sudden rise suggests return of circulation.

> **Closing point:** Quality and ROSC marker.

items.title: How do you manage local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
items.q: How do you manage local anaesthetic systemic toxicity?
items.a:
- Stop injection and call for help.
- Intralipid 20% bolus then infusion.
- Reduce adrenaline doses.
- Prolonged resuscitation.

> **Closing point:** Lipid early.

items.title: What post-resuscitation care follows cardiac arrest?
items.q: What post-resuscitation care follows cardiac arrest?
items.a:
- Oxygenation 94 to 98% and normocapnia.
- MAP above 65.
- Temperature control.
- ECG, PCI and ICU.

> **Closing point:** Protect the brain and heart.

items.title: What are the causes of collapse after induction?
items.q: What are the causes of collapse after induction?
items.a:
- Anaphylaxis.
- Hypovolaemia and drug effects.
- Tension pneumothorax.
- Arrhythmia, embolism or cardiac tamponade.

> **Closing point:** Consider the common first.

items.title: What are the indications for NIV in COPD?
items.q: What are the indications for NIV in COPD?
items.a:
- Persistent hypercapnic acidosis, pH below 7.35; lower pH increases failure risk and monitoring needs.
- PaCO2 above 6.5 kPa.
- Persisting after medical therapy.
- Respiratory rate above 23.

> **Closing point:** Acidotic hypercapnia.

items.title: What are the contraindications to NIV?
items.q: What are the contraindications to NIV?
items.a:
- Respiratory arrest.
- Reduced consciousness or uncooperative.
- Facial trauma or vomiting.
- Undrained pneumothorax.

- A contraindication assessment is contextual; an unsafe airway or immediate intubation need overrides a mask trial.

> **Closing point:** Unprotected airway or instability.

items.title: How do you set up NIV for COPD?
items.q: How do you set up NIV for COPD?
items.a:
- IPAP 10 to 15, EPAP 4 to 5.
- Titrate to comfort and gases.
- Oxygen to 88 to 92%.
- Check gases at 1 to 2 hours.

- Reassess early and escalate immediately for deterioration rather than waiting for a fixed repeat-gas time.

> **Closing point:** Early gas check decides.

items.title: What are the indications and timing of tracheostomy?
items.q: What are the indications and timing of tracheostomy?
items.a:
- Prolonged ventilation.
- Airway protection.
- Failure to wean.
- Early versus late shows no mortality difference.

> **Closing point:** Individualise timing.

items.title: What are the complications of percutaneous tracheostomy?
items.q: What are the complications of percutaneous tracheostomy?
items.a:
- Bleeding and loss of airway.
- Posterior wall injury.
- Pneumothorax.
- Late stenosis and fistula.

> **Closing point:** Guidance reduces risk.

items.title: What are the features of restrictive lung disease?
items.q: What are the features of restrictive lung disease?
items.a:
- Reduced lung volumes with normal ratio.
- Reduced compliance.
- DLCO reduced in parenchymal disease.
- Risk of hypoxia and pulmonary hypertension.

> **Closing point:** Small, stiff lungs.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues in pulmonary fibrosis?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues in pulmonary fibrosis?
items.a:
- Poor oxygen reserve and low compliance.
- Pulmonary hypertension.
- Risk of barotrauma and acute exacerbation.
- Titrate oxygen and ventilation; ask separately about prior pneumotoxic treatment such as bleomycin.

> **Closing point:** Little reserve, high risk.

items.title: When do you initiate chronic NIV in neuromuscular disease?
items.q: When do you initiate chronic NIV in neuromuscular disease?
items.a:
- Use symptoms and trajectory, sleep-related hypoventilation, muscle tests and awake CO2 rather than waiting for one FVC threshold.
- Assess sitting/supine FVC, inspiratory strength, cough and overnight CO2/oximetry.
- Plan a tailored NIV/backup-rate trial with respiratory-team follow-up.
- Pair it with cough/aspiration support and shared decisions about escalation.

items.title: What matters before choosing long-term invasive ventilation?
items.q: What matters before choosing long-term invasive ventilation?
items.a:
- Discuss prognosis, quality of life, goals and the option of symptom-focused care.
- Assess bulbar function, secretion burden, NIV tolerance and caregiver capacity.
- Plan communication, nutrition, home equipment, backup power and emergency support.
- Record advance preferences and review them as disease changes.

items.title: How do you distinguish liberation from extubation readiness?
items.q: How do you distinguish liberation from extubation readiness?
items.a:
- Liberation means breathing without ventilator assistance; extubation also needs a safe airway.
- After an SBT, assess cough, secretions, consciousness and upper-airway risk.
- Use a cuff-leak test selectively, not in every patient.
- Plan prophylactic NIV/HFNC for appropriate high-risk patients and timely reintubation if failing.

items.title: What changed in the AARC 2024 SBT guidance?
items.q: What changed in the AARC 2024 SBT guidance?
items.a:
- RSBI is not required before an SBT.
- An SBT may use low pressure support or no pressure support.
- Assess readiness systematically each day.
- Do not increase FiO2 solely to make the SBT pass.

items.title: A fresh tracheostomy stops ventilating: what are your first actions?
items.q: A fresh tracheostomy stops ventilating: what are your first actions?
items.a:
- Call airway/ENT help and give oxygen to face and stoma.
- Remove valve/cap and inner cannula; assess with capnography and a suction catheter.
- Deflate the cuff and remove a non-functioning tube if necessary; do not force ventilation through a false passage.
- Use available oral/stoma oxygenation routes and expert endoscopic replacement; avoid blind reinsertion in a fresh tract.

items.title: What daily care prevents tracheostomy emergencies?
items.q: What daily care prevents tracheostomy emergencies?
items.a:
- Humidify and clear secretions; check inner cannula, cuff, ties and skin.
- Record type/size, upper-airway patency and emergency plan at the bed.
- Keep suction, appropriate spare tubes and rescue equipment immediately available.
- Plan swallowing, speech, first change, weaning and decannulation with the team.

items.title: Why can a low ETCO2 coexist with a raised PaCO2?
items.q: Why can a low ETCO2 coexist with a raised PaCO2?
items.a:
- Low pulmonary blood flow or increased dead space widens the arterial–end-tidal gradient.
- Consider PE, shock or severe lung disease.
- Check waveform, ventilation, circulation and an arterial gas.
- Treat the cause; do not reflexively increase ventilation for a low ETCO2.

items.title: How useful is VBG in respiratory failure?
items.q: How useful is VBG in respiratory failure?
items.a:
- Useful for acid–base screening/trends and selected CO2/lactate assessment.
- PvCO2 does not precisely substitute for PaCO2, especially in shock.
- PvO2 cannot assess arterial oxygenation.
- Use SpO2 plus ABG/co-oximetry when accurate oxygenation/ventilation is needed.

items.title: How do you recognise a restrictive PFT pattern?
items.q: How do you recognise a restrictive PFT pattern?
items.a:
- Restriction requires a low TLC; FVC is often low with a preserved/high FEV1/FVC.
- Low FVC alone may be obstruction with air trapping.
- Assess DLCO with haemoglobin, alveolar volume and clinical context.
- Distinguish parenchymal fibrosis from neuromuscular/chest-wall causes.

items.title: What ultrasound findings help assess pneumothorax?
items.q: What ultrasound findings help assess pneumothorax?
items.a:
- Absent sliding is suggestive but not specific.
- A lung point supports the diagnosis; sliding, B-lines or lung pulse exclude air at the scanned site.
- Scan multiple appropriate sites and interpret with tube position and clinical physiology.
- Do not delay decompression for imaging in tension physiology.

items.title: How do you treat a persistent air leak on a ventilator?
items.q: How do you treat a persistent air leak on a ventilator?
items.a:
- Check for drain obstruction, external leak and trapped lung.
- Maintain pleural drainage and reduce mean airway pressure as feasible.
- Use suction only when necessary, at the least effective level.
- Seek early thoracic/respiratory advice for isolation, valves, surgery or selected ECMO.

items.title: What are the main mechanisms of perioperative atelectasis?
items.q: What are the main mechanisms of perioperative atelectasis?
items.a:
- Reduced FRC and dependent compression/airway closure.
- Absorption after nitrogen washout or airway obstruction.
- Surfactant dysfunction and retained secretions.
- Pain, residual drugs/block and immobility maintain postoperative collapse.

items.title: Does high PEEP with recruitment prevent all pulmonary complications?
items.q: Does high PEEP with recruitment prevent all pulmonary complications?
items.a:
- No: effects on oxygenation do not guarantee clinical benefit.
- Excess PEEP/recruitment can overdistend lung and impair circulation.
- Titrate to mechanics, gas exchange and haemodynamics; use recruitment selectively.
- iPROVE was abdominal and neutral for its primary outcome; PROTHOR was thoracic OLV.

items.title: What is the current steroid position in ARDS and pneumonia?
items.q: What is the current steroid position in ARDS and pneumonia?
items.a:
- ATS 2024 conditionally supports steroids for ARDS.
- ATS 2025 conditionally supports severe adult CAP, excluding influenza pneumonia.
- Do not extrapolate to all non-severe CAP or VAP.
- Consider cause, timing, contraindications and the strength of evidence.

items.title: How do you investigate and start treatment for suspected VAP?
items.q: How do you investigate and start treatment for suspected VAP?
items.a:
- Combine new infiltrates, clinical infection and gas-exchange deterioration; consider mimics.
- Take appropriate respiratory/blood cultures without delaying urgent antibiotics.
- Choose empirical therapy by severity, resistance risk and local antibiogram.
- Reassess and de-escalate, with individual response-based duration.

items.title: What should you say about newer VAP-prevention trials?
items.q: What should you say about newer VAP-prevention trials?
items.a:
- VAP adjudication and colonisation can bias apparent prevention effects.
- A reduction in VAP incidence is not proof of survival benefit.
- SDD or prophylactic inhaled/systemic antibiotics need local multidisciplinary evaluation.
- Maintain liberation, hygiene, safe airway care and avoid routine chlorhexidine.

items.title: How do you manage intraoperative PE with shock?
items.q: How do you manage intraoperative PE with shock?
items.a:
- Call help, pause surgery, oxygenate and exclude competing emergencies.
- Use echo and haemodynamic/CO2 assessment; CT only if stable enough.
- Support RV perfusion without indiscriminate fluid loading.
- Urgently decide anticoagulation/reperfusion with the team and the operative bleeding risk.

items.title: What do the 2026 AHA/ACC PE categories add?
items.q: What do the 2026 AHA/ACC PE categories add?
items.a:
- A–E categorisation spans incidental/low-severity disease through cardiopulmonary failure.
- It recognises incipient failure before sustained hypotension.
- Use RV findings, biomarkers, respiratory and haemodynamic status together.
- Do not translate categories directly into automatic thrombolysis.

items.title: What determines oxygenation versus CO2 removal in VV-ECMO?
items.q: What determines oxygenation versus CO2 removal in VV-ECMO?
items.a:
- Oxygenation depends on effective blood flow relative to cardiac output, haemoglobin and native-lung function.
- Recirculation reduces effective flow.
- Sweep gas principally governs CO2 clearance.
- Check patient, cannula, circuit and oxygenator before changing settings blindly.

items.title: What does SOHO change about HFNC claims?
items.q: What does SOHO change about HFNC claims?
items.a:
- In selected acute hypoxaemic failure, 28-day mortality was unchanged.
- Intubation was lower as a secondary outcome.
- This does not establish a universal survival benefit.
- Monitor failure and do not substitute HFNC for ventilatory support in acidotic COPD.

items.title: When might bronchoscopic toileting follow aspiration?
items.q: When might bronchoscopic toileting follow aspiration?
items.a:
- After oxygenation/airway stabilisation, selected severe or particulate aspiration may justify expert bronchoscopy.
- The available Blue Book preview describes an emerging local protocol.
- Routine lavage for every aspiration is not established.
- Watch for ETT obstruction, auto-PEEP, hypoxaemia and instability; pause to reoxygenate.

items.title: What do you do in respiratory arrest with a pulse?
items.q: What do you do in respiratory arrest with a pulse?
items.a:
- Call help, open the airway and ventilate effectively with oxygen.
- Use airway adjuncts/two-person technique and capnography; secure the airway if needed.
- Treat the cause, including drugs, obstruction, weakness, bronchospasm or pneumothorax.
- Reassess circulation; begin CPR if cardiac arrest develops.

items.title: How do you recognise FES rather than simple fat embolisation?
items.q: How do you recognise FES rather than simple fat embolisation?
items.a:
- Look for delayed respiratory, neurological and petechial features after risk exposure.
- Fat emboli alone do not establish the clinical syndrome.
- Exclude thrombotic PE, sepsis, aspiration and traumatic brain injury.
- Support organs and coordinate fracture care; routine therapeutic heparin is not FES treatment.

items.title: What should prompt an alternative diagnosis to ICU-acquired weakness?
items.q: What should prompt an alternative diagnosis to ICU-acquired weakness?
items.a:
- Weakness predating ICU or disproportionate to illness.
- Focal/asymmetric findings, sensory level or prominent cranial involvement.
- Residual drugs or correctable electrolyte/metabolic disturbance.
- Investigate selectively with early neurology help; do not label every failed SBT as ICUAW.

items.title: Why can respiratory depression recur after naloxone?
items.q: Why can respiratory depression recur after naloxone?
items.a:
- Naloxone may wear off before the opioid.
- A potent/high-affinity exposure may require repeated treatment.
- Other co-administered depressants are not reversed.
- Continue monitoring and ventilatory support, with repeat dosing/infusion when indicated.

items.title: How do you interpret a saturation that does not fit the patient?
items.q: How do you interpret a saturation that does not fit the patient?
items.a:
- Treat plausible hypoxaemia while checking probe, waveform, perfusion and an alternative site.
- Consider skin-pigmentation bias, dyshemoglobins and dyes.
- Use arterial gas/co-oximetry when needed.
- Separate saturation from ventilation, Hb content and cardiac-output-dependent delivery.

items.title: How do you help a patient stop smoking before surgery?
items.q: How do you help a patient stop smoking before surgery?
items.a:
- Ask about use, dependence and previous attempts; give personalised non-judgemental advice.
- Combine behavioural support with suitable medication, often combination NRT or varenicline.
- Check contraindications/interactions and agree a quit plan with follow-up.
- Encourage cessation now; brief abstinence is not a reason to continue smoking.

items.title: What changes after smoking cessation, and how certain is the timing?
items.q: What changes after smoking cessation, and how certain is the timing?
items.a:
- COHb and nicotine-related cardiovascular effects improve early.
- Airway clearance, symptoms and wound/pulmonary risk improve over ensuing weeks.
- Lung-function and immune recovery vary; do not promise exact normalisation dates.
- Combustion-product CYP1A2 induction wanes, which can matter for theophylline or clozapine.

items.title: How does OSA alter your perioperative plan?
items.q: How does OSA alter your perioperative plan?
items.a:
- Assess severity, PAP adherence, hypoventilation and cardiopulmonary comorbidity.
- Plan airway management, minimise sedatives and use opioid-sparing analgesia.
- Confirm NMBA recovery and an appropriate awake head-up extubation/recovery plan.
- Resume PAP and decide monitoring/admission from disease, procedure and actual recovery events.

items.title: When is a patient with OSA suitable for day surgery?
items.q: When is a patient with OSA suitable for day surgery?
items.a:
- Consider control/comorbidity rather than AHI alone.
- Match surgery and expected opioid needs to facility capability.
- Plan PAP, rescue equipment, monitoring and an admission pathway.
- Discharge only after a stable observed recovery with support and clear instructions.

items.title: How does childhood OSA affect tonsillectomy analgesia?
items.q: How does childhood OSA affect tonsillectomy analgesia?
items.a:
- Use weight-based regular non-opioid multimodal analgesia.
- Titrate opioids cautiously if required with respiratory/sedation monitoring.
- Avoid codeine/tramadol after tonsillectomy in children.
- Plan hydration, antiemesis, discharge instructions and monitored admission when indicated.

items.title: When would you postpone surgery for a respiratory infection?
items.q: When would you postpone surgery for a respiratory infection?
items.a:
- Assess fever, systemic illness, wet cough, wheeze, hypoxaemia and lower-airway signs.
- Consider reserve, age/comorbidity, procedure, airway manipulation and urgency.
- Optimise/defer important active illness; mild symptoms may permit an individual plan.
- Do not use one universal waiting interval for every infection.

items.title: How do you compare nasal prongs, simple and reservoir masks?
items.q: How do you compare nasal prongs, simple and reservoir masks?
items.a:
- All are variable-performance oxygen systems; delivered FiO2 depends on demand and fit.
- Prongs are comfortable for modest needs; mouth breathing does not make them useless.
- Simple masks need sufficient flow to avoid rebreathing, commonly at least 5 L/min.
- A reservoir mask supplies high oxygen for emergencies; keep its bag inflated and monitor/escalate.

items.title: What makes a Venturi mask fixed performance?
items.q: What makes a Venturi mask fixed performance?
items.a:
- A jet entrains air in a device-defined ratio.
- Use the manufacturer-labelled driving flow and keep entrainment ports unobstructed.
- Total flow must meet inspiratory demand for the intended FiO2.
- Use controlled oxygen with clinical/gas reassessment in hypercapnia-risk patients.

items.title: What does a normal capnograph show?
items.q: What does a normal capnograph show?
items.a:
- Time is the horizontal axis and CO2 pressure/concentration the vertical axis.
- Early expiration starts with dead-space gas, then the upstroke and alveolar plateau.
- The end-expiratory point is ETCO2; inspiration produces the downstroke towards baseline.
- A sustained waveform supports tracheal placement, but the PaCO2 gradient varies with perfusion/dead space.

items.title: What are the key safety steps in percutaneous tracheostomy?
items.q: What are the key safety steps in percutaneous tracheostomy?
items.a:
- Confirm indication, consent, anatomy, coagulation and physiological tolerance.
- Plan oral-airway rescue and surgical conversion with a trained team.
- Use appropriate ultrasound/bronchoscopic guidance for puncture, wire and dilation.
- Confirm tracheal position and ventilation, secure the tube and record aftercare/emergency plans.

items.title: What can make percutaneous tracheostomy inappropriate?
items.q: What can make percutaneous tracheostomy inappropriate?
items.a:
- Emergency rescue-airway need or unidentifiable/unfavourable anatomy.
- Anterior vessels, local infection or major bleeding risk.
- Cervical instability and severe oxygen/PEEP dependence can add risk.
- Choose timing/technique individually with surgical and ICU expertise.

items.title: What is new in the global ARDS definition?
items.q: What is new in the global ARDS definition?
items.a:
- It includes selected non-intubated patients on HFNC ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP.
- P/F ≤300 or S/F ≤315 can qualify when SpO2 ≤97%, with support requirements.
- Bilateral imaging may include ultrasound; acute non-cardiogenic criteria remain.
- Resource-variable adaptations differ; do not blend the definition indiscriminately with Berlin.

items.title: How do you reduce postoperative pulmonary complications?
items.q: How do you reduce postoperative pulmonary complications?
items.a:
- Optimise respiratory disease/infection, smoking and functional reserve.
- Use protective ventilation and avoid residual NMBA with quantitative assessment.
- Provide effective opioid-sparing analgesia, mobilisation and coached breathing/coughing.
- Use targeted PAP/respiratory support and monitoring; no single device or exercise guarantees prevention.

items.title: How does an acute PE cause circulatory collapse?
items.q: How does an acute PE cause circulatory collapse?
items.a:
- Abrupt RV afterload rise causes dilation/ischaemia, septal shift and reduced LV filling.
- Hypotension reduces RV coronary perfusion and worsens the cycle.
- Give oxygen, support systemic pressure, avoid automatic large fluids and excessive airway pressure.
- Intubation may precipitate RV collapse; prepare vasoactive and reperfusion rescue.

items.title: How does fresh surgery change PE treatment?
items.q: How does fresh surgery change PE treatment?
items.a:
- Balance therapeutic anticoagulation against wound/neuraxial bleeding; agree agent with surgeon and PE team.
- Thrombolysis in life-threatening PE can be necessary but recent major surgery creates major bleeding risk.
- Consider catheter or surgical reperfusion and selected ECMO bridging when appropriate.
- Prophylactic LMWH dosing is not adequate treatment for established PE.

items.title: Give a practical VTE prevention plan for an allocated Set 11 patient.
items.q: Give a practical VTE prevention plan for an allocated Set 11 patient.
items.a:
- Assess patient/procedure VTE risk, bleeding, renal function and any neuraxial catheter.
- Mobilisation and appropriate mechanical measures; avoid stockings in significant arterial disease.
- Choose indicated drug/dose/duration from the operation-specific pathway; pelvic lymphadenectomy differs from low-risk robotic prostatectomy.
- Time prophylaxis separately around neuraxial insertion/removal and ensure discharge adherence/reassessment.

items.title: 1. During general anaesthesia for a laparotomy, the oxygen saturation falls from 99
items.q: During general anaesthesia for a laparotomy, the oxygen saturation falls from 99% to 85% over two minutes. Discuss your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Immediate response

Tell the surgeon, give 100% oxygen, and check the oximeter (waveform, probe position, cold or poorly perfused finger, nail varnish, methaemoglobin, dyes) against a second site or an arterial gas. Hand-ventilate, listen to the chest, look at capnography, airway pressure and the circuit. Confirm the problem is real before assuming a probe fault: a true fall from 99% to 85% in two minutes is a hypoxic emergency.

## Differential, checked from the machine to the patient

- **Oxygen supply and circuit:** disconnection, wrong gas mixture, empty cylinder, pipeline crossover, failure of the oxygen analyser. Check FiO2 and use a self-inflating bag attached to an independent, known oxygen source; room air is the fallback if oxygen is unavailable.
- **Airway:** endobronchial intubation (most likely after patient positioning or laparoscopic insufflation), tube kink, obstruction by secretions or a mucus plug, bronchospasm, laryngospasm on a supraglottic device.
- **Breathing:** pneumothorax (tension), atelectasis, aspiration, pulmonary oedema, pleural effusion, anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism (a sudden fall in ETCO2), and in this laparotomy case gas embolism or diaphragmatic splinting.
- **Circulation:** low cardiac output (bleeding, tamponade), shunt and dyshemoglobinaemia. Severe anaemia lowers oxygen content and tissue delivery but does not, by itself, cause a low PaO2 or saturation.
- **Patient factors:** morbid obesity, one-lung ventilation (if thoracic), Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum.

## Management

- **1.** Increase FiO2 to 1.0 and ventilate by hand with a PEEP valve to feel compliance; consider a cautious recruitment manoeuvre only after excluding tube obstruction, pneumothorax and dangerous haemodynamic instability.
- **2.** Pass a suction catheter and check the tube position with auscultation and bronchoscopy if endobronchial or obstructed.
- **3.** Treat the cause: bronchodilators and deepening anaesthesia for bronchospasm, adrenaline for anaphylaxis, decompress a tension pneumothorax (needle, then drain), stop nitrous oxide, suction for aspiration.
- **4.** If saturation does not recover, ask the surgeon to stop, remove positioning or insufflation, check haemodynamics, take a gas, order a chest X-ray or ultrasound, and consider CPAP, PEEP titration or ICU.
- **5.** Report the incident and document the cause.

## Evidence

Management is based on physiology, closed-claims and incident data (NAP and the Australian Incident Monitoring Study), not trials.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Check patient and equipment simultaneously; do not postpone oxygenation to prove monitor artefact. Ordinary pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb reliably and may overestimate saturation in darker skin pigmentation. Compare the waveform and clinical picture, and request arterial co-oximetry when discordant. A normal SpO2 on supplemental oxygen does not establish adequate ventilation or oxygen delivery. Source: Blue Book 2025 pulse oximetry chapter, targeted error sections; BJA Education 2025 impaired gas exchange review.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

## Self-marking checklist

- Immediate 100% oxygen and manual ventilation
- Checks equipment and monitors
- Airway and tube position
- Lung causes (bronchospasm, pneumothorax, atelectasis)
- Cardiovascular and metabolic causes
- Bronchoscopy, ultrasound and gas
- Specific treatments
- Escalation and postoperative plan

items.title: 2. The peak airway pressure rises suddenly from 20 to 45 cmH2O during general anaes
items.q: The peak airway pressure rises suddenly from 20 to 45 cmH2O during general anaesthesia. Discuss the differential diagnosis and your management.
items.a:
## Immediate steps

Ask whether it is the patient or the machine. Disconnect from the ventilator and hand-ventilate with 100% oxygen: a normal feel after isolating the suspect ventilator/circuit supports an equipment cause; a stiff bag suggests airway, lung or chest-wall pathology but requires systematic checking. Check capnography, SpO2 and blood pressure, and tell the surgeon.

## Differential in order of speed of onset

- **Circuit and equipment:** kinked or blocked circuit, closed APL valve, filter or HME blocked by secretions, ventilator fault, oxygen flush stuck.
- **Tube:** kink, biting, cuff herniation, obstruction by secretions or blood, endobronchial migration. A suction catheter may detect or clear obstruction, but its passage does not exclude partial obstruction, cuff problems or malposition.
- **Airway:** bronchospasm (wheeze, prolonged expiratory capnograph, "shark-fin"), anaphylaxis (hypotension, rash), aspiration, laryngospasm on a supraglottic device.
- **Lung and pleura:** tension pneumothorax (unilateral breath sounds, hypotension, tracheal shift), pulmonary oedema, atelectasis, abdominal causes (pneumoperitoneum, Trendelenburg, tight packs).
- **Inadequate anaesthesia or paralysis:** coughing, bucking, chest wall rigidity from opioids.

## Management

- **1.** 100% oxygen and manual ventilation with a PEEP valve.
- **2.** Pass a suction catheter, then check the tube with a bronchoscope if resistance remains.
- **3.** **Bronchospasm:** deepen with volatile or propofol, salbutamol 5 to 10 puffs through the circuit, IV adrenaline 10 to 50 micrograms if severe, IV magnesium 2 g, hydrocortisone, and a long expiratory time.
- **4.** **Anaphylaxis:** stop the trigger, give oxygen and reassessed IV fluid, and administer adrenaline appropriate to severity. In continuously monitored perioperative grade-3 reactions, experienced clinicians may titrate 50–100 micrograms IV under ANZAAG/ANZCA guidance; this is not a blanket dose for every reaction or an unmonitored setting.
- **5.** **Tension pneumothorax:** needle decompression and chest drain; stop nitrous oxide.
- **6.** Ask the surgeon to deflate the abdomen or remove packs; apply a muscle relaxant if there is rigidity.
- **7.** Take a gas, get a chest X-ray or lung ultrasound, and replace the circuit if in doubt.

## Evidence

The systematic approach (disconnect, check the tube, then the patient) is taught in difficult-situation algorithms. Incident reporting shows circuit and tube problems are the commonest causes.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

A normal feel when bagging through the same circuit does not exclude circuit failure; isolate it with an independent bag and oxygen source. Passing a suction catheter does not exclude partial obstruction, cuff herniation or endobronchial migration. Measure plateau pressure during passive zero-flow conditions and total PEEP with an expiratory hold; Ppeak minus Pplat reflects the resistive component, while Pplat minus total PEEP reflects driving pressure. Treat suspected tension pneumothorax immediately without waiting for tracheal deviation or imaging. Decompression technique depends on available expertise and the setting, followed by definitive drainage.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

## Self-marking checklist

- Peak versus plateau pressures
- Resistance causes
- Compliance causes
- Pneumothorax and bronchospasm recognised
- Surgical and positional causes
- Stepwise check with hand ventilation and bronchoscope
- Specific treatments
- Ventilation adjustment

items.title: 3. Discuss the causes, effects and management of an acute rise in end-tidal CO2 dur
items.q: Discuss the causes, effects and management of an acute rise in end-tidal CO2 during general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Causes of a rising ETCO2

Assess the patient immediately and check the sampling line/capnograph in parallel. A true rise means production exceeds elimination.

- **Increased CO2 production:** malignant hyperthermia (with tachycardia, rigidity and rising temperature), sepsis, fever, shivering, thyroid storm, absorption of CO2 from laparoscopic insufflation, sodium bicarbonate or tourniquet release, light anaesthesia.
- **Decreased elimination (hypoventilation):** inadequate minute ventilation, circuit leak or disconnection, bronchospasm, airway obstruction, high dead space, reduced compliance, endobronchial intubation, residual block or opioid in a spontaneously breathing patient.
- **Rebreathing and equipment:** exhausted soda lime, a faulty one-way valve, inadequate fresh gas flow in a Mapleson circuit, or a closed APL valve.
- **Pulmonary:** pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema, and a rise after a fall in ETCO2 following embolism.

## Effects of acute hypercapnia

Respiratory acidosis (falling pH by about 0.08 per 1.3 kPa PaCO2), sympathetic activation (tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmia), direct myocardial depression and vasodilatation, raised cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, pulmonary vasoconstriction, hyperkalaemia, a right shift of the haemoglobin curve, and in the awake patient narcosis. Extreme levels cause arrhythmia and cardiac arrest.

## Management

- **1.** Increase oxygen, check the patient and the breathing circuit, and confirm the capnograph with a gas.
- **2.** Increase minute ventilation (rate and tidal volume, limited by airway pressure and auto-PEEP).
- **3.** Treat the cause: replace soda lime or the circuit, relieve bronchospasm, remove the obstruction, and drain a pneumothorax.
- **4.** If there is an unexplained hypermetabolic pattern, think malignant hyperthermia without waiting for a temperature rise: stop triggers, call for help, dantrolene initially 2.5 mg/kg IV by actual body weight, with the current ANZCA per-dose maximum of 300 mg and repeat treatment according to the MH protocol, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen at high flow.
- **5.** For laparoscopy, lower insufflation pressure, change position, or convert to open.
- **6.** In permissive hypercapnia (ARDS, asthma), accept a pH above 7.2 to 7.25, unless raised intracranial pressure or pulmonary hypertension.

## Evidence

Management is based on physiology and incident reports. Permissive hypercapnia is supported by ARDSNet-type data.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

A rapidly increasing ETCO2 despite verified effective ventilation, tachycardia and rigidity warrants immediate treatment for possible malignant hyperthermia while excluding other causes; fever may be late. Assess sampling faults in parallel with the patient. Increase ventilation only within safe pressure, volume and expiratory-time limits. Hypercapnia targets are individual, especially with raised intracranial pressure or right ventricular failure; pH 7.2 is not a universal safe threshold.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

## Self-marking checklist

- Increased production causes
- Decreased elimination and dead space
- Rebreathing and equipment
- Physiological effects
- Increase ventilation and check circuit
- Malignant hyperthermia in the differential
- Blood gas confirmation
- Permissive hypercapnia and exceptions

items.title: 4. Outline the causes and physiological effects of hypocapnia in the anaesthetised
items.q: Outline the causes and physiological effects of hypocapnia in the anaesthetised patient.
items.a:
## Causes in the anaesthetised patient

Hypocapnia (a low PaCO2; low ETCO2 is only a surrogate) usually reflects hyperventilation but must be separated from a falling cardiac output or increased dead space, where the ETCO2 falls despite normal minute ventilation.

- **Iatrogenic hyperventilation:** the commonest cause, with excessive minute ventilation (rate or tidal volume) during controlled ventilation.
- **Low cardiac output or reduced pulmonary blood flow:** hypotension, haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism (thrombus, air, fat or amniotic fluid), and cardiac arrest.
- **Increased dead space:** bronchospasm, pulmonary embolism, reduced lung perfusion.
- **Reduced production:** hypothermia, deep anaesthesia, neuromuscular blockade, hypothyroidism.
- **Equipment and sampling:** leak, disconnection, an obstructed or dislodged sampling line, oesophageal intubation (absent trace).
- **Spontaneous breathing:** pain, anxiety, or high altitude.
- **Intentional:** hyperventilation for raised intracranial pressure.

## Physiological effects

- **Cerebral:** vasoconstriction (cerebral blood flow falls about 2 to 4% per mmHg), which lowers ICP but may cause cerebral ischaemia, particularly with prolonged severe hypocapnia (below 25 mmHg).
- **Respiratory alkalosis:** pH rises, which causes a left shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve (less oxygen release), hypokalaemia, ionised hypocalcaemia (tetany, paraesthesia, arrhythmia), and hypophosphataemia.
- **Cardiovascular:** reduced cardiac output, coronary vasoconstriction, and arrhythmia.
- **Respiratory:** bronchoconstriction, and reduced respiratory drive afterwards.
- **Pulmonary vascular:** alkalosis may lower PVR, but induced hypocapnia is not routine pulmonary-hypertension therapy.

## Management

- **1.** Check the capnograph and the patient (circulation first): a sudden fall in ETCO2 with hypotension is pulmonary embolism, haemorrhage or arrest until proven otherwise.
- **2.** Reduce excessive minute ventilation towards an appropriate PaCO2 target if hypocapnia is confirmed; use ETCO2 trends with awareness of a variable arterial–end-tidal gradient.
- **3.** Treat the cause: restore cardiac output, treat embolism, correct equipment faults.
- **4.** Give calcium if there is symptomatic hypocalcaemia, and manage electrolytes.
- **5.** Use intentional hyperventilation only for a defined indication, such as brief rescue for impending cerebral herniation, with an individual PaCO2 target and definitive treatment underway.

## Evidence

Evidence for the effects is physiological; brain trauma data show harm from prolonged hyperventilation (Muizelaar).

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Distinguish actual hypocapnia, confirmed by PaCO2, from a low ETCO2 caused by poor pulmonary perfusion or increased dead space. A sudden ETCO2 fall during shock or embolism can coexist with a normal or raised PaCO2: increasing ventilation reflexively can worsen haemodynamics. Routine prophylactic hyperventilation in brain injury is harmful; brief controlled hyperventilation is a rescue bridge for impending herniation while definitive treatment is arranged.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

## Self-marking checklist

- Iatrogenic hyperventilation
- Reduced production
- Low cardiac output and embolism as causes of low ETCO2
- Equipment causes
- Cerebral vasoconstriction
- Alkalosis, left shift and low ionised calcium
- Cardiovascular effects
- Management and appropriate targets

items.title: 5. Classify respiratory failure and outline the pathophysiology, causes and managem
items.q: Classify respiratory failure and outline the pathophysiology, causes and management of type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure.
items.a:
## Classification and mechanism

- **Type 1 (hypoxaemic):** PaO2 below 60 mmHg with normal or low PaCO2. The mechanisms are V/Q mismatch (pneumonia, atelectasis, asthma, COPD), shunt (ARDS, pulmonary oedema, collapse; poorly responsive to oxygen), diffusion limitation (fibrosis; oxygen helps), and low inspired oxygen or alveolar hypoventilation; low mixed-venous oxygen can amplify hypoxaemia in the presence of venous admixture.
- **Type 2 (hypercapnic):** PaCO2 above approximately 45–50 mmHg; acute cases usually have respiratory acidaemia, while chronic compensated cases may have a near-normal pH. The mechanisms are reduced respiratory drive (opioids, sedatives, brainstem injury), neuromuscular failure (myasthenia, Guillain-Barre, spinal injury, residual block), chest wall disease (flail, obesity, kyphoscoliosis), airway obstruction (COPD, asthma, OSA) and increased dead space with CO2 production.
- **Acute versus chronic:** in chronic type 2 failure, renal bicarbonate retention compensates, so pH is near normal; a new fall in pH with a further PaCO2 rise suggests acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure, but superimposed metabolic acidosis must be excluded.
- Some classifications add type 3 (perioperative, from atelectasis) and type 4 (shock-related).

## Clinical assessment

Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, accessory muscle use, paradox, confusion, cyanosis, and fatigue. Arterial gas shows PaO2/FiO2 and the A-a gradient (a raised gradient indicates V/Q or shunt; a normal gradient suggests hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen, interpreted for age and FiO2), plus chest X-ray, ECG, lung ultrasound and bedside spirometry.

## Management

- **1.** **Treat the cause:** bronchodilators and steroids for COPD, antibiotics for pneumonia, diuretics for oedema, drain pleural fluid, naloxone for opioids, reverse residual block.
- **2.** **Type 1:** oxygen titrated to SpO2 94 to 98%, HFNC, CPAP, then intubation with PEEP and lung-protective ventilation if refractory; prone positioning in severe ARDS; ECMO for refractory cases.
- **3.** **Type 2:** controlled oxygen (SpO2 88 to 92% in COPD), non-invasive ventilation for persistent acidotic hypercapnia after initial treatment; a pH below 7.25 increases failure risk but does not automatically exclude a closely monitored ICU trial, intubation if pH worsens, fatigue or reduced consciousness, and ventilator settings that avoid auto-PEEP.
- **4.** Optimise secretion clearance, analgesia, physiotherapy, nutrition and fluid balance; wean with daily trials.
- **5.** Escalate to ICU early, set a ceiling of care, and discuss goals.

## Evidence

NIV reduces intubation and mortality in COPD exacerbations (Brochard, BTS audit) and in cardiogenic oedema (3CPO showed symptom benefit only). FLORALI did not significantly reduce its primary overall intubation endpoint; its secondary survival finding should not be generalised. SOHO (2026) found no 28-day mortality difference between HFNC and standard oxygen; see the worked respiratory-support evidence case.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Choose support from physiology and urgency, rather than a compulsory oxygen → HFNC → CPAP → intubation ladder. NIV is strongly supported in acidotic COPD; use much greater caution in de novo hypoxaemic pneumonia/ARDS because failure and delayed intubation are dangerous. Cardiogenic oedema often improves with CPAP or bilevel support, although mortality estimates vary by study. Hypoventilation can be concealed by oxygen: assess respiratory effort, PaCO2 and consciousness.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Berlin boundaries:** mild 200 < P/F ≤300, moderate 100 < P/F ≤200, severe P/F ≤100 mmHg, with the specified PEEP/support and other criteria. Do not double-count the boundary values between groups.

Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

## Self-marking checklist

- Definitions of types 1 and 2
- Mechanisms (V/Q, shunt, diffusion, hypoventilation)
- Causes of each
- A–a gradient concept
- Controlled oxygen in type 2
- NIV and indications for intubation
- Lung-protective ventilation and rescue therapy
- Treat underlying cause

items.title: 6. Discuss the evidence for, and your approach to, lung-protective ventilation in a
items.q: Discuss the evidence for, and your approach to, lung-protective ventilation in a patient having a long open abdominal operation under general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Approach and evidence

Intraoperative ventilation can injure healthy lungs (volutrauma, atelectrauma, barotrauma and biotrauma), contributing to postoperative pulmonary complications. My approach is a bundle:

- **Tidal volume 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight** (calculated from height and sex, not actual weight). Meta-analyses and the IMPROVE trial (about 400 patients, abdominal surgery) showed fewer pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications with 6 to 8 mL/kg plus PEEP 6 to 8 and recruitment than with 10 to 12 mL/kg and no PEEP.
- **PEEP 5 cmH2O at least,** and an individually titrated level; PROVHILO (12 versus 2 with recruitment) and PROBESE (obese, 12 versus 4) showed no benefit of high PEEP with recruitment and more intraoperative hypotension, while the abdominal iPROVE trial did not show a significant reduction in its primary complication outcome with the tested individualised open-lung approaches. The balance favours moderate PEEP with titration to the best compliance and lowest driving pressure.
- **Driving pressure** (plateau minus total PEEP, measured in a passive patient) kept below 13 to 15 cmH2O; its association with complications is strong in observational data, so I treat it as a target in major surgery.
- **Plateau pressure** below 30 cmH2O.
- **Recruitment manoeuvres** only for atelectasis or hypoxaemia, rather than automatically after induction and before extubation; avoid in hypovolaemia, bullae or right heart failure; high PEEP lowers cardiac output.
- **FiO2** as low as needed for SpO2 94 to 98% (about 0.3 to 0.5); a high FiO2 (0.8) during induction/emergence promotes absorption atelectasis, but the PROXI trial showed no difference in infection with 0.8 compared with 0.3.
- **Respiratory rate** to keep ETCO2 35 to 45 mmHg, accepting mild hypercapnia.
- Pre-oxygenate with CPAP in obese patients, keep the abdomen free of unnecessary packing, and avoid prolonged periods of apnoea.

## Patient-specific changes

- **Obese:** ramped position, low tidal volume by predicted body weight and individual PEEP; recruitment only if indicated and tolerated, rather than a compulsory PEEP 8–12/recruitment package.
- **COPD:** long expiratory time, low rate, lower PEEP (to avoid hyperinflation), permissive hypercapnia.
- **ARDS:** 4 to 6 mL/kg, plateau below 30, higher PEEP.
- **One-lung ventilation:** 4 to 6 mL/kg and PEEP 5.

## Postoperative

Avoid residual neuromuscular block, extubate semi-recumbent, early CPAP or HFNC in at-risk patients, analgesia that allows deep breaths, and mobilise.

## Evidence

Blue Book 2017 recommends 6 mL/kg predicted body weight or less, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O, PEEP in the range 5 to 15 depending on severity, and driving pressure below about 14 cmH2O (Amato's analysis of nine trials). It reports Futier 2013 (400 abdominal surgery patients, 6 to 8 mL/kg with PEEP 6 to 8): non-invasive ventilation or reintubation fell from 17% to 5%. A 2014 Cochrane review of 12 studies (1012 patients) found fewer postoperative pneumonias and less need for ventilation, with no consistent mortality difference. The chapter notes no clinically relevant benefit of recruitment in large trials, and poor uptake: in LUNG-SAFE fewer than two thirds of ARDS patients received 8 mL/kg or less. PROTHOR was an adult thoracic one-lung ventilation trial, published online in 2025, comparing PEEP 10 with recruitment against PEEP 5 without routine recruitment. Its primary pulmonary-complication outcome was not significantly improved; it was not a 2022 open-abdominal-surgery trial.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Do not treat a driving-pressure threshold as a universally validated interventional target. Use predicted body weight, passive plateau measurement, total PEEP, compliance, gas exchange and blood pressure together. Obesity does not mandate a fixed PEEP of 12 or routine sustained recruitment. The January 2026 BJA Education atelectasis review emphasises both collapse at insufficient PEEP and overdistension/circulatory harm at excessive PEEP. Sources: iPROVE primary abstract (PMID 29371130); PROTHOR primary publication, DOI 10.1016/S2213-2600(25)00330-3; BJA Education 2026;26:20–29.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
