A normal daytime SpO2 does not exclude nocturnal hypoventilation. Interpret trends, symptoms, bulbar impairment and measurement reliability together.

CHEST 2023 supports NIV for chronic respiratory failure in neuromuscular disease and an individual initiation decision using symptoms, respiratory-muscle impairment, sleep testing and hypercapnia. Illustrative triggers include symptomatic FVC below 80%, FVC below 50%, weak inspiratory pressures or awake PaCO2 above 45 mmHg; these are prompts for specialist assessment, not a compulsory wait-until threshold. Arrange an elective acclimatisation trial before crisis where possible. Bilevel ventilatory support with a backup rate and tailored interface/settings is often needed; CPAP alone treats obstruction but does not correct muscle-related hypoventilation.

Pair ventilation with cough augmentation, secretion clearance and aspiration management. Teach assisted cough and consider mechanical insufflation–exsufflation when cough is ineffective. Address mask fit/pressure injury, leak, synchrony, humidification, nutrition and communication; review nocturnal gas exchange and symptoms after changes. Oxygen alone can conceal hypoventilation and worsen hypercapnia, so add it only for a defined oxygenation indication while ensuring ventilation.

Explain burden, likely progression, benefit/limitations and the possibility of increasing daytime dependence. Discuss tracheostomy/invasive ventilation if NIV fails or bulbar/secretion issues make it unsuitable, alongside the option of symptom-focused care. Record capacity, advance preferences, ceiling of care, caregiver training, backup power/equipment, emergency access, follow-up and support needs. Starting ventilation does not commit the patient irrevocably to invasive support; goals can be reviewed.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Symptoms/trajectory and multidisciplinary assessment
- **2** — Objective awake/sleep/muscle/cough tests
- **2** — Individual timing and NIV approach
- **2** — Cough/aspiration/secretion support and monitoring
- **2** — Goals, invasive options and home contingency

items.title: 27. Interpret a gas in chronic respiratory disease and a postoperative CXR; show how
items.q: Interpret a gas in chronic respiratory disease and a postoperative CXR; show how the result changes management.
items.a:
**Worked educator-created gas.** A drowsy COPD patient on controlled oxygen has pH 7.25, PaCO2 80 mmHg, HCO3 34 mmol/L, PaO2 58 mmHg and lactate 1.2 mmol/L. This is hypercapnic respiratory failure with acidaemia; elevated bicarbonate suggests a chronic component, but prior gases and metabolic causes are necessary to distinguish acute-on-chronic from another mixed disorder. Acute respiratory compensation raises bicarbonate roughly 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg CO2 increase; chronic compensation roughly 3–4. These are approximations and must not replace clinical interpretation. At PaCO2 80, bicarbonate 34 is more than acute compensation but less than some fully chronic expectations, supporting deterioration in a chronically affected patient. Document FiO2, sample source and units before calculating oxygenation indices.

Assess airway, respiratory effort, sedation/opioids, infection, bronchospasm and fatigue immediately. Titrate oxygen to 88–92%, treat an exacerbation/cause and initiate suitable monitored bilevel NIV if the patient can protect the airway. Reassess clinically and with an early gas; worsening consciousness, inability to clear secretions, shock, exhaustion or failure warrants intubation rather than persevering with a mask. Do not give bicarbonate merely to normalise respiratory pH.

**Worked educator-created CXR description.** A postoperative film shows a dense lower-zone opacity with fissure/hilar displacement towards that side, raised hemidiaphragm and reduced volume. This favours lobar atelectasis rather than simply pneumonia; assess a mucus/blood plug, mainstem tube, pain and hypoventilation. Check airway and tube depth, use suction/bronchoscopy when obstructed, analgesia/physiotherapy and appropriate PEEP/CPAP, with follow-up response. Consolidation without volume loss, pleural effusion, oedema and aspiration can overlap.

Use a systematic image approach: identity/date, projection/rotation/inspiration, airway and devices, lungs/pleura, heart/mediastinum, diaphragm and bones/soft tissue; compare previous films. A supine CXR may miss anterior pneumothorax or obscure fluid distribution. Lung ultrasound helps at the bedside; CT resolves selected stable cases. No supplied radiographic image is claimed for this constructed example. Interpret the gas and image with physiology; a normal saturation on oxygen does not refute ventilatory failure.

## Self-marking checklist

- **3** — Correct acid–base and chronicity interpretation
- **2** — Oxygenation/source/units and clinical response
- **3** — CXR volume-loss pattern and systematic approach
- **2** — Targeted management with imaging limitations

items.title: 28. Outline complete treatment of an acute COPD exacerbation, including failure of i
items.q: Outline complete treatment of an acute COPD exacerbation, including failure of initial therapy.
items.a:
Assess ABC, work of breathing, mental state, haemodynamics and gas exchange, looking for infection, pneumonia, oedema, PE, pneumothorax, arrhythmia and medication problems. Establish usual function, oxygen/PAP, prior admissions/intubation, baseline PaCO2 and preferences. Obtain gas, CXR, ECG and appropriate blood/microbiology tests without delaying support.

Give controlled oxygen to an initial 88–92% target in a hypercapnia-risk patient and repeat gases after intervention. Treat with inhaled short-acting beta-agonist, with a short-acting antimuscarinic for a significant exacerbation, using a suitable device and avoiding unnecessary oxygen-driven nebulisation that defeats controlled oxygen. Use a short systemic steroid course for a moderate/severe exacerbation, and antibiotics when bacterial features or ventilatory support/local guidance indicate; select drug and duration by local resistance, allergy, renal function and microbiology. Avoid routine methylxanthines. Correct fluid/electrolyte derangement and treat the trigger.

For persistent hypercapnic acidosis initiate monitored NIV with a clear intubation or ceiling-of-care plan. Titrate inspiratory pressure support, EPAP, interface/leak and oxygen to the patient and reassess promptly. Severe acidosis needs higher supervision, not an arbitrary exclusion rule. Intubate for failure, exhaustion, unsafe airway, arrest or severe instability; ventilate with a low rate, modest predicted-weight tidal volume and long expiration, following auto-PEEP/plateau pressure and accepting an appropriate CO2 near baseline rather than forcing a normal PaCO2.

Provide VTE prophylaxis when indicated, nutrition, secretion clearance, mobilisation and avoidance of excess sedation. Before discharge optimise maintenance LABA/LAMA and assess the indication for ICS rather than prescribing it to everyone. Check inhaler technique, smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen reassessment, an action plan and follow-up. Persistent hypercapnia after recovery may prompt specialist long-term NIV assessment; an acute gas alone does not automatically establish that indication.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Assessment and alternate diagnoses
- **2** — Controlled oxygen with gases
- **2** — Bronchodilator/steroid/antibiotic decisions
- **2** — NIV, escalation and safe invasive ventilation
- **2** — Recovery, maintenance and follow-up

items.title: 29. A patient on day six of ventilation develops fever, purulent secretions and wors
items.q: A patient on day six of ventilation develops fever, purulent secretions and worse oxygenation. Evaluate VAP and justify treatment/prevention.
items.a:
VAP is suspected pneumonia arising after at least 48 hours of invasive ventilation. New/progressive infiltrates, fever/leukocyte change, purulent secretions and worsened oxygenation support it, but no single score or positive tracheal culture proves infection. Consider colonisation/tracheobronchitis, mucus-plug collapse, oedema, ARDS, infarction and extrapulmonary sepsis. Examine, review imaging/mechanics and obtain respiratory and blood samples before antibiotics when this will not delay urgent therapy.

Tracheal aspirate is easy and low risk but can detect colonisation; bronchoscopic BAL may improve targeted sampling yet is invasive, resource intensive and can worsen hypoxaemia. International guidelines differ on preferred sampling. PCR can speed pathogen/resistance identification but may detect non-viable organisms. Interpret microbiology with the clinical syndrome rather than treating every result.

In clinically important suspected infection begin empirical antibiotics based on illness severity, prior antibiotics/colonisation, local antibiogram and resistance risk. A suitable antipseudomonal beta-lactam may be required; add MRSA or second Gram-negative coverage only when justified by risk and local guidance. Review dosing, renal function and infusion strategy. Reassess diagnosis and narrow/stop treatment with results and response, typically within 48–72 hours. About seven days is a common uncomplicated course with good response; abscess, empyema, structural disease or immunocompromise needs individual advice. REGARD-VAP supports selected shorter response-based courses, not automatic three-day therapy for all VAP. Support oxygenation, lung-protective ventilation, perfusion and drainage of complications; steroids for severe CAP cannot simply be extrapolated to VAP.

Prevent avoidable invasive-ventilation days using appropriate NIV selection, sedation minimisation and daily liberation assessment; minimise reintubation, use head-up positioning when safe, maintain sensible cuff pressure, appropriate secretion drainage and oral care with toothbrushing, and follow hand/equipment hygiene. Routine circuit changes, chlorhexidine, probiotics or prophylactic antibiotics are not universal outcome-proven measures. SDD and newer inhaled/prophylactic antibiotic studies require local resistance assessment and multidisciplinary policy; lowering adjudicated VAP incidence does not necessarily improve survival. Use stress-ulcer prophylaxis for bleeding risk and do not claim PPIs necessarily cause pneumonia.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Clinical diagnosis versus colonisation and alternatives
- **2** — Sampling methods and limitations
- **3** — Local empirical therapy, reassessment and duration
- **1** — Supportive treatment/complications
- **2** — Prevention and evidence limits

items.title: 30. A ventilated patient has a pneumothorax with a persistent large air leak despite
items.q: A ventilated patient has a pneumothorax with a persistent large air leak despite a drain. Discuss diagnosis, ventilation and escalation.
items.a:
Treat tension or respiratory/circulatory compromise immediately. Check drain patency, connection, position and side holes, and exclude external air entrainment masquerading as a pulmonary leak. Persistent bubbling, failure of re-expansion and a large inspired–expired tidal-volume difference suggest an ongoing leak; define its phase, magnitude and trend. A leak continuing beyond about five days is commonly called persistent. Distinguish proximal bronchopleural from distal alveolopleural fistula, and consider necrotising infection, postoperative stump failure, trauma, malignancy or ventilatory injury.

Use CXR/CT when stable to identify undrained air, infection, parenchymal disease and trapped/non-expandable lung. A residual space does not always mean a drain must be placed on stronger suction. Bronchoscopy and sequential balloon occlusion can localise a culprit airway when intervention is considered. Seek early thoracic/respiratory/ICU input.

Maintain adequate pleural drainage and reduce mean airway pressure as feasible: lower tidal volume/pressure, the lowest effective PEEP, shorter inspiratory time and lower respiratory rate, balancing oxygenation and permissible CO2. Monitor expired volume and haemodynamics rather than trusting inspired volume. Avoid aggressive recruitment/APRV strategies that maintain high mean pressure across a fistula. Transition towards spontaneous ventilation/extubation when safe, balancing respiratory effort/P-SILI against prolonged mandatory ventilation.

Avoid automatic strong continuous suction: use it when necessary to maintain expansion, at the least effective level with specialist guidance. A larger/repositioned/additional drain may be needed for a substantial leak, proximal injury or infected space. If ventilation is failing, expert temporary isolation with a blocker, DLT or selective intubation may protect the better lung. Persistent problems may need endobronchial valves/other occlusion, surgery or selected extracorporeal support; each has infection, migration, airway and procedural risks. Treat underlying infection and nutrition and discuss goals/prognosis. Do not clamp an actively leaking drain in a patient at risk of tension.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Urgent stabilisation and true-leak assessment
- **2** — Fistula/trapped-lung diagnosis and imaging
- **2** — Ventilator changes linked to mean pressure
- **2** — Individual drainage/suction and monitoring
- **2** — Specialist isolation/intervention/rescue

items.title: 31. Discuss the newer ARDS definition and how contemporary evidence changes manageme
items.q: Discuss the newer ARDS definition and how contemporary evidence changes management.
items.a:
Berlin remains important for historical papers and intubated ARDS. The newer global definition broadens recognition to selected non-intubated patients supported with HFNC at at least 30 L/min or NIV/CPAP, permits oxygen-saturation-based criteria when SpO2 is no higher than 97%, and accommodates lung ultrasound and resource-limited settings under defined conditions. The underlying syndrome still requires acute onset, bilateral lung abnormalities and an explanation beyond purely cardiac oedema/overload. Do not apply an intubated severity category to every oxygen-dependent patient without checking the definition's support and measurement requirements.

For practice preserve the established foundation: treat cause, low predicted-weight tidal volumes, limited plateau pressure, appropriate PEEP, early prolonged prone positioning in suitable moderate/severe disease and reassessed fluid management after shock resuscitation. ATS 2024 conditionally supports steroids, selected VV-ECMO, early severe-ARDS NMBA and higher PEEP without recruitment, and strongly recommends against prolonged recruitment manoeuvres. These are conditional choices, not a mandate to paralyse or cannulate everyone. Steroid drug/timing and contraindications depend on cause; influenza is a distinct concern in pneumonia guidance.

Monitor respiratory effort and dyssynchrony, dead space, RV function and gas exchange. Avoid accepting a reassuring SpO2 while effort or hypercapnia worsens. Inhaled vasodilators can bridge refractory hypoxaemia but have not shown a survival benefit; HFOV and aggressive recruitment must not be listed as equivalent outcome-proven rescue options. Seek early specialist/ECMO advice for potentially reversible refractory failure rather than waiting for arrest.

**Audit addition:** For non-intubated global-definition ARDS, oxygenation is P/F ≤300 mmHg or S/F ≤315 when SpO2 ≤97%, on HFNC ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP with ≥5 cmH2O expiratory pressure. Use the specified timing and acute bilateral imaging/non-cardiogenic criteria. Resource-variable adaptations have different support requirements and should be identified explicitly rather than blended with Berlin.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Historical versus global definition and measurement conditions
- **2** — Protective ventilation/prone foundation
- **2** — Conditional ATS adjuncts and evidence strength
- **2** — Avoids harmful recruitment/HFOV generalisation
- **2** — Monitoring, cause-specific care and timely escalation

items.title: 32. Evaluate HFNC versus NIV and standard oxygen in acute respiratory failure, using
items.q: Evaluate HFNC versus NIV and standard oxygen in acute respiratory failure, using recent trials.
items.a:
Select support by failure mechanism, severity and airway safety. HFNC supplies humidified high flow, a more stable inspired oxygen fraction and upper-airway dead-space washout, with variable modest pressure. Bilevel NIV adds pressure support to unload respiratory muscles and improve CO2 clearance; CPAP supplies continuous pressure without the same inspiratory assistance. None protects the airway like an ETT.

Acidotic COPD is a strong indication for NIV when suitable. CPAP/bilevel is useful in acute cardiogenic oedema, with treatment of the cardiac cause. In de novo hypoxaemic pneumonia/ARDS, HFNC is often a reasonable closely monitored option; NIV may fail and can generate large tidal volumes/high effort. Device selection does not substitute for intubation when airway protection, work of breathing, gases or haemodynamics deteriorate. Use serial bedside assessment; scores such as ROX can support trends but must not impose a waiting period in a failing patient.

Interpret outcomes separately. FLORALI was not positive for its primary overall intubation endpoint; its secondary mortality signal does not prove HFNC survival benefit in all acute failure. SOHO (2026) enrolled acute hypoxaemic failure and found identical 28-day mortality of 14.6% in both groups. Intubation was lower with HFNC (42.4% versus 48.4%), but this was a secondary endpoint and the trial was open-label. These findings support a possible reduction in intubation, not a guaranteed survival advantage. A trial result in selected hypoxaemic patients does not establish equivalence to bilevel NIV for acidotic COPD.

Set an explicit reassessment and escalation plan, document FiO2/flow or pressure/interface, check skin/leak/humidification and allow necessary breaks. Oxygenation may look normal despite rising CO2 or severe respiratory effort. In high-risk post-extubation patients choose prophylactic support before failure develops; in established post-extubation failure, avoid delaying reintubation with prolonged unsuccessful rescue NIV.

**Audit addition:** RENOVATE (published online 2024, JAMA 2025) used Bayesian dynamic borrowing across five acute-failure groups and met its prespecified non-inferiority threshold for intubation/death at seven days in four groups; the immunocompromised group stopped for futility. Non-inferiority used an odds-ratio margin of 1.55, and group size/borrowing limit interpretation. It does not show HFNC is physiologically identical or superior to NIV, and should not erase established NIV practice for acidotic COPD. Source: primary report, DOI 10.1001/jama.2024.26244.

## Self-marking checklist

- **3** — Physiological differences and disease-specific selection
- **2** — Failure recognition and escalation
- **3** — Accurate primary/secondary trial interpretation
- **2** — Monitoring and extubation distinctions

items.title: 33. How would you assess a severely hypoxaemic patient on VV-ECMO and adjust the cir
items.q: How would you assess a severely hypoxaemic patient on VV-ECMO and adjust the circuit?
items.a:
Assess the patient and circuit immediately with the ECMO team. Verify the saturation, arterial gas, haemoglobin, perfusion, temperature and metabolic demand; check oxygenator gas supply, effective blood flow, pressures/alarms, cannula position, circuit clot and native-lung ventilation. A sudden change may reflect oxygen-supply failure, cannula migration, flow limitation, oxygenator failure, haemorrhage or new native-lung pathology.

VV drainage blood is oxygenated and returned to venous circulation; systemic saturation reflects mixing with venous blood that bypasses the circuit plus native-lung gas exchange. The ratio of effective ECMO flow to cardiac output matters, as do venous oxygen content and haemoglobin. Recirculation returns freshly oxygenated blood directly to the drainage cannula, reducing effective support. Increasing pump speed can worsen drainage limitation or recirculation rather than fixing saturation. Evaluate volume/cannula position and the circuit systematically with specialist input.

Sweep gas principally governs CO2 clearance; oxygen transfer is more dependent on effective blood flow, oxygenator function and blood/gas oxygen content. Do not reflexively increase sweep alone for isolated low arterial oxygenation. Avoid abrupt large PaCO2 changes and prevent excessive respiratory effort while using lung-protective native ventilation. Treat fever, agitation, shivering or sepsis increasing demand, and assess whether a modest saturation is compatible with adequate total oxygen delivery rather than chasing SpO2 with harmful ventilator pressure.

VV provides no direct systemic circulatory flow. If severe circulatory failure persists, investigate its cause and whether another configuration is needed. Bleeding, haemolysis, thrombosis and neurological injury must be considered, not just the saturation number. Escalation and circuit adjustments belong to an experienced ECMO team with a clearly communicated plan.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Patient/circuit emergency check
- **2** — Flow-to-output and oxygen-content physiology
- **2** — Recognition of recirculation/flow limitation
- **2** — Sweep versus oxygen-transfer distinction
- **2** — Native-lung, demand and circulatory/rescue plan

items.title: 34. Evaluate early bronchoalveolar toileting after severe pulmonary aspiration
items.q: Evaluate early bronchoalveolar toileting after severe pulmonary aspiration.
items.a:
The available 2027 Blue Book preview proposes a local early-toileting approach for selected severe, large-volume or particulate aspiration. It is a developing strategy with limited evidence, not a standard requirement to lavage every aspirating patient. Immediate priorities remain suction, airway protection and oxygenation; life-saving ventilation must not be delayed while assembling a bronchoscope.

After stabilisation consider whether retained material/obstruction makes bronchoscopy useful and whether the patient can tolerate it. Consult experienced anaesthesia/ICU/respiratory colleagues, ensure appropriate ETT/scope compatibility, effective suction, trained assistance and continuous physiological monitoring. An additional clinician should manage ventilation/perfusion while the proceduralist works. Scope occupation of an ETT reduces available lumen and can impair expiration, causing hypercapnia, auto-PEEP and barotrauma; suction also promotes derecruitment. Pause or withdraw to reoxygenate if deterioration occurs.

Target visual removal of particulate/obstructing material and follow an institutionally approved technique if toileting is selected; do not adopt a case-report saline volume as a universal prescription. Reassess oxygenation, airway pressures and haemodynamics throughout. Subsequently manage aspiration pneumonitis supportively, evaluate infection/contaminated aspirate, and decide antibiotics, surgery continuation and ICU on the actual clinical course. Routine steroids and prophylactic antibiotics are not established treatment for uncomplicated chemical pneumonitis.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Recognises selective/emerging nature
- **2** — Oxygenation and airway first
- **2** — Patient selection and skilled preparation
- **2** — Procedure-related gas-exchange/barotrauma hazards and stopping
- **2** — Post-event cause-specific monitoring/disposition

items.title: 35. What would you do for respiratory arrest with a palpable pulse
items.q: What would you do for respiratory arrest with a palpable pulse?
items.a:
Call the emergency team, check responsiveness, breathing and circulation rapidly and begin effective assisted ventilation with oxygen. Open the airway, remove visible obstruction/suction, use airway adjuncts and a two-person bag-mask technique where possible, observing chest rise and capnography. Give approximately 10 breaths/min in an adult with a pulse, titrated to chest rise and physiology; avoid excessive pressure or hyperventilation. Insert a definitive airway if mask support is inadequate or ongoing protection/support is required, with a difficult-airway rescue plan.

Treat the precipitant immediately: opioid/sedative depression with ventilation and titrated reversal, upper-airway obstruction/laryngospasm, residual NMBA, severe bronchospasm, aspiration, pneumothorax, neuromuscular failure, high neuraxial block or a central/metabolic cause. A reversal drug does not replace oxygenation. Confirm quantitative recovery where relevant and monitor for recurrence after shorter-acting antidotes.

Reassess pulse and perfusion continually. If there is no definite pulse or other evidence of cardiac arrest, begin high-quality CPR and follow the applicable ALS algorithm. A low ETCO2 or a monitor alarm alone does not determine pulselessness or justify withholding resuscitation. After recovery use monitored care, gas analysis, investigation of cause, safe oxygen/CO2 targets and an explicit observation/escalation plan. Communicate, document and disclose the event where appropriate.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Recognises arrest with pulse and calls help
- **2** — Effective oxygenation/ventilation
- **2** — Airway escalation and cause-directed treatment
- **2** — Detects progression to cardiac arrest
- **2** — Recurrence prevention and monitored care

items.title: 36. A postoperative patient has low SpO2 but an unusual clinical picture
items.q: A postoperative patient has low SpO2 but an unusual clinical picture. Evaluate pulse-oximeter error and oxygen delivery.
items.a:
Treat plausible hypoxaemia immediately while checking the signal. Assess airway, ventilation, circulation, inspired oxygen and the waveform against the measured pulse. Check probe fit/site, cold or low-perfusion extremity, motion, venous pulsation, ambient light, nail/skin interference and dyes. Move to a better-perfused/alternative site or second device if appropriate; do not dismiss a falling saturation as artefact without examination.

Two-wavelength oximetry estimates saturation and cannot reliably quantify COHb or distinguish all dyshemoglobins. CO poisoning may look reassuring, and methaemoglobinaemia tends to distort readings towards the mid-80s. Accuracy is limited at low saturation and can be biased by skin pigmentation; a high reading does not override a concerning clinical picture. Obtain arterial gas with co-oximetry when the saturation, PaO2, exposure or phenotype is discordant. ABG-calculated saturation without co-oximetry may also be misleading in dyshemoglobinaemia.

Separate oxygen tension, saturation, content and delivery. Anaemia reduces oxygen content without necessarily lowering PaO2/SpO2. Low cardiac output can cause tissue hypoxia despite a normal saturation. High FiO2 can maintain saturation during severe hypoventilation, so assess respiratory effort, CO2 and sedation independently. Treat the identified airway, lung, perfusion, Hb or measurement problem and document response; do not chase a number with oxygen alone.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Treats real hypoxaemia while checking signal
- **2** — Common technical/perfusion faults
- **2** — Dyshemoglobin and pigmentation limitations
- **2** — Correct use of ABG/co-oximetry
- **2** — Distinguishes tension/saturation/content/delivery and ventilation

items.title: 37. Use lung ultrasound to evaluate postoperative hypoxaemia: findings, actions and
items.q: Use lung ultrasound to evaluate postoperative hypoxaemia: findings, actions and limitations.
items.a:
Begin with physiology and emergency treatment, then scan systematically across anterior, lateral and accessible posterior/dependent areas, comparing sides and integrating heart assessment where appropriate. Choose a probe and settings for the question, identify pleural line/ribs and look for sliding, artefacts, fluid and consolidation. A rapid focused examination must not replace airway/circuit checks or delay treatment of tension pneumothorax.

Sliding, B-lines or lung pulse rule out pneumothorax at that site; absent sliding alone has several causes. A lung point supports pneumothorax but may be absent with a very large collection. Diffuse B-lines suggest interstitial/alveolar fluid but are not specific for cardiogenic oedema; integrate distribution, pleural appearance and cardiac findings. Pleural effusion appears as fluid adjacent to lung/diaphragm, and depth/loculation matter before any drainage. Tissue-like consolidation with volume-loss clues may represent atelectasis; dynamic air bronchograms favour pneumonia but no isolated sign is perfectly diagnostic. Ultrasound can follow recruitment/diuresis or drainage response.

Treat the cause: decompress tension physiology, clear a plugged airway, provide suitable PEEP/respiratory support for collapse, treat infection or manage cardiac/fluid overload according to the full assessment. Do not automatically recruit every consolidated region or diurese every B-line pattern. Limitations include operator dependence, inaccessible dressings/obesity/subcutaneous air, lesions not reaching pleura, focal sampling and overlapping patterns. CXR/CT remain appropriate when uncertainty persists or anatomy must be defined. Document sites, findings, interpretation and the management decision rather than merely writing “ultrasound normal”.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Systematic technique integrated with resuscitation
- **2** — Pneumothorax signs and site-specific interpretation
- **2** — B-lines, effusion and consolidation differential
- **2** — Cause-directed action and reassessment
- **2** — Limits and complementary imaging

items.title: 38. A patient is awake after critical illness but cannot lift their limbs and repeat
items.q: A patient is awake after critical illness but cannot lift their limbs and repeatedly fails weaning. Evaluate ICU-acquired weakness.
items.a:
Consider ICU-acquired weakness after severe sepsis, multiorgan failure, prolonged ventilation, deep sedation and immobility, but do not assume every weakness is caused by ICU care. Establish whether it preceded admission or is disproportionate to the course. Check residual NMBA, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance including phosphate, hypoxia, malnutrition and concurrent cardiac/pulmonary causes of weaning failure.

Examine for diffuse symmetrical limb and respiratory weakness, cough/secretion clearance, swallowing and axial function; relative facial/ocular sparing is typical. When cooperative, quantify limb strength with an MRC sum score; below 48/60 is a commonly used threshold. Functional assessment complements it because limb strength alone misses respiratory/bulbar problems. Focal/asymmetrical weakness, prominent cranial involvement, sensory level, rapid progression or a discordant trajectory prompts urgent neurological investigation rather than a routine ICUAW label. Electrophysiology is selective for atypical presentations and alternative diagnoses; CK can be normal.

Management is multimodal and phase-sensitive: treat ongoing illness, minimise unnecessary sedation, review NMBA/steroid exposure without withholding an indicated short course automatically, correct metabolic contributors, provide appropriate nutrition and conventional glucose control, assess readiness for SBTs daily and support cough/swallowing. Mobilise and rehabilitate as safely tolerated with daily team review. More intensive exercise is not invariably better: TEAM found no improvement in its main outcome with intensified early active mobilisation and more adverse events. There is no established disease-modifying drug or universal high-intensity mobilisation prescription.

Distinguish inability to sustain breathing from inability to protect the airway after an SBT. Discuss tracheostomy individually if prolonged support is likely, without promising it cures weakness or improves survival. Involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech/swallowing, nutrition and the patient/family. Explain uncertain and sometimes prolonged recovery, track function, and document rehabilitation goals and follow-up after ICU.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Risk/course and reversible contributors
- **3** — Clinical pattern, respiratory/bulbar function and atypical red flags
- **3** — Individual prevention/rehabilitation with evidence limits
- **2** — Weaning, airway, communication and follow-up

items.title: 39. A patient becomes apnoeic after postoperative opioid administration
items.q: A patient becomes apnoeic after postoperative opioid administration. Explain rescue, recurrence and prevention.
items.a:
Call for help, stop further opioid/sedative administration, open the airway and give effective assisted ventilation with oxygen while checking circulation. Severe depression can progress to arrest; do not wait for naloxone before oxygenating. Assess respiratory rate/pattern, effort, consciousness, capnography and SpO2. Supplemental oxygen may conceal hypoventilation. If cardiac arrest develops follow ALS.

Give titrated naloxone by an appropriate route, commonly small IV increments in a monitored postoperative patient, aiming to restore ventilation and airway safety without unnecessary pain/withdrawal. A major overdose or profound arrest-risk state needs prompt effective reversal rather than slow undertreatment. Reassess repeatedly; naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so repeat dosing or an infusion and monitored care may be needed. High-affinity/potent opioid exposure and co-administered non-opioid depressants complicate reversal. Naloxone does not reverse benzodiazepine, gabapentinoid or other non-opioid effects; failure to wake requires continued airway support and a wider differential.

Risk assessment includes age, opioid naivety, sleep-disordered breathing, heart failure, organ dysfunction, dose/route, concurrent sedatives and previous recovery events. The PRODIGY study used continuous monitoring to detect episodes; its high event frequency is not a rate of fatal clinical overdose. Chronic tolerance does not eliminate respiratory risk. Use opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, appropriate dose/interval/route, sedation assessment and suitable monitoring/observation; restart analgesia safely after rescue. Novel respiratory stimulants are research developments, not a reason to delay standard airway/ventilatory treatment. Document, disclose and revise the postoperative care plan.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Immediate airway/ventilation/circulation rescue
- **2** — Titrated effective naloxone and monitoring
- **2** — Recurrence/high-affinity and co-depressant limitations
- **2** — Individual risk and careful evidence interpretation
- **2** — Prevention and revised analgesia/disposition

items.title: 40. How does a current or recent respiratory infection change the decision to procee
items.q: How does a current or recent respiratory infection change the decision to proceed with surgery?
items.a:
Assess severity, trajectory, infectivity, baseline reserve and urgency rather than the diagnostic label alone. Ask about fever, cough and sputum, wheeze, breathlessness, exercise tolerance, chest pain, systemic illness and oxygen needs; examine respiratory effort and saturation and seek lower-airway signs. Consider asthma/COPD/OSA, frailty, smoking and previous respiratory events. In children add age/prematurity, passive smoke, secretion burden and airway surgery/instrumentation.

Mild isolated upper-airway symptoms in an otherwise well patient may be compatible with proceeding after an informed individual assessment. Significant fever/systemic illness, lower-respiratory infection, hypoxaemia or active bronchospasm usually favours deferring elective surgery and treating/optimising the illness. Do not impose a universal interval after every cold, pneumonia or COVID infection; recovery, ongoing symptoms, surgical risk and current local infection guidance determine timing. Urgent source-control surgery may need to proceed despite high risk, with explicit mitigation and postoperative critical-care planning.

Use tests to answer a clinical question: CXR/gas for important lower-airway/gas-exchange concern, viral tests for infection-control or treatment decisions, spirometry only where it will alter management. Avoid routine antibiotics for viral URTI. Continue indicated inhalers, manage secretions and hydration and plan an appropriate airway device/technique with experienced staff. Ensure adequate depth during airway manipulation, gentle suction, protective ventilation, full quantitative NMBA recovery if used, effective analgesia and a recovery/escalation plan. Consent must explain the increased respiratory risk and why proceeding or postponing is the better choice for this patient.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2** — Severity/trajectory and baseline reserve
- **2** — Age/procedure/airway risk
- **2** — Individual proceed/postpone reasoning
- **2** — Targeted tests/treatment without routine viral antibiotics
- **2** — Technique, recovery and informed communication

items.title: 41. On postoperative day 2 after hip surgery, a patient develops sudden dyspnoea, sy
items.q: On postoperative day 2 after hip surgery, a patient develops sudden dyspnoea, syncope, tachycardia and hypotension. Outline the diagnosis, severity assessment and initial management of suspected pulmonary embolism, including the implications of fresh surgery.
items.a:
### Immediate priorities and diagnosis
Call senior anaesthesia/ICU and the PE response/cardiology team; monitor, oxygenate, gain IV access and assess perfusion. Consider bleeding, MI, tamponade, pneumothorax, sepsis and anaphylaxis in parallel. PE acutely raises RV afterload, causing RV dilation/ischaemia, septal shift, reduced LV filling and obstructive shock. Avoid routine large-volume resuscitation; use small reassessed fluid only for demonstrated underfilling, and noradrenaline for poor perfusion.

If sufficiently stable, **CT pulmonary angiography** is usual definitive imaging. V/Q imaging can suit selected contrast-contraindicated patients. A postoperative D-dimer is often elevated and is poor for confirming PE; in high clinical probability do not use a negative screening pathway to delay imaging. Bedside TTE/TOE and compression venous ultrasound can support decisions when too unstable to transfer. RV strain/McConnell-type findings are not specific, and a negative focused scan does not exclude PE.

### Severity and triage
Assess BP trend and end-organ perfusion, oxygen/ventilatory requirement, RV imaging, troponin and clinical severity scores. Normotension alone does not exclude impending failure. The 2026 AHA/ACC scheme spans **A incidental/asymptomatic; B symptomatic low clinical severity; C symptomatic elevated severity; D incipient cardiopulmonary failure; E established cardiopulmonary failure**. Do not confuse this with SCAI cardiogenic-shock staging. Older ESC low/intermediate-low/intermediate-high/high terminology remains useful when named explicitly. This hypotensive postoperative patient needs monitored critical care and urgent reperfusion assessment.

### Anticoagulation and reperfusion
Anticoagulate promptly if PE is likely/confirmed and bleeding permits, with surgeon and PE-team input. LMWH suits many stable patients; UFH is often practical when rapid reversal/procedure or severe renal impairment is anticipated. This is **treatment dosing**, distinct from prophylaxis. Assess surgical haemostasis, neuraxial catheter, platelet count and renal function; document the drug/dose and monitoring plan.

Systemic thrombolysis can reverse high-risk PE but fresh major surgery creates major bleeding risk. Review contraindications and alternatives immediately: catheter-directed treatment/mechanical thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy may suit when thrombolysis is unsafe or unsuccessful. Do not give routine thrombolysis to every normotensive patient with RV strain. VA-ECMO can bridge selected refractory collapse in an expert centre, with a definitive clot-treatment strategy.

### Anaesthetic implications and follow-through
Intubation can precipitate RV collapse through vasodilation and positive-pressure loading; use experienced staff, preoxygenation, vasopressor support and a planned rescue route. Avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Use ECG, invasive pressure and repeat RV/perfusion assessment as appropriate.

After stabilisation, agree anticoagulant duration (usually at least three months, then individual risk review), education, mobilisation and follow-up for persistent dyspnoea/CTEPH. An IVC filter is selective for an important contraindication to anticoagulation, not a routine add-on.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains acute RV/obstructive-shock physiology and treats ABC/perfusion
- Uses definitive imaging when safe and bedside support when unstable
- Explains postoperative D-dimer and focused-echo limitations
- Assesses RV, biomarkers and clinical/perfusion severity; recognises normotensive deterioration
- Distinguishes treatment anticoagulation from prophylaxis and checks bleeding/neuraxial risk
- Weighs thrombolysis against fresh surgery and names catheter/surgical alternatives
- Anticipates induction/RV collapse and avoids unnecessary fluids/airway pressure
- Plans critical care, anticoagulant duration and persistent-symptom follow-up

**Evidence:** AHA/ACC acute PE guideline 2026; BJAEd POCUS in shock 2026; ASRA 2025; see source key and audit register.

items.title: 2026.2 Q8: Pathophysiology, diagnostic features and clinical management of fat em
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q8 · pass rate not available
items.q: Pathophysiology, diagnostic features and clinical management of fat embolism syndrome.
items.model:
**Pathophysiology.** Marrow fat enters the venous circulation after long-bone/pelvic trauma or manipulation, obstructing pulmonary microvessels and provoking endothelial injury. Fat breakdown/free fatty acids and inflammatory/coagulation activation add capillary leak and ARDS; systemic embolic/inflammatory effects produce neurological and skin manifestations, sometimes through a right-to-left shunt or passage through the pulmonary microcirculation. Distinguish common fat embolisation from the less frequent clinical syndrome.

**Diagnosis.** Suspect delayed deterioration, often 24–72 hours after injury, with hypoxaemia/respiratory distress, neurological change and an upper-body/conjunctival petechial rash; the full triad need not be present. Fever, tachycardia, falling Hb/platelets and retinal changes support it. Assess oxygenation, organ dysfunction, chest imaging and relevant neurological imaging, excluding thrombotic PE, aspiration, pneumonia, haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury. Gurd or other criteria can structure the assessment but no isolated laboratory finding confirms FES. Explain how the injury/timing and clinical pattern fit rather than merely listing a mnemonic.

**Management.** Stabilise airway, breathing and circulation, involve ICU and the trauma team, and give oxygen with timely protective ventilation when needed. Treat shock and concurrent injury, avoiding unnecessary fluid overload, maintain cerebral perfusion/oxygenation and monitor renal, neurological and haematological complications. Coordinate appropriate fracture stabilisation and minimise further embolic insult. Use VTE prophylaxis according to trauma/bleeding risk, but do not prescribe therapeutic heparin solely for fat emboli. Steroids are not established routine treatment; selected refractory ARDS may justify specialist extracorporeal rescue. Document trajectory and provide rehabilitation/support after survival.
rubric: **3** — Clinical pattern, timing and exclusion of mimics
**4** — Supportive organ care, fracture strategy and treatment limitations

items.title: 2026.2 Q13: Mechanisms of atelectasis during/after general anaesthesia (30%); prev
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q13 · pass rate not available
items.q: Mechanisms of atelectasis during/after general anaesthesia (30%); prevention strategies and rationale (70%).
items.model:
**Mechanisms, 30%.** Loss of respiratory muscle/diaphragmatic tone, supine position and cephalad diaphragmatic displacement reduce FRC; dependent airway closure occurs when closing capacity exceeds end-expiratory lung volume. Compression is amplified by obesity, abdominal distension, Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum. Denitrogenation with high FiO2 permits rapid gas absorption behind poorly ventilated or obstructed airways. Mucus/blood plugging and altered surfactant/surface tension add obstructive and adhesive mechanisms. Postoperative pain, splinting, residual drugs/NMBA, impaired cough and immobility maintain collapse. Perfusion of unventilated units produces shunt; repeated opening/closing adds atelectrauma, while overdistending open lung to compensate can produce VILI.

**Strategies and rationale, 70%.** Identify high-risk patients, optimise obstructive disease/infection, support smoking cessation and preoperative physiotherapy/inspiratory training where suitable. Plan less invasive surgery and regional/opioid-sparing analgesia to preserve cough and deep breathing. Preoxygenate effectively for safety, head-up/ramped where appropriate; selected CPAP/PEEP can limit collapse in patients with reduced reserve. Do not compromise an airway safety margin merely to lower FiO2.

During GA use 6–8 mL/kg predicted-weight tidal volumes with individual PEEP, monitor plateau/driving pressure and delivered volume, and avoid zero/insufficient PEEP where collapse is likely. Adjust to compliance, oxygenation and haemodynamics rather than prescribing universal high PEEP. A recruitment manoeuvre is selective treatment for likely recruitable collapse after excluding dangerous causes; prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres can cause harm. Minimise avoidable disconnections. Titrate oxygen to an appropriate target once the airway is safe, maintain normothermia and adequate perfusion without overload, and avoid unnecessary prolonged paralysis.

Before extubation confirm quantitative NMBA recovery and adequate airway/ventilatory function. Use awake head-up recovery when appropriate, effective analgesia, early mobilisation, coached deep breathing/coughing and secretion clearance. Investigate persistent hypoxaemia rather than assuming atelectasis. Lung ultrasound can identify consolidation/effusion and follow response, with CXR/CT when needed. Use CPAP/NIV for appropriate postoperative respiratory failure and prophylaxis in selected high-risk/PAP-dependent patients; routine prophylactic CPAP for all major abdominal cases has not reduced important outcomes. HFNC can support oxygenation but cannot guarantee ventilation or prevent all atelectasis. Incentive spirometry alone is not an established complete prevention programme.
rubric: **3** — Compression, absorption, obstruction/surfactant and postoperative mechanisms
**3** — Protective ventilation, individual PEEP/oxygen and recruitment cautions
**2** — Recovery, mobilisation, targeted respiratory support and assessment

items.title: 2026.2 Q15: Severe hypoxaemia during VATS lobectomy on one-lung ventilation throug
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q15 · pass rate not available
items.q: Severe hypoxaemia during VATS lobectomy on one-lung ventilation through a double-lumen ETT.
items.model:
Tell the surgeon immediately, stop hazardous manipulation, give FiO2 1.0 and verify the saturation waveform, pulse and perfusion. With severe or rapidly worsening hypoxaemia, restore two-lung ventilation in coordination with the surgeon while obtaining senior assistance. Oxygenation takes priority over maintaining the surgical view.

Check oxygen supply/circuit and DLT connections, clamps, kinks and secretions. Use flexible bronchoscopy to confirm and correct DLT position, including after patient positioning or surgical traction; assess both lumens and the ventilated bronchus. Suction blood/mucus and verify delivered volumes, capnography and airway pressures. Exclude tension pneumothorax in the dependent lung, major haemorrhage, embolism and RV failure; use examination and ultrasound/echo, and treat tension physiology immediately. Take an ABG and Hb, but do not wait for results before rescue.

Once the airway and circulation are satisfactory and OLV is resumed, optimise the dependent lung with low predicted-weight tidal volumes and individually titrated PEEP, avoiding overdistension that diverts perfusion to the non-ventilated lung. Consider cautious recruitment only in a suitable stable patient with likely reversible collapse. Treat bronchospasm and maintain cardiac output, Hb and perfusion; both very low mixed-venous oxygen and excessive airway pressure can worsen oxygenation. Avoid unnecessary inhibition of HPV but do not claim that all modern volatile anaesthesia must be stopped.

With the surgeon, apply low CPAP/oxygen to the non-ventilated lung if compatible with VATS exposure, or use intermittent two-lung ventilation. Persistent hypoxaemia may require alteration of the operation or specialist surgical manoeuvres such as pulmonary-artery occlusion to the operative lung where appropriate. Reassess causes and consider abandoning unsafe OLV. Plan postoperative critical care according to cause and residual gas exchange; communicate and document the event.

Prevention includes reviewing reserve and anticipated OLV risk, bronchoscopic DLT confirmation before/after turning, suitable protective settings and a shared hypoxaemia rescue plan. Fixed high PEEP and repeated recruitment are not proven universal prophylaxis: PROTHOR did not significantly improve its primary pulmonary-complication outcome.
rubric: **3** — Immediate oxygenation, surgeon communication and two-lung rescue
**3** — Bronchoscopic device correction and life-threatening alternatives
**2** — CPAP/intermittent two-lung and definitive surgical/disposition decisions

items.title: 2025.2 Q1: Outline management of respiratory distress on the ward three days afte
items.q: Outline management of respiratory distress on the ward three days after tracheostomy formation during radical base-of-tongue resection.
items.model:
Call the emergency/airway team and ENT surgeon, take the emergency tracheostomy equipment and apply high-flow oxygen to BOTH face and stoma while assessing breathing and pulse. Check the bedhead information, operation, tracheostomy type/size, upper-airway patency, reason for the tracheostomy and last known function. This is a fresh tract: blind reinsertion can create a false passage and surgical emphysema.

Remove any speaking valve/cap and inner cannula. Check waveform capnography and attempt to pass a suction catheter beyond the tube tip. Suction if it passes, but a passing catheter does not by itself exclude every partial malposition or other respiratory cause. If it will not pass, suspect blockage or displacement; do not repeatedly force positive-pressure ventilation through a potentially misplaced tube. Deflate the cuff and reassess airflow through mouth and stoma. If patency is not restored, remove the non-functioning tube promptly according to the tracheostomy emergency algorithm.

If oxygenation remains inadequate, use the route that is anatomically available. For a patent upper airway, bag-mask or supraglottic ventilation with the stoma occluded can be used; oral intubation may be difficult after tongue surgery and must be planned with ENT and difficult-airway backup. For stoma ventilation, use a paediatric face mask or an appropriate supraglottic device over the stoma with a seal. Expert endoscopic-guided intubation of the stoma may be needed; advance only far enough for the cuff to lie in the trachea, confirm waveform CO2 and avoid endobronchial placement. In a laryngectomy patient, the mouth is not a route to the lungs; establish whether this is a tracheostomy rather than assuming anatomy.

Once ventilation is established evaluate mucus plugging, displacement, bleeding/clot, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, pneumonia, aspiration, bronchospasm, pulmonary oedema and PE. Major bleeding needs simultaneous haemorrhage control and airway management with urgent surgical help; consider tracheo-innominate fistula, including a preceding sentinel bleed. Obtain gas, imaging and bronchoscopy as clinically appropriate, arrange ICU/theatre, secure the definitive airway, document and debrief. Later prevention includes humidification, inner-cannula/suction care, secure ties, spare tubes and a clearly recorded emergency plan.
rubric: **2** — Calls help; oxygen to face/stoma and identifies anatomy
**2** — Removes attachments/inner cannula and checks patency
**2** — Deflates cuff/removes ineffective tube without dangerous repeated bagging
**3** — Safe alternative oxygenation with fresh-tract precautions

items.title: 2025.1 Q7: Evaluate the utility of venous blood gas measurement.
items.q: Evaluate the utility of venous blood gas measurement.
items.model:
VBG is a rapid, less painful and often easier assessment of acid–base state when an arterial sample is unnecessary or unavailable. Specify whether peripheral, central or mixed venous; site, tourniquet, tissue metabolism and perfusion influence values. It is particularly useful for initial acid–base assessment and serial trends in suitable patients, but is not a complete substitute for ABG.

Peripheral venous pH is usually slightly lower and bicarbonate close to arterial values, so VBG can identify clinically important metabolic acidosis/alkalosis and support serial assessment, for example in ketoacidosis. Small average biases do not guarantee narrow individual agreement, especially in shock or severe derangement. Interpret with electrolytes, anion gap, lactate, history and expected compensation rather than the pH alone.

PvCO2 is usually higher than PaCO2, but the difference is variable. A reassuring venous value can sometimes help screen for important hypercapnia within a validated clinical pathway. An elevated PvCO2 does not accurately quantify PaCO2: obtain ABG when precise ventilatory assessment, acute respiratory-failure severity, NIV decisions or response requires it, particularly with shock or discordant clinical findings.

PvO2 cannot determine arterial oxygenation: it reflects extraction and local blood flow. Use reliable pulse oximetry for saturation trends and ABG/co-oximetry for PaO2, severe hypoxaemia, saturation discordance or dyshemoglobinaemia. Central venous oxygen saturation can contribute to assessment of supply–demand balance but is not peripheral venous saturation, is not identical to mixed venous saturation and does not exclude regional tissue hypoxia when normal.

Venous lactate can identify a clinically important elevation and follow trends, but arterial and venous lactate are not always interchangeable. Explain sampling/analysis quality, time to analysis and serial consistency. The main utility is acid–base and selected CO2/lactate assessment, not simply the analyser's ability to report glucose or potassium.
rubric: **2** — Practical benefits and appropriate clinical uses
**2** — PvCO2 versus PaCO2 and when ABG is needed

items.title: 2024.2 Q4: Outline the assessment and immediate management of a patient in the po
items.q: Outline the assessment and immediate management of a patient in the post anaesthesia care unit (PACU) with respiratory failure after emergency open abdominal surgery.
items.model:
## Immediate approach: assess and treat together

Call for help early. Apply **high-flow oxygen** (non-rebreather mask or HFNC), sit the patient up if haemodynamically safe, apply monitoring (SpO2, ECG, NIBP, capnography), and check **airway, breathing (rate, effort, auscultation), circulation, disability (sedation score, glucose) and exposure** (temperature, wound, abdomen).

## Differential diagnosis (emergency abdominal surgery)

- **Airway**: obstruction (tongue, laryngospasm, secretions, oedema, haematoma), aspiration.
- **Central/pharmacological**: residual **neuromuscular block**, opioid and sedative effect, hypoventilation, OSA.
- **Pulmonary**: **atelectasis**, pain-limited breathing (splinting), pneumonia/aspiration, **pulmonary oedema** (fluid overload, cardiac), **bronchospasm**, pneumothorax, pleural effusion, **ARDS**, pulmonary embolism, TRALI.
- **Abdominal**: distension, **raised intra-abdominal pressure**, ascites, diaphragmatic splinting.
- **Cardiac and systemic**: myocardial ischaemia, sepsis, anaemia, metabolic acidosis.

## Investigations

**ABG** (type 1 versus type 2 failure, lactate), **chest X-ray**, **ECG** and troponin if indicated, FBC, electrolytes, glucose, **point-of-care ultrasound** (lung, heart, IVC), quantitative TOF (neuromuscular), and CT if PE or abdominal cause suspected.

## Immediate management

- **Oxygen** titrated to SpO2 above 92% (88–92% in hypercapnic COPD); **HFNC or NIV (CPAP/BiPAP)** for atelectasis, oedema and fatigue, unless contraindicated (vomiting, anastomosis concerns, reduced consciousness).
- **Reverse**: sugammadex/neostigmine for residual block, **naloxone** titrated for opioid effect (small doses to preserve analgesia), treat bronchospasm, drain tension pneumothorax.
- **Analgesia**: effective multimodal and regional (epidural, TAP, wound catheter) to permit deep breathing and coughing; physiotherapy.
- **Treat the cause**: diuretic for oedema, antibiotics for pneumonia/sepsis, decompress the abdomen, therapeutic anticoagulation for PE.
- **Escalate**: failure to improve, worsening acidosis, exhaustion or reduced consciousness → **reintubation and ICU**.

## Disposition

Post-PACU care in **ICU/HDU** with continuous monitoring, documented ceilings of care, and handover to the intensive care team.

> **Examiner's point:** show logical steps of escalation, with simultaneous assessment and management, a differential specific to the context, and the plan for disposition.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Systematic assessment with simultaneous oxygen therapy
Differential diagnosis specific to emergency abdominal surgery
Reversal of drug effects and analgesia

items.title: 2024.2 Q9: Discuss the perioperative management of a patient with severe asthma w
items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of a patient with severe asthma who is scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy in two weeks' time.
items.model:
## Preoperative (two weeks lead time)

- **Assess control**: frequency of symptoms, nocturnal waking, reliever use, recent exacerbations, steroid courses, **ICU admissions or intubations** (the strongest risk marker), triggers (NSAIDs, aspirin-exacerbated disease, allergy), and current treatment.
- **Examination and tests**: wheeze, peak flow or spirometry (FEV1 and reversibility), pulse oximetry; ABG and chest X-ray only if indicated.
- **Optimise now**: ensure inhaled corticosteroid–LABA adherence and technique, treat infection, stop smoking, and if poorly controlled or FEV1 below 80% predicted, **a short oral prednisolone course (e.g. 30–40 mg for 5–7 days)** or step-up therapy in conjunction with respiratory physician; **postpone** if there is an active exacerbation or infection.
- **Consent and plan**: discuss risks (bronchospasm, postoperative pulmonary complications), continue all inhalers including on the morning of surgery, and **hydrocortisone cover** if on chronic oral steroids.
- **Premedication**: bronchodilator (salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulised or 4–8 puffs) before induction; anxiolysis if needed.

## Intraoperative

- **Technique**: avoid airway instrumentation where possible, but laparoscopy needs **GA with an ETT**; ensure **adequate depth** before laryngoscopy, with **propofol or ketamine** (bronchodilator) and **lidocaine/opioid** to blunt reflexes. A second-generation supraglottic airway can be suitable in selected fasted laparoscopic patients; choose a cuffed ETT here according to severe asthma, ventilation requirements, aspiration risk and access rather than a blanket prohibition.
- **Avoid triggers**: histamine-releasing drugs (morphine, atracurium, mivacurium), beta-blockers, NSAIDs (aspirin-sensitive), desflurane; prefer **sevoflurane** (bronchodilator) or propofol TIVA.
- **Ventilation strategy**: tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg, **low respiratory rate, prolonged expiratory time (I:E 1:3 to 1:4)**, minimal PEEP, avoid dynamic hyperinflation (watch the flow–time curve), accept **permissive hypercapnia**; low-pressure pneumoperitoneum to limit CO2 load; head-up (reverse Trendelenburg) is favourable.
- **Bronchospasm**: 100% oxygen, deepen anaesthesia, disconnect to release air trapping, salbutamol, ipratropium, IV magnesium 2 g, hydrocortisone, ketamine, adrenaline for severe; exclude anaphylaxis, tube obstruction and pneumothorax.
- **Reversal**: sugammadex (avoids neostigmine and atropine effects); extubate awake or deep depending on the plan.

## Postoperative

Multimodal analgesia (paracetamol, local anaesthetic, avoid NSAIDs if sensitive; judicious opioids), continue inhalers, early mobilisation and physiotherapy, supplemental oxygen, and monitoring for bronchospasm, with an HDU bed if brittle asthma.

> **Examiner's point:** include pre-, intra- and postoperative factors; ventilation strategy and postoperative care were often omitted.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Do not start oral steroids solely because FEV1 is below an arbitrary 80% cutoff: assess current control, recent exacerbations and respiratory-team advice. Systemic steroid supplementation depends on adrenal-suppression risk and procedure stress. Avoid deep extubation in a patient with aspiration risk or difficult airway without a clear rescue plan. Quantitative TOF recovery remains necessary whichever reversal agent is selected. GINA 2026 uses a titrated 92–95% adult acute-asthma oxygen target; brief 100% oxygen remains appropriate during a hypoxic airway emergency.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Assessment of asthma control and risk markers
Optimisation within two weeks (inhalers, steroids, postpone if unwell)
Induction and drug choices to avoid triggers
Ventilation strategy to avoid air trapping

items.title: 2024.1 Q9: Perioperative analgesia for a 20 kg four-year-old undergoing elective
items.source: Past SAQ 2024.1 Q9 · pass rate not available
items.q: Perioperative analgesia for a 20 kg four-year-old undergoing elective adenotonsillectomy.
items.model:
Assess expected tonsillectomy pain, OSA severity, previous analgesic exposure, allergies, hydration/renal function, bleeding history and family ability to give medicines. Agree an analgesia/antiemesis and monitored recovery plan with ENT and parents. OSA changes opioid safety, but the answer must still treat pain: inadequate analgesia impairs drinking, sleep and recovery.

Use regular paracetamol; an example oral dose is 15 mg/kg (300 mg for 20 kg), with interval and daily maximum verified against the local paediatric formulary and all combination products counted. Use ibuprofen when appropriate under local tonsillectomy guidance; an example oral dose is 10 mg/kg (200 mg), with local interval/maximum and contraindications checked, especially dehydration, renal dysfunction, NSAID sensitivity or relevant bleeding concerns. Do not infer that all NSAIDs are contraindicated merely because this is tonsil surgery. A single intraoperative dexamethasone dose provides antiemetic and modest analgesic benefit; verify local dose, maximum and patient factors rather than mixing incompatible regimens.

If pain is not controlled, titrate a small IV opioid dose to observed response in a monitored setting, reducing exposure in significant OSA; reassess respiratory rate, sedation, airway obstruction and oxygenation. Have naloxone and airway rescue available. Avoid codeine and tramadol after tonsillectomy in children. Consider selected adjuncts such as dexmedetomidine or low-dose ketamine with an experienced paediatric anaesthetist, balancing sedation and recovery; local infiltration has limited/variable benefit and must avoid toxicity/injection complications.

Prevent/treat nausea, provide appropriate fluids and a clear take-home regular non-opioid regimen with written dose/interval/maximum instructions. Explain administration, pain with swallowing, hydration targets, bleeding signs and when to seek care. Persistent pain, inability to drink, opioid-related obstruction/sedation or recurrent desaturation changes disposition. Significant OSA or complications may require overnight monitored admission. Do not discharge simply because supplemental oxygen normalises saturation.
rubric: **2** — Safe rescue opioid/adjuncts and contraindicated drugs

items.title: 2024.1 Q15: Describe the assessment and management of suspected pneumothorax in PA
items.q: Describe the assessment and management of suspected pneumothorax in PACU following a paravertebral block for mastectomy.
items.model:
Attend immediately, call senior assistance and inform the surgeon. Give oxygen, monitor ECG/SpO2/BP, obtain IV access and assess airway, respiratory effort, consciousness and perfusion together. Severe respiratory compromise or shock makes tension pneumothorax a clinical emergency: decompress without waiting for radiography, using the fastest appropriate technique and trained operator, then establish definitive pleural drainage.

Establish timing after the block, pleuritic pain, breathlessness, cough, block technique, ventilation and baseline lung disease. Examine both hemithoraces, chest expansion, air entry and the block/surgical side. Tracheal deviation and raised venous pressure are late or unreliable signs; their absence does not exclude tension. Consider alternative or concurrent bronchospasm, aspiration, atelectasis, pulmonary oedema, PE, opioid depression, local-anaesthetic toxicity and haemorrhage.

In a stable patient obtain lung ultrasound and an erect CXR if possible. Absent sliding alone is not diagnostic; a lung point supports pneumothorax, while sliding/B-lines/lung pulse exclude it only where seen. CT may resolve uncertainty in a stable patient but must not delay urgent treatment. Check an ABG if significant hypoxaemia/ventilatory failure, Hb if bleeding and ECG as indicated.

Management depends on symptoms, physiology, size, evolution, underlying disease and anticipated positive-pressure ventilation. A small stable iatrogenic pneumothorax may be observed with oxygen when needed and repeat assessment/imaging under an appropriate protocol. Larger, symptomatic, progressive or ventilated cases generally need aspiration or a drain after specialist discussion; do not apply spontaneous-pneumothorax rules uncritically. Provide analgesia, monitor for re-expansion oedema, confirm drain function/position and document an admission and review plan.

Explain the complication candidly to the patient, document the procedure and event, perform open disclosure and arrange follow-up. A drain must be secured, patent and safely managed during transfer; avoid routine clamping of an ongoing air leak.
rubric: **2** — Recognises severity and treats tension immediately

items.q: Clinical features of PE under general anaesthesia (30%) and immediate management (70%).
items.model:
**Features, 30%.** Suspect PE with a sudden otherwise unexplained ETCO2 decrease/widened PaCO2–ETCO2 gradient, hypoxaemia, tachycardia, hypotension and acute RV strain or PEA. ECG may show new right-heart changes; high CVP, echo RV dilatation/dysfunction and septal flattening support the diagnosis but are not specific. Symptoms such as chest pain and dyspnoea are masked by anaesthesia. Absence of hypoxaemia or S1Q3T3 does not exclude PE.

**Management, 70%.** Call for help, tell the surgeon, pause the procedure and give oxygen while supporting ventilation and perfusion. Exclude disconnection, tube obstruction, pneumothorax, haemorrhage, anaphylaxis and gas embolism; maintain continuous capnography/ECG/SpO2, frequent or invasive BP and obtain blood gases/lactate. Use focused TTE/TOE and venous ultrasound if unstable; obtain CTPA only if stable enough and it will guide treatment. Do not move a collapsing patient merely for confirmation.

Support RV perfusion with carefully titrated noradrenaline and an individual inotrope if low output persists. Avoid excessive fluid loading of an overloaded RV; give a small reassessed fluid challenge only when underfilling is likely. Prevent hypoxia, severe hypercapnic acidosis and excessive mean airway pressure. Intubation can precipitate collapse: prepare haemodynamic support and an expert plan if not already intubated.

Discuss immediately with PE/ICU/cardiology and surgical teams. Anticoagulate when appropriate after evaluating operative bleeding, often with a readily titratable/reversible agent if intervention is likely. Shock, arrest or impending failure needs urgent consideration of reperfusion—systemic thrombolysis, catheter intervention or surgical embolectomy—balancing bleeding and availability. Recent surgery may make alternatives preferable but must not produce therapeutic paralysis in a dying patient. If arrest occurs follow ALS and consider PE-specific reperfusion and specialist extracorporeal rescue. Normotensive RV strain/troponin elevation alone does not warrant routine thrombolysis.

Arrange ICU, definitive imaging when stable, anticoagulation/reperfusion follow-through and communication/documentation. The 2026 AHA/ACC categories recognise incipient failure as well as persistent shock; use the physiology to escalate before arrest rather than relying only on a BP threshold.
rubric: **3** — Low ETCO2, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxaemia and masked signs
items.title: 2023.2 Q7: List the clinical features that suggest a diagnosis of pulmonary embol
2023.2 Q10: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of supranormal oxygen levels
items.q: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of supranormal oxygen levels in the perioperative setting.
items.model:
## Definition

Supranormal oxygen means **FiO2 above that needed to maintain normal saturation**, producing **hyperoxia** (an elevated arterial oxygen tension; thresholds vary by context and do not require an FiO2 of 0.8).

## Potential benefits

- **Surgical site infection**: higher tissue oxygen tension supports neutrophil oxidative killing; early trials (Greif 2000) showed lower SSI with 80% oxygen, but later large trials (PROXI, 2009) and meta-analyses are **inconsistent**, with recent guidelines (WHO) recommending it but evidence heterogeneous.
- **Safety margin/reservoir**: preoxygenation extends apnoea time and buys time in airway emergencies or sudden desaturation.
- **Reduced PONV** (small effect, inconsistent).
- **Treat specific conditions**: carbon monoxide poisoning, air or gas embolism, decompression illness, severe anaemia, pneumothorax resorption.
- **Pulmonary vasodilatation** and reduced pulmonary vascular resistance (neonatal, pulmonary hypertension).

## Potential risks

- **Absorption atelectasis** (nitrogen washout) with reduced FRC, shunt, and postoperative pulmonary complications; **reduced mucociliary clearance**.
- **Oxygen toxicity**: reactive oxygen species, lung injury with prolonged exposure (FiO2 above 0.6 for over 24 hours), tracheobronchitis, ARDS-like injury.
- **Cardiovascular**: coronary and systemic vasoconstriction, reduced cardiac output; **harm in myocardial infarction** (AVOID suggested possible harm, while DETO2X did not show a mortality benefit from routine oxygen in non-hypoxaemic MI; current guidance is to give oxygen only if SpO2 below 90–94%); possible increased mortality in meta-analyses of hyperoxia in sepsis and cardiac arrest.
- **Late detection of deterioration**: high FiO2 masks hypoventilation and shunt (a normal SpO2 despite worsening lung disease); **hypercapnia in COPD** (V/Q redistribution and the Haldane effect, with a variable contribution from hypoventilation).
- **Retinopathy of prematurity** in neonates, **fire risk** in the airway and theatre, **bleomycin and paraquat** toxicity, and **neurological** effects (cerebral vasoconstriction; possible harm after stroke or cardiac arrest).
- **Potential increase in mortality**: a meta-analysis (Chu 2018) linked liberal oxygen therapy in acutely ill adults to higher mortality.

## Balance

Use **titrated oxygen** with a target SpO2 (94–98%, 88–92% for hypercapnia), reserve high FiO2 for **preoxygenation, emergencies and specific indications**, and wean promptly. The benefit for SSI is modest and uncertain, while risks of absorption atelectasis and late detection are real.

> **Examiner's point:** list five significant risks or benefits with brief explanation, discuss controversy, and reconcile the safety reservoir benefit with the risk of late detection of problems.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Hyperoxia is elevated arterial oxygen tension; its definition is context dependent and it does not require FiO2 ≥0.8. PaO2 and FiO2 are not interchangeable. Oxygen-related hypercapnia in COPD mainly reflects V/Q redistribution and the Haldane effect, with variable hypoventilation; avoid the simplistic claim that loss of hypoxic drive is the main mechanism. AVOID suggested possible harm whereas DETO2X did not show a mortality benefit from routine oxygen in non-hypoxaemic MI; do not describe both as proving harm. There is no abrupt universally safe/unsafe FiO2-duration boundary. Prescribe an individual target and reassess clinical perfusion and ventilation.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Surgical site infection evidence and controversy
Masking deterioration and hypercapnia in COPD

items.title: 2023.1 Q15: Label spirometry-loop axes A/B and points C–H; changes in COPD, IPF an
items.q: Label spirometry-loop axes A/B and points C–H; changes in COPD, IPF and extrathoracic tracheal obstruction.
items.model:
The original diagram was inspected rather than reconstructing letters from memory. **A** is flow (L/s), positive for expiration and negative for inspiration. **B** is volume (L); this drawing increases expired volume to the right. **C** is the effort-dependent ascending expiratory limb. **D** is peak expiratory flow. **E** is the descending expiratory limb, progressively limited by airway dynamics. **F** marks the end of forced expiration (the FVC endpoint on this volume convention; absolute lung volume is RV). **G** is peak inspiratory flow. **H** is the horizontal vital-capacity excursion. The same physiology can be drawn with an absolute-lung-volume axis reversed; label the displayed convention, not a memorised orientation.

**COPD:** reduced expiratory peak, a concave/scooped descending limb and reduced FEV1/FVC. Dynamic compression can make FVC less than slow VC; RV and TLC may rise with air trapping/hyperinflation. DLCO falls in emphysema but may be preserved in other obstructive patterns. **IPF:** reduced TLC and FVC with preserved or increased FEV1/FVC; the loop is small/narrow, often relatively tall for its volume, and DLCO usually falls. Low FVC alone cannot prove restriction. **Variable extrathoracic obstruction:** flattening/limitation of the inspiratory limb because negative intraluminal pressure tends to narrow the extrathoracic airway; expiratory flow is relatively preserved. Fixed obstruction can flatten both limbs and must not be conflated with variable extrathoracic obstruction.

Check manoeuvre quality, reproducibility and clinical context. A loop suggests a physiological pattern and cannot by itself localise every lesion or establish a diagnosis without history, imaging or endoscopy. Explain the mechanism behind each change rather than only naming the disease.
rubric: **4** — Correct displayed axes/units and C–H interpretation
**2** — Variable extrathoracic inspiratory flattening versus fixed obstruction

items.title: 2021.2 Q3: Persistent SpO2 82% immediately after intubation for severe bacterial
items.q: Persistent SpO2 82% immediately after intubation for severe bacterial pneumonia; actions and oxygenation pending retrieval.
items.model:
Call senior/ICU/retrieval help immediately, give FiO2 1.0, verify oxygen supply and hand-ventilate while checking waveform CO2, chest expansion, tube depth and pulse/pressure. Treat as a real emergency while checking the saturation signal. Rapidly exclude oesophageal/endobronchial intubation, displacement, tube/filter/circuit obstruction, disconnection and tension pneumothorax. Pass suction, use bronchoscopy/ultrasound if available and decompress tension physiology without awaiting imaging. Use an independent bag and oxygen source to isolate equipment failure.

Obtain an ABG, assess the arterial–end-tidal gradient and calculate P/F with known FiO2; CXR or lung ultrasound and bedside echo assess pneumonia/ARDS, collapse, oedema, effusion and ventricular function. Restore haemodynamic perfusion, recognising that excessive PEEP or fluids can worsen the situation. Check haemoglobin and sepsis treatment.

If severe intrapulmonary shunt remains, ventilate protectively at about 6 mL/kg predicted weight, reducing volume if plateau is excessive, and individualise PEEP to oxygenation, mechanics and circulation. Avoid aggressive prolonged recruitment. Ensure sedation/analgesia and consider a short NMBA course if severe dyssynchrony prevents safe ventilation. Use early prolonged prone positioning when moderate/severe ARDS persists and a trained team can do it safely; arrange retrieval around the effective respiratory strategy. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilator may be a temporary bridge where available, with no proven survival benefit; discuss early ECMO referral for refractory potentially reversible failure.

Give appropriate antibiotics promptly after samples when feasible, manage sepsis and drain a complicated pleural collection. After resuscitation avoid fluid overload. Confirm retrieval staffing, ventilator capability, oxygen/battery reserve and contingency before transfer; do not dismantle effective support merely to fit an inadequate transport system. Reassess continuously and communicate current settings, gases, airway, pressors and escalation plan.
rubric: **3** — Justified protective ventilation, PEEP and rescue

items.title: 2021.1 Q9: Evaluate the equipment available for the delivery of oxygen to postope
items.q: Evaluate the equipment available for the delivery of oxygen to postoperative patients on a general surgical ward.
items.model:
## Classification

**Variable performance (low-flow) devices**: FiO2 depends on flow, tidal volume and respiratory rate (the patient entrains room air).
