**Fixed performance (high-flow) devices**: delivered flow exceeds peak inspiratory flow, so FiO2 is stable.

## Devices

| Device | Flow and FiO2 | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nasal prongs (cannulae)** | 1–4 L/min; FiO2 about 0.24–0.40 | Comfortable, allows eating and talking, cheap, good compliance | Variable FiO2, nasal drying above 4 L/min, effect may vary with breathing pattern; nasal obstruction impairs delivery |
| **Simple (Hudson) face mask** | 5–10 L/min; about 0.35–0.60 | Higher FiO2 than prongs, simple | Needs minimum 5 L/min to flush CO2 (rebreathing), variable FiO2, claustrophobic, interferes with eating, drinking and communication |
| **Non-rebreather (reservoir) mask** | 10–15 L/min; up to 0.80–0.90 | Highest FiO2 on the ward, emergency use | Needs a good seal and flow to keep the reservoir inflated; variable; not suited to long-term use |
| **Venturi mask** | Fixed FiO2 of 0.24–0.60 with colour-coded valves (e.g. 24%, 28%, 35%, 40% at 2–15 L/min) | **Precise FiO2** by air entrainment, suited to COPD and CO2 retention | Noisy, requires correct flow settings; entrainment ratio fixed, total flow often below peak inspiratory flow at high FiO2 |
| **High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC)** | 20–60 L/min; FiO2 0.21–1.0 | Warmed, humidified; washes out dead space; low-level PEEP (about 3–5 cmH2O); comfortable | Cost, needs trained staff and supply, may delay escalation, usually limited to HDU/ward-based protocols |
| **Humidified systems and tracheostomy masks** | Variable | Comfort for prolonged therapy | Equipment and infection control |

**Other**: oxygen source (wall outlet, cylinder, concentrator), flow meters, humidification, and **monitoring**: SpO2, escalation protocols, and **safety** (oxygen alerts, fire risk, no smoking, cylinder security). CPAP and BiPAP lie beyond a general ward (HDU).

## Evaluation

Choose by required FiO2, risk of CO2 retention, need for humidity, patient comfort, and staff skills. Start low-flow (prongs) for most; **Venturi** for COPD; **non-rebreather** for the acutely hypoxic while awaiting review; HFNC if available. Targets: SpO2 94–98%, or 88–92% if hypercapnic risk. Pitfall: unmonitored high-flow oxygen masks hypoventilation.

> **Examiner's point:** the non-rebreather mask was most often omitted, and the Venturi mask the least understood. Differentiate variable from fixed delivery and quote realistic FiO2 and flows.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Device FiO2 figures are approximate and depend on demand, fit and manufacturer. Mouth breathing does not render standard nasal oxygen ineffective. A Venturi system is fixed-performance only when its total flow meets inspiratory demand and entrainment ports are unobstructed; jet entrainment involves momentum transfer, not a simplistic Bernoulli explanation alone. Follow the labelled valve flow, not a universal colour/flow table. HFNC pressure and FiO2 are variable with leak and demand; HFNC and NIV require an appropriately staffed location and escalation protocol, which may include a designated ward service.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Nasal prongs flows, FiO2, pros and cons
Simple mask minimum flow and rebreathing
High-flow nasal cannula as an option

items.title: 2019.2 Q6: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of non-invasive ventilation m
items.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of non-invasive ventilation methods in the intensive care unit.
items.model:
## Methods (to interpret the question both ways)

**CPAP** (single pressure, no inspiratory support), **bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP: IPAP/EPAP, pressure support)**, **volume-targeted/assured modes**, **proportional-assist ventilation (PAV) and NAVA**, **high-flow nasal oxygen** (not strictly NIV), and interfaces: oronasal mask, full-face mask, nasal mask, **helmet**.

## Advantages of NIV (versus intubation)

- **Avoids intubation** and its complications: airway trauma, sedation, **VAP**, haemodynamic collapse, delirium, ventilator weaning difficulty.
- May preserve spontaneous cough and communication, but **does not protect the airway**; swallowing/intake need assessment and planned breaks.
- Reduces **mortality and intubation rate** in selected groups: **acute COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic acidosis (strong evidence)**, **cardiogenic pulmonary oedema**, selected immunocompromised patients (benefit is context-dependent), post-extubation prophylaxis in high-risk patients, and OSA/obesity hypoventilation; useful in chest wall trauma and as a **palliative or ceiling-of-care** option.
- Easy to apply and titrate, intermittent use possible, and lower costs and ICU stay.

## Disadvantages

- **Needs a cooperative, conscious patient with intact airway reflexes**, and **no airway protection**: aspiration risk; unsuitable for vomiting, bowel obstruction or reduced GCS.
- **Failure and delayed intubation** worsen outcomes (late intubation of a fatigued patient is hazardous), so close monitoring is essential.
- **Interface problems**: leak, pressure sores, skin necrosis, claustrophobia, conjunctivitis, gastric distension, intolerance, and air swallowing.
- **Physiological**: hyperinflation, barotrauma, hypotension (reduced preload), and less reliable delivery of tidal volume and PEEP; cannot control ventilation precisely.
- **Contraindications**: respiratory arrest, **untreated pneumothorax**, life-threatening hypoxaemia, haemodynamic instability, facial trauma or surgery, severe encephalopathy, upper GI surgery or bleeding.
- Staff time, expertise, and aerosolisation risk in infectious disease.

## Differences between modes

CPAP is simple and effective in oedema; BiPAP assists ventilation and reduces CO2 in COPD; helmets tolerate high pressures with less leak; PAV/NAVA improve synchrony but need expertise.

> **Examiner's point:** advantages (avoids intubation, groups that benefit) and disadvantages (cooperation, no airway protection, contraindications) were the core, and the different modes may also be compared.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

NIV does not secure the airway, even if the patient can cough or speak. Oral intake usually needs interruption or a planned break. Do not generalise a mortality benefit to every immunocompromised patient or to de novo hypoxaemic failure. Compare CPAP/bilevel pressure and mask/helmet interfaces explicitly; NAVA via an ETT is invasive, although NIV-capable NAVA systems exist. NIV prophylaxis after extubation differs from rescue NIV in established post-extubation failure, which can delay reintubation.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Avoidance of intubation and associated complications
Patient groups with evidence of benefit
Need for cooperation and airway protection absent
Comparison of CPAP, BiPAP and other modes

items.title: 2018.1 Q10: Describe the physiological effects of a high-flow nasal cannula device
items.q: Describe the physiological effects of a high-flow nasal cannula device (HFNC) e.g. Optiflow or Airvo. (50%) Justify its use in an adult endoscopy suite. (50%)
items.model:
## Physiological effects (50%)

HFNC delivers **heated (37 degrees) and humidified (44 mg/L) oxygen–air mix at 20–70 L/min** through wide nasal prongs. Effects:
- **Washout of anatomical dead space** in the nasopharynx, reducing rebreathing and improving CO2 clearance and alveolar ventilation.
- **Generation of low-level positive airway pressure** (about 3–7 cmH2O at 30–60 L/min with the mouth closed; less with open mouth), improving **FRC, alveolar recruitment, compliance and oxygenation**, and reducing atelectasis.
- **Stable FiO2** (flow exceeds peak inspiratory flow, avoiding air entrainment), so a precise FiO2 up to 1.0.
- **Reduced work of breathing** (reduced upper airway resistance, dead space, and inspiratory demand) and fewer respiratory rate.
- **Humidification** improves mucociliary clearance, comfort and tolerance, reduces airway drying and bronchospasm.
- **Apnoeic oxygenation** (THRIVE: transnasal humidified rapid-insufflation ventilatory exchange): continued oxygen delivery during apnoea, extending the oxygenation window while CO2 still rises; cardiogenic mixing does not guarantee adequate ventilation.

## Justification in the endoscopy suite (50%)

- **Safer sedation**: endoscopy (especially upper GI, ERCP, bronchoscopy) with sedation risks airway obstruction and hypoxia; HFNC **increases the margin of safety** with lower desaturation rates (RCTs in gastroscopy and bronchoscopy).
- **Preoxygenation** before induction and **apnoeic oxygenation** during intubation or procedures with shared airway, giving **hands-free airway management**, as the endoscopist works without mask interruption.
- **Spontaneously breathing patients**: supports oxygenation and may reduce hypoventilation and the need for jaw support.
- **High-risk patients** (obesity, OSA, COPD, frailty, ASA 3 or more): fewer hypoxic events.
- **Patient comfort and compatibility** with oral instrumentation.

**Limitations**: **does not eliminate CO2 retention or guarantee ventilation** (capnography still needed), masks hypoventilation, gastric insufflation, fire risk with diathermy and high oxygen concentrations, cost and set-up, and noise.

> **Examiner's point:** physiology including humidification and generation of CPAP, and a reasoned use beyond apnoeic oxygenation, including preoxygenation and spontaneous ventilation.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

HFNC is an oxygenation technique, not a guarantee of ventilation or sustained apnoeic CO2 removal. During apnoea PaCO2 still increases substantially. Positive airway pressure is flow- and mouth-dependent and is lower with an open mouth during endoscopy. Monitor airway patency and ventilation independently, with capnography adapted to the interface or transcutaneous CO2 where indicated. A good SpO2 must not justify continuing deep sedation in an apnoeic patient.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Physiological effects 5; justified endoscopy use including limitations 5. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.

items.title: 2017.2 Q1: Persistent hypoxia after VATS left upper lobectomy with DLT still in s
items.q: Persistent hypoxia after VATS left upper lobectomy with DLT still in situ: causes (30%), management (70%).
items.model:
**Causes, 30%.** Consider DLT malposition, retained clamps or incorrect connections, kinking, blood/mucus plugging, residual one-lung ventilation and inadequate ventilator settings. Pulmonary causes include dependent or re-expanded-lung atelectasis, shunt/V/Q mismatch, bronchospasm, aspiration, oedema and pneumothorax of the remaining ventilated lung. Also assess air leak, chest-drain function, haemorrhage/low output, anaemia, PE and acute RV dysfunction. Persistent desaturation after resection should not automatically be attributed to the expected shunt.

**Management, 70%.** Call help and inform the surgeon; give FiO2 1.0, support perfusion, verify the saturation waveform, inspect chest movement, auscultate and review capnography/pressures/volumes. Restore two-lung ventilation if still isolated and safe for the operative situation. Check the entire circuit and DLT connections/clamps, then bronchoscopically inspect both lumens, confirm position and clear secretions/blood. Treat tension pneumothorax immediately and assess drain patency, avoiding clamping a leaking drain.

Obtain ABG, Hb and appropriate CXR/lung ultrasound/echo after immediate rescue. If collapse is likely, optimise PEEP and consider a haemodynamically tolerated recruitment manoeuvre while avoiding high pressure in a newly operated lung or air leak. Treat bronchospasm, aspiration, cardiac failure or embolism according to findings; reassess pressure, oxygenation and perfusion after each intervention. Decide whether the DLT should be exchanged for a single-lumen tube under controlled expert conditions if postoperative ventilation is needed; do not destabilise a marginal airway simply for routine extubation. Arrange ICU/HDU as indicated, communicate the event, and document ongoing ventilation/drain plans.
rubric: **3** — Immediate stabilisation, examination and equipment checks
**2** — Safe recruitment, airway transition and disposition

items.title: 2017.2 Q12: Define FEV1, FVC, VC and DLCO; interpret the supplied PFT table and po
items.q: Define FEV1, FVC, VC and DLCO; interpret the supplied PFT table and possible diagnoses (50% each).
items.model:
**Definitions, 50%.** FEV1 is the volume forcibly expired in the first second after full inspiration. FVC is the total volume expired during a complete forced expiration after full inspiration. VC is the maximal volume between full inspiration and full expiration, often measured slowly; it can exceed FVC in obstructive disease because forced expiration produces dynamic airway closure. DLCO measures carbon-monoxide transfer from alveolar gas into blood, reflecting membrane properties and pulmonary capillary blood volume; interpretation depends on haemoglobin, alveolar volume and test quality. State appropriate units rather than confusing a volume with a flow.

**Table and interpretation, 50%.** The source image was checked: FEV1 1.19 L (34%), FVC 4.23 L (95%), reported FER 23% (29% predicted), VC 5.11 L (115%), DLCO 11.7 (37%) and PEF 3.9 L/s (44%). There is marked airflow obstruction with severely reduced FEV1, a large slow-VC/FVC difference consistent with dynamic closure, and impaired gas transfer. FEV1/FVC from the displayed volumes is about 28%; the printed FER of 23% approximates FEV1/VC. Explicitly recognise the denominator/table discrepancy instead of silently altering data. A near-normal FVC does not exclude severe obstruction. TLC/RV were not supplied: do not diagnose measured hyperinflation from invented values.

COPD with emphysema is a leading diagnosis; asthma with persistent obstruction, bronchiectasis/other obstructive disease and combined pathology are alternatives. Reduced DLCO supports emphysema but may also reflect anaemia, pulmonary vascular disease or parenchymal disease. Assess smoking/exposure history, symptoms, exacerbations, reversibility, haemoglobin correction, lung volumes, imaging and exercise oxygenation. A numerical pattern does not itself establish operability or fitness for an unrelated operation.
rubric: **5** — Four accurate definitions and measurement limitations
**5** — Actual numbers, severe obstruction, DLCO and differential with table discrepancy

items.title: 2017.2 Q15: Features required of a transport ventilator for severe ventilator-depe
items.q: Features required of a transport ventilator for severe ventilator-dependent ARDS.
items.model:
Choose a device that can reproduce the patient's effective ICU lung-protective support throughout the expected transfer, with reserve for delays. A list of generic transport equipment does not answer the question.

It must deliver accurately controlled low tidal volumes based on predicted weight, suitable volume- or pressure-controlled assist/control modes, independently adjustable respiratory rate, inspiratory flow/time and I:E ratio, and sufficiently high reliable PEEP. It must support the required FiO2, pressures and minute ventilation without losing PEEP, measure delivered and exhaled volumes and pressures, and enable plateau/total-PEEP assessment where available. It needs adjustable pressure limits and appropriate trigger/synchrony or sedation/paralysis to avoid harmful dyssynchrony. Check compatibility with a high-resistance circuit, HME, humidification and any inhaled pulmonary vasodilator if essential.

Require disconnection, low minute-volume, high pressure, apnoea, oxygen-supply and power alarms that are audible/visible in transport; pressure/flow waveforms and trend monitoring are desirable. Continuous waveform capnography, SpO2 and haemodynamic monitoring are separate required monitors even if not built into the ventilator. Do not rely on ETCO2 as an exact PaCO2 surrogate in high dead space.

The unit must be compact, robust, securely mounted, operable by the escort and suitable for the vehicle/environment. Calculate battery and oxygen consumption for settings, device drive gas and the entire journey with a generous contingency; have charged spare power and oxygen plus an independent bag/oxygen/PEEP rescue system. Test on the patient before leaving, check tube/circuit/drain security, minimise disconnections, ensure skilled escort and communicate with the receiving unit. If oxygenation cannot be supported safely, reconsider timing/platform or specialist retrieval/ECMO rather than transferring with inadequate equipment.
rubric: **4** — ARDS-specific modes, settings, accurate volumes and PEEP
**2** — Patient trial, escort, contingency and safe transfer decision

items.title: 2017.1 Q4: Determine suitability for day surgery in a patient with known obstruct
items.q: Determine suitability for day surgery in a patient with known obstructive sleep apnoea.
items.model:
Make an individual assessment of OSA severity/control, surgery, analgesia, recovery and the capabilities of the facility. OSA alone is not an automatic reason to prohibit day surgery, and a favourable AHI alone does not make it safe.

Review the sleep study, symptoms, daytime somnolence, witnessed apnoeas, prior perioperative obstruction, PAP prescription/adherence and response. Assess obesity hypoventilation, daytime hypoxaemia/hypercapnia, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, resistant hypertension and other unstable disease. A high-risk untreated or poorly controlled patient may need optimisation, investigation or an inpatient setting.

Consider invasiveness, operative site, duration, airway access, expected opioid requirement and any postoperative obstruction/bleeding risk. Prefer local/regional techniques and effective non-opioid analgesia where suitable. Avoid unnecessary sedatives; prepare for difficult mask ventilation/intubation, quantitative NMBA recovery, awake head-up extubation and resumption of prescribed PAP. Major surgery, significant opioid needs or an airway procedure may exceed the day unit's safe capability.

Confirm appropriate postoperative monitoring, trained staff, rescue equipment, ability to use the patient's PAP and an admission/transfer pathway. Observe the actual course: recurrent obstruction, hypoxaemia, excessive sedation, uncontrolled pain or unexpectedly high opioid requirements should trigger longer monitoring/admission. Oxygen must not conceal hypoventilation. Discharge only when stable at baseline, with acceptable saturation in an unstimulated setting, controlled pain on a safe oral regimen, no concerning recurrent events and a responsible adult/support plan. Provide PAP, medicine, driving, warning-sign and emergency advice. Monitoring duration is individual; do not quote a universal fixed extra-hours rule as sufficient.

items.title: 2016.1 Q9: Considering the indications and limitations, compare the rationale for
items.q: Considering the indications and limitations, compare the rationale for the use of: Hudson masks; Non-rebreathing masks; Nasal prongs.
items.model:
## Comparison

| Feature | **Nasal prongs** | **Hudson (simple) mask** | **Non-rebreathing mask** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Flow** | 1–4 L/min (up to 6) | 5–10 L/min (minimum 5 to flush CO2) | 10–15 L/min |
| **Maximum FiO2** | About 0.40 (0.24 at 1 L/min, about 0.04 per additional litre) | About 0.50–0.60 | About 0.80–0.90 (up to 0.95 with perfect seal) |
| **Type** | Variable performance | Variable performance | Variable performance |
| **Mechanism** | Oxygen mixes with the nasopharyngeal reservoir and room air | Mask acts as a reservoir (about 100–200 mL); room air entrained through side holes during inspiration | Reservoir bag plus one-way valves on mask and ports: gas only from reservoir; exhalation vented |
| **Rationale/indication** | Mild hypoxaemia, long-term and postoperative use, comfort, speaking and eating | Moderate hypoxaemia in short-term use (recovery, ward) | Severe hypoxaemia and emergencies, transport, carbon monoxide poisoning, resuscitation |
| **Limitations** | FiO2 is variable; nasal obstruction impairs delivery, while mouth breathing does not make nasal oxygen ineffective; irritation and drying at higher flows; low FiO2 | Rebreathing at low flows; variable FiO2; no precision for COPD; claustrophobia, interferes with eating and communication | FiO2 depends on seal and reservoir inflation; valves can stick; does not deliver precise FiO2; cannot be used for long-term; less tolerated |

## Rationale

- **Prongs** for mild requirements with high comfort; **Hudson** as a step up (also used for nebulisers); **non-rebreather** for the acutely hypoxic patient needing maximal oxygen.
- All are **variable-performance**: FiO2 depends on respiratory rate, tidal volume and peak inspiratory flow, so **cannot be relied on for exact FiO2** (use a Venturi mask in patients with hypercapnia risk).
- **Monitor** SpO2 (and ABG if CO2 retention), humidify for long-term therapy, and review for escalation to high-flow nasal oxygen or NIV.

> **Examiner's point:** quote the correct maximal FiO2, differentiate the Hudson and non-rebreather masks, show limitations, and justify each use.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Device FiO2 figures are approximate and depend on demand, fit and manufacturer. Mouth breathing does not render standard nasal oxygen ineffective. A Venturi system is fixed-performance only when its total flow meets inspiratory demand and entrainment ports are unobstructed; jet entrainment involves momentum transfer, not a simplistic Bernoulli explanation alone. Follow the labelled valve flow, not a universal colour/flow table. HFNC pressure and FiO2 are variable with leak and demand; HFNC and NIV require an appropriately staffed location and escalation protocol, which may include a designated ward service.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Correct flow rates and maximum FiO2 for each device

items.title: 2016.1 Q11: As a perioperative physician, what strategies can you offer to assist
items.q: As a perioperative physician, what strategies can you offer to assist a patient to cease smoking tobacco and how will you best communicate them?
items.model:
## Why act at the perioperative visit

Surgery is a **teachable moment**: smoking raises the risk of pulmonary complications, wound infection and dehiscence, cardiovascular events, and delayed bone healing, and benefit begins within days, with larger effects after 4 or more weeks of abstinence.

## Communication

- **Ask, Advise, Assist** (the 5As: Ask, Advise, Assess readiness, Assist, Arrange follow-up), using **brief intervention** in the preadmission clinic.
- Use **non-judgemental, personalised, motivational interviewing**: explore the patient's goals, link smoking to their surgery and recovery, ask permission to give advice, acknowledge past attempts, and set a quit date.
- Provide written materials and refer to Quitline (0800 778 778 in NZ) and the GP or pharmacist.

## Non-pharmacological interventions

**Behavioural support** (individual or group counselling, cognitive behavioural therapy, telephone coaching such as Quitline, text-message programmes, apps) has effective medium- to long-term abstinence rates; combined with medication it is the most effective.

## Pharmacological therapy

- **Nicotine replacement therapy** (NRT): patches (21 mg/24 h for over 10 cigarettes a day) plus short-acting gum, lozenge or inhaler (**combination NRT is more effective**); safe perioperatively and in cardiac disease.
- **Varenicline** (partial nicotine agonist; 0.5 mg daily increasing to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks; the most effective single agent; nausea, vivid dreams).
- **Bupropion** (150 mg daily to twice daily; seizure risk, interactions).
- Nicotine e-cigarettes may help but evidence and safety are debated.

## Perioperative practice

Advise stopping as early as possible (ideally 4–8 weeks before), but **any abstinence helps, including the day before surgery** (carboxyhaemoglobin falls within 12–24 hours). Continue support after discharge and address relapse.

> **Examiner's point:** to pass, describe an effective non-pharmacological intervention and at least one suitable replacement therapy.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Tailor medication to contraindications and renal function: varenicline often needs renal dose adjustment; bupropion is unsuitable in seizure disorders and several interacting conditions. Continue behavioural follow-up. Do not promise normal pulmonary risk after a short fixed period of abstinence. The benefits of stopping start early and increase over time; there is no reason to advise continued smoking because surgery is close.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.

items.title: 2015.2 Q6: A three-year-old requires adenotonsillectomy for OSA: outline and just
items.source: Past SAQ 2015.2 Q6 · pass rate not available
items.q: A three-year-old requires adenotonsillectomy for OSA: outline and justify perioperative management.
items.model:
Assess OSA severity with snoring/apnoea, work of breathing, sleep study/oximetry where available, growth/behaviour, recurrent infection and previous anaesthetic problems. Seek severe desaturation, daytime symptoms, obesity, craniofacial/neuromuscular disease, pulmonary hypertension and cardiac impairment. Adult AHI/STOP-BANG thresholds cannot be applied to a three-year-old. Consider whether surgery should occur in a paediatric centre and plan postoperative admission/monitoring from severity, age, comorbidity and local capability.

Discuss with parents and ENT, including obstruction, respiratory depression, bleeding and analgesia. Avoid routine sedative premedication in significant OSA; if necessary use an individual monitored plan. Prepare age/weight-appropriate difficult-airway and laryngospasm equipment. Coordinate induction/airway management with the surgical team; choose an appropriate protected/shared-airway technique, monitor ventilation and temperature, and ensure quantitative recovery if NMBA is used.

Provide multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, an NSAID when appropriate under local tonsillectomy guidance and intraoperative dexamethasone for antiemesis/analgesic benefit. Dose all drugs by actual weight and local paediatric protocol; do not derive weight from age alone. Opioids, if required, need conservative titration and close monitoring because OSA increases respiratory risk. Avoid codeine/tramadol after tonsil surgery in children. Manage hydration, PONV and bleeding risk without unnecessary opioids or sedation.

Clear blood/secretions, remove and account for any throat pack and plan extubation according to airway risk and expertise, with rescue available. Recover in a staffed paediatric setting, monitor for recurrent obstruction/desaturation, haemorrhage and opioid sedation, and use PAP/respiratory support with ENT/ICU advice when indicated. Significant OSA or an adverse recovery course warrants monitored admission. Discharge only with stable breathing, adequate fluids/analgesia, responsible care, written bleeding/respiratory warning signs and access to urgent review.
rubric: **3** — Paediatric OSA severity/comorbidity and suitable facility
**3** — Weight-based multimodal analgesia and opioid safeguards

items.title: 2013.2 Q14: Intensive care patients may be at risk of ventilator-associated pneumo
items.q: Intensive care patients may be at risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). a. Describe the likely aetiology of, and risk factors for, VAP. (50%) b. Outline prevention strategies that reduce the incidence of VAP. (50%)
items.model:
## (a) Aetiology and risk factors (50%)

**Definition**: pneumonia developing **48 hours or more after intubation** (early onset under 5 days; late onset after 5 days), occurring in about 10–20% of ventilated patients.
**Aetiology**
- **Aspiration of colonised oropharyngeal and gastric secretions** past the ETT cuff is the key mechanism (micro-aspiration), along with **biofilm** on the tube, contaminated equipment and hands, and (less often) haematogenous spread.
- The ETT bypasses the cough reflex and upper airway defences and impairs mucociliary clearance.
- **Organisms**: early (community-type) Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus, MSSA; late and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, MRSA, Klebsiella, Enterobacteriaceae.

**Risk factors**
- **Patient**: extremes of age, COPD, immunosuppression, depressed consciousness, trauma and burns, aspiration, malnutrition, and chronic illness.
- **ICU/device**: duration of ventilation, **reintubation**, supine position, high cuff leak or low cuff pressure, enteral feeding with gastric distension, nasogastric tube, sedation, prior antibiotics, stress ulcer prophylaxis (acid suppression), transport, tracheostomy, and cross-infection.

## (b) Prevention strategies (50%)

- **1.** **Avoid or minimise intubation**: use NIV or high-flow nasal oxygen where suitable, daily **sedation interruption** and weaning protocols, early extubation, and avoid reintubation.
- **2.** **Positioning**: **semi-recumbent position (30–45 degrees head-up)**.
- **3.** **Airway management**: **subglottic secretion drainage** ETT, **cuff pressure 20–30 cmH2O**, avoid unnecessary circuit changes, closed suction, and heat–moisture exchangers versus heated humidifiers (equivalent).
- **4.** **Oral care**: toothbrushing; do not use routine **chlorhexidine** solely for VAP prevention; efficacy and potential harm are concerns.
- **5.** **Medication strategies**: minimise sedation, avoid unnecessary stress ulcer prophylaxis (balance GI bleeding risk), **selective digestive decontamination** (reduces VAP and mortality but resistance concerns), restrict antibiotic exposure.
- **6.** **General ICU protocols/bundles**: hand hygiene, equipment care, staff education, surveillance, early enteral nutrition (post-pyloric if aspiration risk), avoid gastric overdistension, and early mobilisation.
- **7.** **Others**: probiotics (uncertain), early tracheostomy (no clear effect).

> **Examiner's point:** only 28% passed. Define VAP, explain aspiration of colonised secretions, include patient and ICU factors, and cover the key daily ICU practices.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

The October 2025 BJA Education review distinguishes VAP incidence from patient-centred benefit and colonisation from infection. Routine chlorhexidine, probiotics, prophylactic inhaled/systemic antibiotics or SDD are not automatic care for every ventilated patient; local microbiology, resistance and patient selection matter. Use stress-ulcer prophylaxis for a justified bleeding-risk indication, not as VAP prevention; contemporary PPI trials have not established increased pneumonia. Early/late timing alone cannot replace local resistance risk. The new Retrieve VAP case works diagnosis, sampling, empirical therapy, de-escalation and duration.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Aetiology/risk factors 5; prevention 5. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.
rubric: Definition and early versus late onset
Aspiration of colonised secretions as key mechanism
Positioning, cuff pressure and subglottic drainage

items.title: 2013.1 Q13: Why hypoxaemia occurs after changing to one-lung ventilation (50%); tr
items.q: Why hypoxaemia occurs after changing to one-lung ventilation (50%); treatment (50%).
items.model:
**Causes, 50%.** OLV creates an obligatory shunt through the non-ventilated lung; HPV limits but does not abolish its perfusion. Dependent-lung atelectasis, low FRC, poor reserve, V/Q mismatch and high airway pressure can worsen gas exchange. Check unrelated equipment/supply faults, DLT/blocker malposition, obstruction by blood/secretions, bronchospasm and pneumothorax. Low cardiac output or anaemia lowers mixed-venous oxygen content and magnifies shunt-related arterial hypoxaemia; excessive overdistension can divert perfusion away from the ventilated lung. Surgical haemorrhage, embolism and RV dysfunction are important alternatives.

**Treatment, 50%.** Call for assistance, inform the surgeon, give FiO2 1.0 and assess signal, circulation, delivered volume and capnography. Severe or rapidly deteriorating hypoxaemia requires immediate two-lung ventilation while identifying the cause. Confirm and correct the isolation device bronchoscopically, suction obstructing material and treat bronchospasm or tension pneumothorax. Optimise dependent-lung ventilation with protective volumes, individual PEEP and selective cautious recruitment, watching blood pressure. Maintain perfusion and appropriate Hb; correct the underlying cause rather than chasing saturation with indiscriminate fluids. If OLV remains necessary, discuss CPAP/oxygen to the operative lung, intermittent two-lung ventilation and feasible surgical pulmonary-artery manipulation. Reconsider proceeding if oxygenation cannot be maintained safely. Record a postoperative support plan.

Escalation is determined by urgency; an orderly list must not delay two-lung rescue in a patient with critical desaturation. Physiological improvement with recruitment is not evidence that routine high PEEP/recruitment improves all postoperative outcomes.
rubric: **5** — Severity-based oxygenation, device correction and justified escalation

items.title: 2012.1 Q10: An adult patient from the intensive care unit with severe adult respir
items.q: An adult patient from the intensive care unit with severe adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requires a laparotomy for an acute abdomen. a. What are the features of ARDS? (30%) b. Explain your perioperative ventilation strategy (70%)
items.model:
## (a) Features of ARDS (30%)

**Causes**: direct (pneumonia, aspiration, contusion, inhalation) and indirect (sepsis, pancreatitis, trauma, transfusion, burns).
**Definition (Berlin)**: acute onset within 1 week of an insult, **bilateral opacities** not explained by effusions or collapse, **respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload**, and **PaO2/FiO2 ratio under 300 with PEEP 5**: mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe under 100.
**Pathophysiology**: diffuse alveolar damage with increased capillary permeability, protein-rich oedema, surfactant loss, **shunt and V/Q mismatch**, reduced compliance ("baby lung"), pulmonary hypertension.
**Effects**: severe hypoxaemia, high work of breathing, hypercapnia from dead space, right ventricular strain.

## (b) Perioperative ventilation strategy (70%)

**Principle**: continue the **ICU lung-protective ventilation** to avoid ventilator-induced lung injury (volutrauma, barotrauma, atelectrauma, biotrauma), and keep the patient on the **ICU ventilator** during transfer if possible. Consider whether surgery can be done in ICU, delayed, or modified (damage-control).
- **Tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg predicted body weight** (ARDSNet), **plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O**, driving pressure below 15.
- **PEEP**: high PEEP tables (10–20 cmH2O) or individually titrated, with **recruitment manoeuvres** used cautiously; minimise disconnections and preserve PEEP with an agreed safe transfer method; clamping an ETT is not routine and must never occur while the patient is actively breathing or the ventilator is delivering a breath.
- **Respiratory rate** 20–35, **permissive hypercapnia** (pH above 7.2–7.25), and I:E ratio adjustments (with PEEP/auto-PEEP monitoring).
- **FiO2** titrated to **SpO2 88–95% or PaO2 55–80 mmHg**; avoid unnecessary high oxygen.
- **Rescue**: **nitric oxide or nebulised prostacyclin** (improve oxygenation, no mortality effect), **neuromuscular blockade** (early in severe ARDS: ACURASYS, though ROSE found no benefit), prone positioning (not feasible for laparotomy, but used pre/postoperatively; PROSEVA), ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia (EOLIA).
- **Anaesthetic**: TIVA or volatile; avoid nitrous oxide; **conservative fluid strategy** (FACTT) balanced against shock; vasopressors for haemodynamics.
- **Monitoring**: arterial line, ABG, plateau pressure and compliance, ETCO2; recognise pneumothorax; abdominal insufflation is not advised.
- **Postoperative**: return to ICU ventilated.

> **Examiner's point:** specify tidal volume, rate, PEEP, acceptable PaCO2 and airway pressures, and other strategies such as nitric oxide and fluid management.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

For the historical stem, retain a short accurate Berlin description; distinguish it from the newer global definition in Retrieve. Current ATS guidance favours selected higher PEEP without prolonged recruitment in moderate/severe ARDS; prolonged recruitment is harmful. Driving pressure is a useful physiological signal, not a universal RCT-proven standalone threshold. Prone sessions should generally last at least 16 hours when indicated. Steroids are now conditionally supported for ARDS overall, but discussion of non-ventilatory treatment must not displace the ventilatory focus of the 2007.1 question.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Features 3; perioperative ventilation 7. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Berlin boundaries:** mild 200 < P/F ≤300, moderate 100 < P/F ≤200, severe P/F ≤100 mmHg, with the specified PEEP/support and other criteria. Do not double-count the boundary values between groups.
rubric: Causes and Berlin criteria for ARDS
Lung-protective ventilation targets (tidal volume, plateau pressure)
PEEP and recruitment, maintaining PEEP during transfer

items.title: 2012.1 Q15: With regard to oxygen therapy for patients in a general postoperative
items.q: With regard to oxygen therapy for patients in a general postoperative ward a. Describe the options available (30%) b. What are the justifications for your choice for a particular patient? (70%)
items.model:
## (a) Options (30%)

- **Variable performance (low-flow)**: nasal prongs (1–4 L/min, FiO2 0.24–0.40), simple Hudson mask (5–10 L/min, 0.35–0.60), **non-rebreather mask** (10–15 L/min, up to 0.9).
- **Fixed performance (high-flow)**: **Venturi mask** (24–60%), **high-flow nasal cannula** (up to 60 L/min, 0.21–1.0, humidified).
- **Others**: humidified systems, tracheostomy mask, CPAP/BiPAP (HDU), and oxygen via T-piece.

## (b) Justification for a particular patient (70%)

Choose on **patient characteristics, surgery and need**:
- **Pre-existing disease**: **COPD with CO2 retention** needs a **Venturi mask** (controlled FiO2, target SpO2 88–92%); **dementia or confusion** (tolerates prongs rather than a mask); asthma; obesity and OSA (CPAP/HFNC, head-up).
- **Ventilation pattern**: tidal volume, respiratory rate, and respiratory pause alter FiO2 with variable devices. A patient with a high respiratory rate or tidal volume entrains more air, so FiO2 is lower than expected; those with rapid, shallow breathing need high flow.
- **Oxygen requirement**: mild hypoxaemia (SpO2 90–94%) → prongs; moderate → Hudson/Venturi; severe or emergency → non-rebreather then HFNC/NIV with escalation.
- **Surgical factors**: abdominal and thoracic surgery (splinting, atelectasis; HFNC, CPAP), **neurosurgery** (avoid hypoxia and hypercapnia), **ENT/airway surgery** (humidification, mask versus prongs; fire risk), oesophageal/upper GI anastomoses (avoid CPAP/NIV pressures where contraindicated).
- **Special groups**: paediatric and neonatal patients (humidified, hoods, prongs; avoid hyperoxia in preterm infants), pregnant patients.
- **Comfort and compliance**, eating, speaking, claustrophobia.
- **Humidification** for prolonged therapy or thick secretions.
- **Monitoring and targets**: SpO2 94–98% (88–92% in hypercapnia), RR, sedation, gas if CO2 retention is suspected; review and wean regularly; early escalation.

> **Examiner's point:** options (variable and fixed) and justification linked to patient and surgical factors, with humidification. Only 32% passed.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Device FiO2 figures are approximate and depend on demand, fit and manufacturer. Mouth breathing does not render standard nasal oxygen ineffective. A Venturi system is fixed-performance only when its total flow meets inspiratory demand and entrainment ports are unobstructed; jet entrainment involves momentum transfer, not a simplistic Bernoulli explanation alone. Follow the labelled valve flow, not a universal colour/flow table. HFNC pressure and FiO2 are variable with leak and demand; HFNC and NIV require an appropriately staffed location and escalation protocol, which may include a designated ward service.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

items.title: 2011.2 Q1: Compare and contrast oxygen delivery by nasal prongs, simple facemask
items.q: Compare and contrast oxygen delivery by nasal prongs, simple facemask and Venturi mask.
items.model:
## Physics of delivery: variable versus fixed performance

- **Variable performance** (nasal prongs, simple mask): oxygen flow is lower than the patient's peak inspiratory flow (about 30–40 L/min, higher in distress), so the patient entrains room air, and FiO2 depends on oxygen flow, tidal volume, respiratory rate, inspiratory flow pattern, and the mask or pharyngeal reservoir.
- **Fixed performance** (Venturi): **high total flow** delivered above the peak inspiratory flow, with a defined FiO2.

## Comparison

| | **Nasal prongs** | **Simple facemask** | **Venturi mask** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Delivery mechanism** | Oxygen into the nares, mixing with the nasopharyngeal reservoir (about 50 mL) | Oxygen into a mask reservoir (100–200 mL); room air entrained via side ports and around the mask | Oxygen passes through a **narrow jet orifice**, **entraining room air by jet momentum transfer**, with device geometry determining entrainment through fixed ports; the orifice size sets the ratio |
| **Flow** | 1–4 L/min | 5–10 L/min (at least 5 to prevent rebreathing) | Specified for each valve (e.g. 24% at 2 L/min, 28% at 4, 35% at 8–10, 40% at 10, 60% at 15 L/min) |
| **FiO2** | 0.24–0.40 (increase of about 0.04 per litre) | 0.35–0.60 | Fixed at 0.24, 0.28, 0.31, 0.35, 0.40, 0.60 |
| **Accuracy** | Variable | Variable | **Accurate** (within a few per cent at the prescribed flow), but total gas flow falls at high FiO2 (ratio of entrainment decreases), which may be below inspiratory flow in distressed patients |
| **Advantages** | Comfortable, cheap, allows eating, drinking and speaking | Simple, higher FiO2 than prongs | **Controlled FiO2** for CO2 retainers (COPD), gives titration, reproducible |
| **Disadvantages** | Low FiO2, drying at higher flows, nasal obstruction impairs delivery | CO2 rebreathing at low flow, claustrophobic, uncertain FiO2 | Noisy, interferes with eating and talking, air entrainment ports may be obstructed, no humidification, costs more |

## Summary

For a patient with COPD and hypercapnia use a Venturi mask (88–92%); for mild hypoxaemia use prongs; for short-term moderate requirements a simple mask; for severe, a non-rebreather or high-flow system.

> **Examiner's point:** physics, oxygen concentration, mechanism, and advantages and disadvantages. Only 5% passed this very core question.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Device FiO2 figures are approximate and depend on demand, fit and manufacturer. Mouth breathing does not render standard nasal oxygen ineffective. A Venturi system is fixed-performance only when its total flow meets inspiratory demand and entrainment ports are unobstructed; jet entrainment involves momentum transfer, not a simplistic Bernoulli explanation alone. Follow the labelled valve flow, not a universal colour/flow table. HFNC pressure and FiO2 are variable with leak and demand; HFNC and NIV require an appropriately staffed location and escalation protocol, which may include a designated ward service.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Mechanism of delivery for each device
Flow rates and FiO2 for each
Importance of minimum flow with masks

items.title: 2011.2 Q8: Active URTI in a child: risk factors for respiratory adverse events (5
items.q: Active URTI in a child: risk factors for respiratory adverse events (50%) and risk reduction (50%).
items.model:
**Risk, 50%.** Assess the actual infection and physiological reserve: fever, wet/productive cough, copious or purulent secretions, wheeze, lower-respiratory signs, hypoxaemia, lethargy and poor intake increase concern compared with isolated mild clear rhinorrhoea. Young age, prematurity, reactive airways/asthma, passive smoke exposure, OSA and relevant comorbidity add risk. Airway surgery, tracheal intubation and repeated/difficult instrumentation increase laryngospasm, bronchospasm, desaturation and secretion-related events. Consider urgency, the procedure and the experience/resources of the team.

**Reduction, 50%.** Discuss an individual proceed/postpone decision with parents and surgeon. Defer elective cases with significant systemic illness, lower-respiratory involvement or uncontrolled wheeze until recovery and optimisation; a single fixed cancellation interval is not appropriate for every child. For time-critical surgery plan a setting and team able to rescue deterioration. Consider preoperative bronchodilator where indicated, effective secretion management and gentle suction without unnecessary stimulation. Routine antibiotics or steroids do not treat an uncomplicated viral URTI.

Use an experienced paediatric anaesthetist, minimise repeated airway instrumentation, choose face mask/supraglottic/ETT according to the procedure and protection requirements rather than assuming an LMA removes the risk, and ensure adequate anaesthetic depth for manipulation. An IV propofol induction can reduce airway reactivity in suitable children; balance this with IV access, cooperation and the safest individual airway plan. Avoid irritant exposure and provide appropriate monitoring, lung ventilation and humidification. Plan extubation with laryngospasm/obstruction rescue equipment immediately available, careful recovery observation and admission/escalation if events recur. Explain residual risk and document the decision.
rubric: **5** — Infection severity, patient factors, airway instrumentation and surgery
**5** — Justified timing, optimisation, technique, secretion care and monitoring

items.title: 2011.2 Q9: Reduce the likelihood of acute lung injury during anaesthesia for perf
items.q: Reduce the likelihood of acute lung injury during anaesthesia for perforated bowel three days after colonoscopy.
items.model:
This patient has sepsis, a likely full stomach, abdominal distension and a high risk of aspiration, shock and postoperative respiratory failure. Reduce pulmonary injury while obtaining timely source control; do not delay lifesaving laparotomy for extensive testing. Explain risk, call senior/ICU assistance and plan postoperative critical care.

Preoperatively assess oxygenation, work of breathing, perfusion, urine output and mental status. Obtain gas/lactate, blood count, electrolytes, renal function, cultures and appropriate imaging without delaying treatment. Give timely local-guideline antibiotics. Resuscitate with reassessed fluid aliquots, blood for an appropriate indication and vasopressor support for persistent hypotension; avoid both prolonged hypoperfusion and indiscriminate fluid loading. Decompress the stomach where indicated with attention to aspiration risk.

Prepare head-up preoxygenation, suction, an experienced operator, aspiration/difficult-airway plan and haemodynamic support before induction. Choose rapid-sequence or another appropriate airway technique to secure a cuffed ETT, adapting ventilation if hypoxaemic. Avoid severe peri-intubation hypotension. Confirm waveform CO2 and tube position; promptly recognise and manage regurgitation/aspiration.

Ventilate with roughly 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, appropriate PEEP, limited plateau/driving pressures and adequate expiratory time. In established ARDS use its lower-volume strategy. Titrate FiO2 after initial safety oxygenation; avoid routine prolonged high-pressure recruitment and unnecessary circuit disconnections. Monitor gas exchange, temperature and mechanics. Support perfusion with goal-directed reassessment and avoid unnecessary transfusion; treat surgical bleeding and sepsis rather than accepting hypoxia or hypotension in the name of a restrictive fluid plan.

Use effective opioid-sparing analgesia, normothermia and antiemetics. Postoperatively retain the airway/ventilate in ICU if unstable; extubate only when physiological and neuromuscular recovery are adequate, with selected NIV/HFNC and early mobilisation/physiotherapy as appropriate. Continue source control, antibiotics and aspiration prevention. Steroids do not prevent ALI routinely; use only for a specific contemporary indication such as selected ARDS or refractory septic shock.
rubric: **2** — Resuscitation, antibiotics and timely source control
**2** — Protective ventilation and avoidance of further injury
**2** — Postoperative support and specific rather than routine steroids

items.title: 2011.1 Q2: A patient with known idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (fibrosing alveolit
items.q: A patient with known idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (fibrosing alveolitis) presents for an open right hemicolectomy. (a) What are the respiratory issues facing this patient with regard to their general anaesthetic? (70%) (b) Explain your intraoperative ventilation strategy. (30%)
items.model:
## (a) Respiratory issues (70%)

Organise by patient, anaesthesia and surgery, and pre-, intra- and postoperative.

**Disease and severity**
- IPF is a progressive **restrictive disease** with **reduced lung volumes (FVC, TLC), low compliance, reduced DLCO**, V/Q mismatch, and **hypoxaemia** (exertional then resting; home oxygen suggests severe disease).
- **Sequelae**: pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure, recurrent infection, **acute exacerbations** (high mortality, triggered by surgery, ventilation or infection), lung cancer, and GORD with aspiration.
- **Treatment effects**: actual prescribed **corticosteroids** or immunosuppressants if used for a specific condition (adrenal suppression, infection/marrow effects); these are not standard chronic IPF therapy. Assess antifibrotics (nintedanib, pirfenidone: liver tests), and **oxygen** therapy; prior bleomycin or amiodarone causes can sensitise to high oxygen.

**Assessment**: functional capacity, FVC and DLCO, oxygen saturation at rest and exertion, ABG, chest CT, echocardiogram (PA pressure), 6-minute walk test, current exacerbation, and discussion with a respiratory physician. Question whether surgery is essential and the alternatives; mortality risk is high.

**Anaesthetic and surgical factors**
- **GA and paralysis** further reduce FRC, causing atelectasis and hypoxia; high airway pressures and **barotrauma/pneumothorax** risk in stiff lungs; ARDS/exacerbation after ventilation.
- Open abdominal surgery: **pain and splinting** of the diaphragm, fluid shifts and overload risk (pulmonary oedema, RV failure), cell salvage, and aspiration.
- **Hyperoxia** may worsen oxidative lung injury; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in pulmonary hypertension.
- **Postoperative**: respiratory failure, prolonged ventilation, pneumonia, need for ICU/HDU, and analgesic regimen (epidural preferred, opioid caution).

## (b) Intraoperative ventilation strategy (30%)

- **Lung-protective ventilation**: **tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight** (4–6 if very stiff lungs), **plateau pressure below 28–30 cmH2O**, moderate **PEEP 5–10**, avoid high peak pressures.
- **Respiratory rate** high enough (to maintain minute ventilation, with individually chosen inspiratory/expiratory times, adequate expiration and monitoring; short time constants do not mandate prolonged inspiration or guarantee absence of trapping).
- **FiO2** as low as needed for SpO2 above 90–92%; permissive hypercapnia if tolerated (not with pulmonary hypertension).
- Arterial line and serial ABG, avoid fluid overload, consider epidural analgesia, and plan extubation to HFNC/NIV and ICU/HDU.

> **Examiner's point:** apportion time to the marks (70:30), and use a pre/intra/postoperative or patient/anaesthesia/surgery format.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is distinct from other causes of fibrotic ILD: chronic corticosteroid/azathioprine treatment is not standard IPF therapy and can be harmful. Assess actual prescribed antifibrotic or immunosuppressive treatment and its indication. Avoid assuming that fibrotic lung is recruitable like oedematous ARDS: excessive PEEP or recruitment can overdistend remaining compliant units. Individualise PEEP, rate and inspiratory time; do not prescribe prolonged inspiration solely because the disease is restrictive. Bleomycin exposure is a separate history item, not an inherent feature of IPF.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Respiratory issues 7; ventilation strategy 3. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.
rubric: Tidal volume, plateau pressure and PEEP

items.title: 2010.2 Q15: Interpret restrictive PFTs, discuss anaesthesia with restrictive loop
items.q: Interpret restrictive PFTs, discuss anaesthesia with restrictive loop B, and analyse the abnormal capnograph.
items.model:
**A: interpretation and causes, one third.** FVC 1.74 L (60% predicted), FEV1 1.47 L (70%), ratio 84.5%, TLC 2.81 L (54%) and RV 0.85 L (39%) show a restrictive defect: low TLC and FVC with preserved/high ratio. DLCO is 8.75 (39% predicted), but assess haemoglobin, alveolar volume and transfer coefficient before attributing all reduction to intrinsic parenchymal disease. The report specifically warned against inferring parenchymal disease without accounting for small lung volumes. Causes include interstitial/parenchymal fibrosis, chest-wall deformity, obesity, pleural disease and neuromuscular weakness; integrate history, examination and imaging rather than selecting one from the numbers alone.

**B: implications, one third.** The source figure was visually checked: loop A is normal and B is small/narrow with preserved general shape, consistent with restriction. Small oxygen reserve and reduced FRC cause rapid desaturation with apnoea; supine posture, anaesthetic drugs and opioids worsen ventilation and V/Q mismatch. Stiff lungs require higher pressure for a given volume, risking distension of remaining aerated units. Rapid shallow spontaneous breathing may be inefficient. Consider regional anaesthesia for arthroscopy when suitable; if GA is needed preoxygenate carefully, minimise apnoea and use small predicted-weight tidal volumes with individual rate/pressure/PEEP and CO2 monitoring. Do not assume every restrictive lung benefits from aggressive CPAP/recruitment: neuromuscular restriction differs from poorly recruitable fibrosis. Plan analgesia, full NMBA recovery and postoperative monitoring to the severity.

**C: capnograph, one third.** The original figure shows the normal initial waveform changing to a slower sloping expiratory upstroke/obstructive shark-fin shape with a lower apparent end-tidal level. The report calls this an abnormal expiratory upstroke and apparent ETCO2 fall; do not answer with every possible waveform cause. Consider mechanical expiratory obstruction, bronchospasm and obstructive-airway disease. Assess oxygenation/ventilation, patient and circuit immediately; inspect the ETT, filter, expiratory limb and valves for kink, clot, foreign body or malfunction. Pass a suction catheter without assuming it excludes every obstruction; use independent bag/oxygen to isolate equipment. Auscultate, inspect flow/pressure waveforms, obtain ABG as needed, use bronchoscopy when indicated and assess response to inhaled bronchodilator. Treat dangerous obstruction or tension physiology immediately.
rubric: **3.33333** — A: restrictive pattern, discriminating measurements and differential
**3.33333** — B: specific physiology and justified anaesthetic implications
**3.33333** — C: actual trace, focused differential and patient plus equipment checks

items.title: 2009.2 Q3: PACU agitation and dyspnoea after abdominal hysterectomy: differential
items.q: PACU agitation and dyspnoea after abdominal hysterectomy: differential (40%), assessment for residual neuromuscular blockade (40%), sugammadex (20%).
items.model:
**Differential, 40%.** Assess and support airway, breathing and circulation immediately while calling assistance. Upper-airway obstruction, laryngospasm, secretions, oedema and OSA; bronchospasm or lower-airway obstruction; atelectasis, aspiration, pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema, pneumonia and PE; residual neuromuscular block, diaphragmatic dysfunction or pain-limited breathing; opioid/sedative depression; haemorrhage, low output, myocardial ischaemia or anaemia; delirium, anxiety and metabolic acidosis. Anaemia may cause dyspnoea without lowering arterial saturation. Prioritise recent drug doses and events rather than giving an unranked list.

**Residual block, 40%.** Review NMBA/antagonist dose, timing, temperature, renal/hepatic function, magnesium/aminoglycosides and other potentiating drugs. Assess airway patency, respiratory pattern, tidal effort, cough, swallowing/voice and muscle strength, but head lift or hand grip cannot exclude clinically significant residual block. Use calibrated quantitative ulnar-nerve/adductor-pollicis monitoring and a technically valid T4/T1 ratio. Confirm at least 0.9 (and appropriate baseline normalisation for acceleromyography) before extubation or regarding recovery as complete. TOF count alone and subjective absence of fade are inadequate. A patient may have diaphragmatic movement despite unsafe pharyngeal weakness. Support ventilation, give appropriate reversal and reassess quantitatively; do not wait for a monitor before treating respiratory compromise.

**Sugammadex, 20%.** It encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium, not atracurium/cisatracurium or suxamethonium. Dose by documented depth and local product information: commonly 2 mg/kg at return of T2, 4 mg/kg with 1–2 post-tetanic counts and no TOF response, and 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal soon after a large rocuronium dose. Maintain airway/ventilation until recovery is confirmed. Consider anaphylaxis, profound bradycardia, inadequate dosing/recurarisation, severe renal impairment and relevant interactions, including contraceptive counselling per product information. Reversal is not treatment for another cause of airway obstruction and must not replace airway rescue.
rubric: **4** — Drug history, clinical limits and quantitative TOF ≥0.9
**2** — Correct spectrum, depth-related sugammadex and precautions

items.title: 2009.2 Q8: 1. Outline the factors that determine oxygen delivery to the tissues.
items.q: 1. Outline the factors that determine oxygen delivery to the tissues. (30%) 2. How might you increase the oxygen delivery to the tissues in an anaesthetised patient. (40%) 3. How does a hyperbaric chamber influence oxygen delivery to the tissues? (30%)
items.model:
## 1. Determinants of oxygen delivery (30%)

**DO2 = cardiac output x arterial oxygen content (CaO2)**, where CaO2 = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2) mL/dL.
- Normal: CO 5 L/min x CaO2 200 mL/L ≈ **1000 mL/min** (about 4 times the resting consumption of 250 mL/min, extraction 25%).
- **Haemoglobin**: 150 g/L carries about 200 mL/L; **SaO2** depends on PaO2 and the oxyhaemoglobin curve (P50, affected by pH, CO2, temperature and 2,3-DPG); **dissolved oxygen** is minor (3 mL/L at 100 mmHg).
- **Cardiac output** = heart rate x stroke volume (preload, contractility, afterload).
- **Regional distribution**: autoregulation (myogenic, metabolic) and extrinsic control (sympathetic tone, pH, nitric oxide, hormones) direct flow to tissues; microcirculation and diffusion distance.

## 2. Increasing oxygen delivery in an anaesthetised patient (40%)

- **Arterial oxygen content**: increase **FiO2**, treat atelectasis and shunt (PEEP, recruitment), correct V/Q mismatch, avoid hypoventilation; **raise haemoglobin** (red cell transfusion, treat anaemia, stop bleeding); keep SaO2 above 95%; shift the curve (rightward shift improves unloading: treat alkalosis and hypothermia).
- **Cardiac output**: optimise **preload** (fluids guided by dynamic indices), maintain **heart rate and rhythm**, **contractility** (inotropes: dobutamine, adrenaline), **afterload** (vasopressors for perfusion pressure; vasodilators when high), reduce positive pressure effects (PEEP, high airway pressures), treat arrhythmia, and use regional anaesthesia with care.
- **Reduce oxygen consumption**: adequate depth of anaesthesia and analgesia, muscle relaxation, treat shivering and fever, maintain normothermia and avoid unnecessary metabolic demand; do not deliberately induce hypothermia solely to improve routine perioperative oxygen balance.
- **Regional/microcirculation**: maintain perfusion pressure (MAP), avoid vasoconstrictors in specific beds, use vasodilators for tissue perfusion, correct acidosis and lactate.

## 3. Hyperbaric oxygen (30%)

Breathing 100% oxygen at 2–3 atmospheres absolute raises PaO2 to **about 1500–2000 mmHg** (at 3 atm). **Dissolved oxygen increases in line with Henry's law** (0.003 mL/dL/mmHg), so CaO2 rises by about **6 mL/dL at 3 atm**, enough to meet resting tissue needs **without haemoglobin** (an important effect in severe anaemia and carbon monoxide poisoning).
- **Effects**: higher diffusion gradient into hypoxic tissue (up to 4 times the distance), **vasoconstriction** (reducing oedema), bubble volume reduction (Boyle's law, for decompression illness/gas embolism), angiogenesis, improved leucocyte killing, and displacement of CO from haemoglobin.
- **Risks**: barotrauma (ears, sinuses, lungs), **oxygen toxicity** (CNS seizures, pulmonary), claustrophobia, fire, and reduced cardiac output via vasoconstriction.

> **Examiner's point:** give the oxygen delivery equation with accurate values and units, an organised list of ways to increase each component, and numerical values for hyperbaric oxygen.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

State Hb units explicitly: CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb(g/dL) × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2(mmHg), in mL O2/dL; multiply CO(L/min) × CaO2 × 10 to obtain mL/min. Lowering consumption improves supply-demand balance but does not itself increase calculated DO2. Do not induce hypothermia or administer vasodilators solely to shift the dissociation curve or chase a supranormal delivery target. At 3 ATA dissolved oxygen may approach 6 mL/dL; this is a physiological explanation, not a routine substitute for transfusion or source control.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Determinants 3; methods to increase delivery 4; hyperbaric physiology 3. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.
rubric: Oxygen delivery equation with units and normal values
Oxygen content, saturation and dissolved oxygen
Ways to increase cardiac output and reduce consumption
Hyperbaric oxygen: dissolved oxygen and numerical values
Indications and risks of hyperbaric therapy

items.title: 2009.2 Q14: A patient has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for over 25 years. 1. What ar
items.q: A patient has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for over 25 years. 1. What are the expected physiological changes that would occur in the first 3 months following cessation of smoking? Include a time frame for the changes you describe. (60%) 2. What are the clinical benefits, with regard to anaesthesia, of smoking cessation in this patient? (40%)
items.model:
## 1. Physiological changes by time frame (60%)

| Time after cessation | Change |
|---|---|
| **12–24 hours** | **Carboxyhaemoglobin falls to normal** (half-life 4–6 hours; was 5–10%), restoring oxygen-carrying capacity; nicotine washes out (half-life about 2 hours), reducing heart rate, blood pressure and **coronary vasoconstriction**; reduced myocardial oxygen demand; improved P50 position of the curve |
| **48–72 hours** | Carbon monoxide fully cleared; airway reactivity begins to fall; improved ciliary function begins |
| **1–2 weeks** | **Sputum production increases transiently** (ciliary recovery, mucus clearance) then settles; reduced laryngeal and bronchial reactivity; improved immune and macrophage function begins; platelet function and viscosity improve |
| **3–4 weeks** | Improved wound healing and tissue oxygenation; decrease in infection risk; polycythaemia/viscosity may improve over time, depending on baseline disease and other causes |
| **6–8 weeks** | analgesic requirements may change variably; smoking-related CYP1A2 induction wanes, affecting drugs such as theophylline or clozapine, rather than being the principal clearance pathway for aminosteroid relaxants; immune function approaches non-smoker levels; airway reactivity and cough reduce |
| **8–12 weeks and by 3 months** | Variable recovery in symptoms and ciliary function; a marked FEV1 increase is not guaranteed, reduced cough and mucus (6–9 months for full effect), further reduction in postoperative pulmonary complications |

## 2. Anaesthetic benefits (40%)

- **Improved oxygen delivery** and tissue oxygenation (lower COHb, lower viscosity).
- **Cardiovascular**: lower perioperative myocardial ischaemia and morbidity, stable haemodynamics.
- **Respiratory**: reduced mucus secretion, airway hyper-reactivity and **laryngospasm/bronchospasm**, less cough, **fewer postoperative chest infections and pulmonary complications** (benefit becomes clear after 4 or more weeks).
- **Wound healing and infection**: fewer wound infections and dehiscence.
- **Pharmacology**: normalised drug metabolism and analgesic requirements.
- **Other**: better lung function and improved long-term outcomes. Note that non-smokers have a slightly higher PONV risk (smoking is protective), so this is accounted for in antiemetic planning.
- **Note**: short-term abstinence of under 4 weeks does not increase respiratory complications as once feared.

> **Examiner's point:** include a time frame for each change, such as COHb, myocardial effects, secretions, reactivity, immune function, and analgesic requirements.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

The historical report listed approximate time-dependent changes; these are not guarantees for every smoker. Avoid promising marked FEV1 recovery by three months, complete immune normalisation, resolution of polycythaemia at a fixed week, or normal analgesic needs at exactly 6–8 weeks. Combustion products induce CYP1A2, principally affecting drugs such as clozapine and theophylline; do not teach CYP1A2 as the principal clearance pathway of aminosteroid relaxants. Transient sputum changes are variable and are not a reason to postpone cessation.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Mark allocation /10, educator-created using the official stem weights:** Timed physiological changes 6; anaesthetic benefits 4. Use the checklist to judge completeness within each part; do not give the parts equal total weight.
rubric: Analgesic and drug metabolism normalise in 6 to 8 weeks

items.title: 2009.1 Q12: Describe management of respiratory distress in PACU after total thyroi
items.q: Describe management of respiratory distress in PACU after total thyroidectomy.
items.model:
Attend immediately, call senior anaesthesia and the thyroid surgeon/ENT, give oxygen, apply monitoring and assess airway, ventilation and circulation. Ask when distress began and review operative/anaesthetic events while looking for rapidly enlarging neck swelling, tightness, dysphagia, altered voice, stridor, tachypnoea, agitation or desaturation. A normal-looking drain does not exclude a compressive haematoma.

In suspected expanding haematoma with airway compromise, do not transfer an unstable patient or wait for imaging. Release dressings and urgently open the wound, including the constricting deeper layer, according to the emergency surgical protocol while preparing airway rescue. Continue oxygenation, positioning and suction. Experienced airway help, video/flexible devices and front-of-neck rescue must be present. The airway may remain oedematous after decompression; plan the safest definitive intubation or surgical airway according to the immediate anatomy and physiology. If the patient is stable without airway compromise, urgent theatre exploration is appropriate with continuous reassessment.

Consider bilateral recurrent-laryngeal nerve dysfunction, airway oedema, laryngospasm, retained secretions, tracheomalacia and pneumothorax following mediastinal dissection. Nasendoscopy/bronchoscopy can clarify a stable airway but must not delay treatment of obstruction. Hypocalcaemic laryngospasm is less likely immediately after surgery but check ionised calcium when appropriate; treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia with monitored IV calcium under protocol.

Also assess residual neuromuscular block, drug depression, bronchospasm/anaphylaxis, aspiration, NPPE, cardiac failure, myocardial ischaemia, pain, metabolic derangement and PE. Quantitative TOF, gas, ECG, chest/neck examination and bedside ultrasound guide management after immediate stabilisation. Treat each confirmed cause, arrange ICU or theatre, plan extubation carefully, document, disclose and debrief.
rubric: **3** — Recognises haematoma and urgent bedside decompression if compromised
**2** — Definitive difficult-airway and surgical rescue plan
**2** — Surgical and general respiratory differential with targeted treatment

items.title: 2008.2 Q15: What symptoms and signs suggest the presence of sleep apnoea in a pati
items.q: What symptoms and signs suggest the presence of sleep apnoea in a patient presenting for pre-operative assessment? How does the presence of sleep apnoea alter your anaesthetic plan?
items.model:
## Symptoms and signs (50%)

**Symptoms**: loud habitual **snoring**, witnessed **apnoeas**, choking or gasping at night, restless sleep, nocturia, morning headache and dry mouth; **daytime somnolence** (Epworth score), poor concentration, irritability, depression, reduced performance, drowsy driving.
**Signs/predisposition**: **obesity** (BMI over 35), **neck circumference** over 40 cm, Mallampati 3–4, retrognathia, macroglossia, enlarged tonsils, craniofacial anomalies (Down syndrome, Pierre Robin), narrow pharynx, hypertension (resistant), AF, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, polycythaemia, and hypothyroidism/acromegaly. **Children**: adenotonsillar hypertrophy, behaviour problems, poor growth.
**Screening**: **STOP-BANG** (snoring, tired, observed apnoea, pressure, BMI, age, neck, gender; 5 or more is high risk); **sleep study** (polysomnography, adult AHI 5–14.9 mild, 15–29.9 moderate and ≥30 severe; paediatric thresholds differ), nocturnal oximetry; ECG and echo if suspected pulmonary hypertension, bicarbonate (≥27 mmol/L can prompt investigation for hypoventilation in the appropriate clinical setting).

## How it alters the plan (50%)

**Preoperative**: confirm diagnosis and severity, optimise comorbidity, ensure **CPAP** (bring the machine), avoid or minimise **sedative premedication**, decide on suitability for day surgery (stable, CPAP compliant, local anaesthetic-based analgesia), and arrange HDU if severe with major surgery.
**Intraoperative**
- **Airway**: anticipate difficult mask ventilation and intubation (ramped position, preoxygenation, video laryngoscope, high-flow nasal oxygen, experienced assistance, difficult airway equipment).
- **Drugs**: short-acting (propofol, remifentanil, sevoflurane/desflurane), reduce long-acting opioids and benzodiazepines (increased sensitivity), **regional or local anaesthesia** when possible, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID, dexamethasone, ketamine, dexmedetomidine, regional block).
- **Reversal**: full neuromuscular reversal (sugammadex) and quantitative monitoring.
**Extubation and recovery**: extubate **awake, semi-upright**, with CPAP available; recover in a monitored area, **oxygen**, continuous SpO2 and capnography.
**Postoperative**: sleep apnoea may worsen on postoperative nights 2–3 (REM rebound after initially suppressed REM), so extend monitoring (HDU, continuous oximetry), restart CPAP early, **minimise opioids**, avoid sedatives, position head-up and lateral, and delay discharge as needed.

> **Examiner's point:** the second section (anaesthetic plan, pre-, intra- and postoperative, REM rebound) was done less well.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

AHI adult cutoffs are 5–14.9 mild, 15–29.9 moderate and ≥30 severe; paediatric thresholds differ. An elevated bicarbonate, commonly ≥27 mmol/L in an appropriate setting, prompts assessment for obesity hypoventilation rather than proving it. Screen for daytime hypercapnia. Bring established PAP therapy, plan opioid-sparing analgesia and a monitored recovery/discharge decision. REM rebound timing varies and should not replace observation of actual obstruction, sedation and desaturation. The mapped paediatric OSA questions are separately labelled shared cases rather than being used to expand this set into the whole ENT curriculum.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Scoring /10:** symptoms/signs 5 and altered perioperative plan 5, as the report explicitly divided these sections evenly.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
