items.title: 2008.1 Q4: Clinical features and treatment of fat embolism syndrome.
items.q: Clinical features and treatment of fat embolism syndrome.
items.model:
Fat embolism is common after long-bone/pelvic injury or intramedullary manipulation, but clinical FES is a distinct inflammatory/microvascular syndrome. Presentation is often delayed 24–72 hours after injury; it is not limited to an intraoperative collapse during reaming. Consider non-traumatic causes such as pancreatitis or fat administration in an appropriate setting.

Clinical features include progressive hypoxaemia/tachypnoea and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates/ARDS, altered cognition, agitation, confusion or coma, and transient petechiae classically over upper chest, axillae or conjunctivae. Fever, tachycardia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia and retinal changes may occur. Findings vary and the classic triad is not always complete. Diagnose from the clinical setting and exclusion of alternatives including thrombotic PE, haemorrhage, aspiration, sepsis and brain injury. CXR/CT can support pulmonary involvement and brain MRI may show a characteristic pattern, but there is no single definitive blood test; diagnostic criteria such as Gurd are aids rather than proof.

Treatment is supportive with early senior/ICU involvement, oxygen and lung-protective ventilation if needed, haemodynamic resuscitation without overload, and treatment of associated trauma. Protect the brain from hypoxaemia/hypotension, monitor other organs, provide VTE prevention when appropriate and coordinate fracture stabilisation/timing with the trauma team. Selected severe refractory respiratory failure may require specialist ECMO consideration. Steroids have uncertain prophylactic/treatment evidence and are not routine established FES therapy. Therapeutic heparin does not remove microvascular fat and is not routine treatment unless another indication exists. Prevention includes appropriate early fracture management and minimising repeated uncontrolled manipulation.
rubric: **6** — Risk context, delayed course, respiratory/neurological/petechial and other features
**4** — Supportive ICU/trauma care, complications and non-routine steroids/heparin

items.title: 2007.2 Q7: A 25 year old, 65kg woman with acute severe asthma requires intubation
items.q: A 25 year old, 65kg woman with acute severe asthma requires intubation and ventilation. Explain the problems associated with initiating ventilatory support in this patient and describe how you would overcome them.
items.model:
## Problems (50%)

- **Patient state**: distressed, exhausted, hypoxaemic and hypercapnic; possibly consent and cooperation issues; **not fasted** (full stomach, swallowed air, gastric distension); remote location (emergency department, ward); ICU team preparedness.
- **Underlying causes**: infection, anaphylaxis, non-adherence, pneumothorax.
- **Treatment effects**: tachycardia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and lactic acidosis from high-dose beta-agonists and steroids; theophylline toxicity.
- **Intubation** can precipitate **severe bronchospasm**, hypotension (loss of sympathetic drive, hypovolaemia, dynamic hyperinflation), arrhythmia, and desaturation (low FRC in airway obstruction).
- **Ventilation**: very high airway pressures, **dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP**, barotrauma (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum), **reduced venous return and hypotension**, impaired CO2 clearance, and cardiac arrest. Choice of drugs (histamine release).

## Overcoming them (50%)

**Preparation**: senior help, resuscitation equipment, experienced operator, a plan for the **full stomach**, preoxygenation (HFNO/NIV), large-bore access, arterial line, and vasopressor ready; **resuscitate before intubation** with bronchodilators (salbutamol, ipratropium, IV magnesium, hydrocortisone, adrenaline), and consider NIV; fluid bolus.
**Induction**: **RSI with ketamine (1–2 mg/kg) or propofol and rocuronium**; attenuate the intubation response (lignocaine, fentanyl); use the **largest tube** (7.5–8 mm) to reduce resistance; confirm tube position, avoid vigorous bagging.
**Ventilator strategy**: **low tidal volume (6–8 mL/kg), low rate (8–10/min), long expiratory time (I:E 1:4 or more)**, low or zero extrinsic PEEP (to match intrinsic PEEP), accept **permissive hypercapnia** (pH above 7.2), pressure limits (plateau pressure under 30), monitor flow–time curves and auto-PEEP; **briefly disconnect and allow passive expiration** for life-threatening trapping; do not routinely compress the chest in a patient with a pulse.
**Haemodynamics**: fluids, vasopressors; treat pneumothorax immediately (needle then drain).
**Ongoing treatment**: continuous nebulised bronchodilators, IV magnesium, steroids, ketamine/sevoflurane infusions, sedation and paralysis as required, correct potassium, treat infection, consider ECMO for refractory cases, and arrange ICU care.

> **Examiner's point:** answer both parts (problems and solutions); those who scored poorly addressed only one.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

Use predicted body weight rather than the supplied actual 65 kg to set tidal volume; height was not provided. Do not routinely add aminophylline or IV beta-agonist; seek specialist rescue advice. Prepare for peri-intubation hypotension, verify expiratory flow returns towards zero, and titrate PEEP rather than claiming zero extrinsic PEEP matches intrinsic PEEP. Briefly disconnect for life-threatening air trapping; forceful chest compression is not routine treatment in a patient with a pulse.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Scoring /10:** problems 5 and how to overcome them 5, matching the examiner report. Do not allocate the whole score to a ventilation prescription without explaining the initiation hazards.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Patient and location problems (distress, full stomach)
Bronchospasm and haemodynamic risks at intubation
Ventilator settings (low rate, long expiration, permissive hypercapnia)
Ongoing asthma therapy and ICU plan

items.title: 2007.1 Q1: What are the principles of ventilatory management of patients with acu
items.source: Past SAQ 2007.1 Q1 · pass rate not available
items.q: What are the principles of ventilatory management of patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?
items.model:
## Definition

ARDS (Berlin): acute (within 1 week), bilateral opacities, not wholly cardiac, **PaO2/FiO2 under 300 with PEEP 5** (mild 200–300, moderate 100–200, severe under 100).

## Priorities

- **1.** **Maintain adequate oxygenation**: target **PaO2 55–80 mmHg or SpO2 88–95%** ("adequate" is not normal), avoiding oxygen toxicity (FiO2 above 0.6 for prolonged periods).
- **2.** **Minimise ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI)**: **volutrauma** (overdistension), **barotrauma** (high pressures), **atelectrauma** (cyclic opening and closing), and **biotrauma** (inflammatory mediator release).

## Strategy

- **Low tidal volume**: 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (range 4–8), **ARDSNet (2000)** showed mortality fell from 40% to 31% versus 12 mL/kg.
- **Plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O** and driving pressure (plateau minus PEEP) below 15, rather than peak pressures.
- **PEEP**: enough to prevent derecruitment and improve oxygenation (high PEEP tables, EPVC); benefit greater in moderate to severe ARDS (ALVEOLI, LOVS and EXPRESS showed no mortality difference overall); excessive PEEP overdistends and reduces cardiac output.
- **Permissive hypercapnia** (pH above 7.20–7.25) accepted to allow low volumes.
- **Recruitment manoeuvres**: may transiently improve oxygenation; ART trial found harm with aggressive manoeuvres.
- **I:E ratio** adjustment (prolonged inspiration, inverse ratio) in selected cases, watching auto-PEEP.
- **Rescue and adjuncts**: **prone positioning** for PaO2/FiO2 under 150 for 16 hours per day (**PROSEVA** mortality benefit), **neuromuscular blockade** early in severe ARDS (ACURASYS; ROSE negative), **inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin** (improve oxygenation, no mortality benefit), **ECMO** in severe refractory ARDS (CESAR, EOLIA), high-frequency oscillation (OSCILLATE showed harm), and conservative fluids (FACTT).
- **Haemodynamic stability** with RV protection (avoid high plateau pressures and hypercapnic acidosis).
- **Weaning**: daily spontaneous breathing trials as oxygenation improves, with early mobilisation.

> **Examiner's point:** short accurate definition, prioritise oxygenation and VILI prevention, explain barotrauma, volutrauma, atelectrauma, and biotrauma, and cite evidence (ARDSNet). Nutrition, steroids and antibiotics were not relevant.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

For the historical stem, retain a short accurate Berlin description; distinguish it from the newer global definition in Retrieve. Current ATS guidance favours selected higher PEEP without prolonged recruitment in moderate/severe ARDS; prolonged recruitment is harmful. Driving pressure is a useful physiological signal, not a universal RCT-proven standalone threshold. Prone sessions should generally last at least 16 hours when indicated. Steroids are now conditionally supported for ARDS overall, but discussion of non-ventilatory treatment must not displace the ventilatory focus of the 2007.1 question.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Historical marking distinction:** the 2007.1 report did provide a detailed scheme (oxygenation and VILI prevention were prioritised), although it did not give a question-specific pass rate. The study checklist remains an educator adaptation and does not replace that report.

## Audit additions and clinical qualifications

**Berlin boundaries:** mild 200 < P/F ≤300, moderate 100 < P/F ≤200, severe P/F ≤100 mmHg, with the specified PEEP/support and other criteria. Do not double-count the boundary values between groups.

**Scoring:** This is an educator-created checklist, not an official ANZCA mark scheme. Award equal credit across the checklist items for a total of 10, while respecting the original percentage allocation between stem parts. Major unsafe management is recorded separately and requires correction even when the numerical total is satisfactory.
rubric: Prioritises oxygenation and prevention of VILI
Prone, paralysis, nitric oxide, ECMO, and weaning
